An effect that edits the `direct+ambient(s)` text itself reaches the base's light alone. | The coat's light adds after the sum, unscaled by the share it leaves the layers under it. | Such an effect leaves a coat highlight in its shadow. `Shadows`, `Clustered` and the other effects in this repository use `pbr`. | Return `direct` from `pbr(group)`. |
| Native glass tint draw | Enforced by method ([shader.ts](../packages/gltf-pro/src/shader.ts)): a loaded transmissive material draws twice, a multiply of the light behind and the lit surface, and both sample the material's maps. Cost measured (quiet-gated, RTX A6000, 1920 × 1080 4x, screen-filling glass, [tint-pass-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/tint-pass-gpu.json)): four maps, one layer 0.52 ms a frame against 0.33 ms with no tint draw and 0.39 ms with the older factors-only draw; 16 layers 4.46, 2.56 and 3.47 ms; eight maps, 16 layers 6.88, 3.41 and 4.65 ms. | Base colour, transmission, metal, sheen and clearcoat maps change how much light passes through, so the multiply has to read them. | The tint draw takes 17 to 57 percent of the GPU time of these glass-only frames at 1920 × 1080, 0.03 to 0.2 ms per million glass pixels. Glass with no maps pays as well: 3.41 ms against 2.69 ms for the factors-only draw at 16 layers, because the surface read also covers metal and thin film. | The `Transmission` pass from `@margoengine/materials`. |
| Native glass on a display-encoded target | Open defect ([known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md#native-glass-on-a-display-encoded-target-adds-its-lit-draw-in-encoded-values)): with no HDR scene target, the lit draw of native glass adds to the light behind in encoded values (0.5 + 0.5 reads 1.0, linear light reads 0.69). | `Tonemap`, any PostStack or `install(model)` give the exact sum; the native path has no way to decode the target without a scene copy or a core change. |
| Materials surfaces outside the colour pass | Enforced ([cutout-passes-browser.mjs](../packages/materials/test/cutout-passes-browser.mjs), [cutout-casters-browser.mjs](../packages/shadows/test/cutout-casters-browser.mjs)): shadow maps, contact shadows, TAA velocity and picking follow `map` alpha, `alphaMap`, UV transforms, `alphaTest`, `vertexColors: false`, `displacementMap` and `clippingPlanes`. Three limits: `triplanar` keeps its whole surface in those passes; a `static` `ContactShadows` redraws every frame while it has an `alphaMap`, displaced or clipped caster, which change on the GPU alone; and TAA gives a displacement that changes between frames no velocity of its own. |
| Projected decals | Enforced ([decals.ts](../packages/post/src/decals.ts)): 4,096 decals per `setDecals`, all drawn every frame (no culling); colour only. Cost measured (diagnostic: other jobs running; [decals-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/decals-gpu.json)): 1280 × 720 4x, 1.64 ms without, 1.64 / 1.97 / 6.36 ms with 1 / 16 / 256 one-metre decals. | Screen-space decals need no change to any material shader: one pass reads the scene depth a post capture already provides. | `Decals need scene depth: attach a post capture (Tonemap, Bloom, PostStack, SSAO, TAA) first`; at 4x MSAA decal edges along silhouettes are per pixel; gltf-pro BLEND primitives are tinted with the surface behind them; `multiply` cannot lighten and nothing changes normals or roughness. | `@margoengine/post/decals` (4,118 B gzip) is itself the opt-in; `mode: 'over'` for light-on-dark marks. Normal and roughness decals: none yet. |
| VFX repeatable particle order (accepted difference in work, Scott 2026-10-30) | Measured (RTX A6000, Edge 156, 2026-10-30, 8 alternating rounds of `examples/package-benchmarks/vfx-gpu.mjs` against the atomic build): simulate compute 0.094 to 0.184 ms at 1,000,000 particles and 0.010 to 0.031 ms at 100,000; draw unchanged. On the WebGL2 layer's CPU tier, simulate wall time 290 to 58 ms at 20,000 and 370 to 250 ms at 100,000 (the package-route row under Platform was measured before this change). | Births take the lowest dead slots and the draw list is in slot order, instead of atomic counters whose order changed from run to run (two runs of one still frame differed on up to 5,965 of 65,536 pixels). The extra work is four small compute passes (workgroup prefix sums) around the simulation; the output is the same particles in a repeatable order. | The same frames draw the same pixels on every run (`packages/vfx/test/browser-check.mjs`, order case). Size: `@margoengine/vfx/base` 7,339 to 7,978 B gzip, the root 12,376 to 12,999 B; the growth of their limits in `scripts/quality/baselines/sizes.json` was approved by Scott on 2026-10-30. | None needed below about 1,000,000 particles; fewer particles (`capacity`) cost proportionally less. |
| Scatter cull in candidate order (accepted difference in work, 2026-11-05) | Measured (8 alternating rounds of [scatter-cull-gpu.mjs](../examples/package-benchmarks/scatter-cull-gpu.mjs) against the atomic build, 1432 x 768 at 4x MSAA, [A6000 result](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/scatter-cull-gpu-a6000.json), [M6 result](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/scatter-cull-gpu-m6.json)): the distribute pass at 10,000 / 110,000 / 1,000,000 candidates takes 0.012 / 0.044 / 0.049 ms atomic and 0.046 / 0.091 / 0.222 ms ordered on the RTX A6000 (Edge 156, D3D12), 0.011 / 0.111 / 0.485 ms and 0.043 / 0.231 / 1.050 ms on an Apple M6 Mac mini (Chrome for Testing 156, Metal); the LOD draw is unchanged (ratio 0.94 to 1.03). | The atomic cull put each frame's instances in the rings in whichever order the GPU's threads ran, and an Apple M6 at 4x MSAA draws an instance's edge pixels by that order: a still biome view changed about 420 of 76,800 pixels every frame. The extra work: each candidate stores its ring flags (and, when kept, its instance) at its own index, a prefix count over the three rings (`packages/shared/prefix.js`, the WebGL2 route's) gives each its slot, and each ring is compacted (`packages/scatter/src/order.ts`). The output is the same instances in every ring (the benchmark compares them), in candidate order every frame. | Still frames draw the same bits at 4x MSAA (`packages/scatter/test/repeat.browser.mjs`: exact on the A6000 and the M6). GPU memory: about 58 B more per candidate (`ScatterTiles`: per record slot; `gpuBytes` counts it), 32 B of it the culled instance: the zero-config biome world's stored objects went from 5.9 to 12.0 MB; `ScatterTiles` holds at most `maxStorageBufferBindingSize / 32` record slots (4,194,304 at the WebGPU default of 128 MiB, 16,777,216 before). Shadow lists keep their atomic append: a depth-only pass gives the same depth in any order. | Fewer candidates (`count`) cost proportionally less; a candidate past every ring costs its flags and its share of the prefix count only. |
| TAA `velocityOnly` (`@margoengine/taa`) | Enforced by check: construction refuses it without `depth`, and a 4x MSAA frame with no PostStack throws `state`. | With no capture of its own it reads the depth and scene target another plugin made. | No anti-aliasing and no `resolved` frame; `gpuState` throws, as there is no history. | Plain `TAA` for anti-aliasing with its vectors. |
| Raw mesh shared buffers (`@margoengine/shader/raw`) | Enforced by method: meshes share a buffer only when every packed byte is equal, compared on upload. | Comparing needs the bytes, so each shared buffer keeps a CPU copy of them until its meshes have left it. | One more CPU copy per distinct stream, and a first write to a shared buffer makes that mesh a new GPU buffer. | Build meshes from different data, or write to them, and they hold their own buffers. |
| SciFiHelmet with default shadows (accepted difference in work, 2026-11-05) | Measured (`helmet`, RTX A6000, Edge 156, 5 runs, `--no-gate`, other jobs running, diagnostic): 0.33 ms GPU a frame against three's WebGL 0.08 and WebGPU 0.07 (0.78 when first measured). Like for like (`helmet-filterpcf-cascades1`, `'pcf'` and one cascade, the setup closest to three's one map): 0.074 ms against 0.085 and 0.068. CPU 0.12 ms against WebGL 0.09 and WebGPU 0.19. | three's side draws one map with one fixed filter. Margo's default draws four cascades and PCSS, so a penumbra widens with the distance to its blocker. Of the 0.33 ms, about 0.12 is the frame with `'pcf'` and four cascades, 0.10 is the pass that finds each layer's nearest depth (it reads all 64 MiB of the four 2048 maps, so memory bandwidth sets its time), and 0.10 is the blocker reads and comparison taps. | Contact-hardening shadows and sharper texels near the camera by default, for about 0.25 ms on this scene. A cheaper filter would change the image, so the default stays. The nearest-depth pass could read only the part of each layer that casters reach and give the same result, but casters carry no bounds yet. | `filter: 'pcf'` and `cascades` on `Shadows`; `@margoengine/quality` sets them on its light and phone tiers. |
| Precise maths against the WGSL builtins (accepted difference in work, 2026-11-05) | Measured ([precise-math-gpu.mjs](../examples/package-benchmarks/precise-math-gpu.mjs), RTX A6000, [result](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/precise-math-gpu.json)): on 16,777,216 values `createCompute()` takes 1.0 to 1.8 times `createCompute({ fastMath: true })` for one call per element, `tan` 2.3 times and `pow` 3.0 times (2.19 against 0.72 ms). The path tracer's panorama and fisheye rays cost 1% to 7% of a traced sample. What Margo does extra: the same answer on every GPU within the bounds in the compute README. Trade-off: `fastMath` is faster and as accurate as the GPU happens to be; the tracer has no such option. |
| Subgroup kernels (`@margoengine/compute/subgroups`, 2026-11-05) | Measured ([compute-subgroups.mjs](../examples/package-benchmarks/compute-subgroups.mjs), RTX A6000, subgroup size 32, 16,777,216 f32 values, busy machine, diagnostic, [result](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/compute-subgroups.json)): sort 11.9 to 7.0 ms (1.7 times), argsort 13.6 to 8.8 ms (1.5 times), sum 0.087 to 0.066 ms (1.3 times), sum along an axis 0.59 ms both, cumsum 0.55 to 0.56 ms (no gain). Correct at subgroup sizes 32 and 4; other sizes not run. | WGSL promises no subgroup size or layout, so each subgroup takes a seat with one atomic, and float sums follow the subgroup size. Sums and scans are limited by memory bandwidth here, so removing barriers saves little. | Float sums differ from the default kernels by rounding and from GPU to GPU; integers, orders and sorts are identical. `f16` arrays, `argmin`, `argmax`, segmented and per-axis scans run the default kernels. | Leave it off where float sums must match across GPUs; `useSubgroups` is a choice per context. |
| Neural networks (`@margoengine/compute/nn`, 2026-11-05) | Enforced by method: f32 only. Convolution and pooling hold their unfolded input, n x output positions x channels x kernel area floats, plus tables of the same shape for one sample, made once per input size and kept until the layer is disposed. Attention holds its [..., t, s] scores. Speed is not measured. | Convolution is a gather and a matrix product, and backward is the gather through the inverse table, so it uses no atomics and runs on every backend, the CPU included, at the price of memory. | A large image or a long sequence runs out of GPU memory before it runs out of time (`failed` on the next wait). `Embedding` gradients add atomically, so their rounding may vary on a GPU. Not included: grouped and transposed convolution, batch normalization, recurrent layers, f16, and GELU's erf form (the tanh form differs by under 0.001). | Split the batch; use a stride or pooling early. |
| Graph algorithms (`@margoengine/compute/graph`, 2026-11-05) | Enforced by method: vertices below 2^30; distances in `shortestPaths` are f32 sums, exact up to 2^24 for whole weights. `bfs` and `shortestPaths` take up to one round per edge of the longest shortest path (`shortestPaths` at most the vertex count, plus one to tell a negative cycle apart), and `connectedComponents` takes about log(vertices) rounds on the graphs tested (2,000-vertex shuffled path: under 64). Speed is not measured. | Each round runs over every edge at once with an atomic minimum, so a graph needs no frontier queue, the code is the same on the GPU and the CPU backend, and negative weights work. | A round visits every edge whether or not its source changed, so a long thin graph costs edges x its depth: a frontier-based search would do less work there. With f32 sums, cycles of total weight 0 that round below it can read as negative; zero-weight cycles can loop `predecessors`. `graph()` builds on the CPU and uses memory for every edge twice over. Not included: strongly connected components, minimum spanning trees, centrality. | Use whole or dyadic weights for exact sums; raise `checkEvery` on deep graphs to read back less often. |
| Workgroup autotuning (`@margoengine/compute/autotune`, 2026-11-05) | Default: 6 candidate sizes, 2 warm-up and 7 timed runs each, so 54 runs of your kernel on the first call and none on later ones. Results last for the context, or across sessions with `store`. | Measuring beats a fixed rule because the best size depends on the GPU and the kernel; timed runs take turns so drift is shared, and the median drops spikes. | The first call pays for those runs and for compiling every candidate. A result holds for the input size measured: name it in `signature`. Browsers round GPU timestamps (steps of 0.066 ms in the Chrome tested), so sizes of a short kernel can tie. Browsers without `device.adapterInfo` (and browsers that hide adapter details) let different GPUs of a store share an entry, which costs speed, never correctness. Driver updates are not seen: use `refresh`. The package's own kernels keep their fixed sizes. | Tune once at start-up, or ship a `store`. |
| Render passes of a package's frame | One colour pass when only packages that `join` draw (`createInstancedMesh`, `CulledInstances`, runs of glTF models): 0.024 ms at 1,000 boxes against 0.039 before (RTX A6000, 2026-11-05, perf-history entry 51). A core mesh in the same scene keeps core's clear pass; a pass after the package keeps core's resolve pass; a glTF model alone in its segment takes core's clear but keeps core's resolve pass, which measured no slower than resolving in the package's pass. |
| Depth-writing lines (`depthWrite` on `LineMaterial`, `@margoengine/lines`) | By method: two draws per line (solid part, then edge ramp) unless `antialias` is false; depth is written where a line is at least half covered, so a crossing line shows through the outer half of the ramp. Depth follows the centre line, not the round profile of a thick line. | Keeping the smooth edge needs the ramp to blend after every solid part. One draw would either cut the ramp or write depth through it. | Twice the vertex work for these lines; a translucent depth-writing line hides what is drawn behind it after it. | Leave `depthWrite` off where lines do not cross, or set `antialias: false` for one draw. |
| GPU picking of lines (`LinePicking` in `@margoengine/lines/pick`) | Enforced: 268,435,456 segments per pick, 8 overlays per `Picking`. By method: a pick answers the nearest thing only; `engine.pick` can only answer meshes, so a line that follows no mesh answers an empty stand-in mesh (`lineOf` maps it back); with an overlay registered every pick draws the 3 x 3 pass with all line vertices, uncropped. | Core is frozen, so `engine.pick` keeps its mesh return type; lines share the pass and depth test of meshes. | Picks cost more with many segments; Picking's cached ID texture goes unused. | Read `hit.line` from `picking.pick`; use `intersectLines` from `@margoengine/bvh/lines` for a sorted list of ray hits. |
| Trails (`Trail` in `@margoengine/lines/trail`) | Enforced: 2 to 65,536 points (`maxPoints`, default 256); past that the oldest point goes and the far end jumps. By method: a trail is a line, so it faces the camera and cannot lie flat on the ground; a dashed trail ignores `tailWidth`, because dash distances use the value widths are stored in. | One line keeps joins, antialiasing, fog, clipping and picking for free. | A tyre track seen from low down looks like a tube, not a flat strip. | Raise `maxPoints`; build a flat strip as a mesh with `@margoengine/splines/mesh`. |
| Massive line batches (`LineBatch` in `@margoengine/lines/batch`) | Enforced: 67,108,864 segments a batch; one draw per 8,388,608 segments at the default 256 MiB `maxBufferSize`. By method: independent segments with square ends: no joins, round caps, dashes, fog, clipping planes, depth writing or picking; colours at 8 bits a channel; a CPU copy of 32 bytes a segment stays for device loss. | Six vertices and 32 bytes a segment, where `Line` draws 78 vertices and reads a storage buffer whose binding size limits it. | Translucent corners are darker where segments overlap; memory is 64 bytes a segment across CPU and GPU. | Use `Line` where those features matter. |
| Hidden lines (`HiddenLine` in `@margoengine/lines/hidden`, `behind` and `depthBias` on `LineMaterial`) | By method: the test is against scene depth, so surfaces that write no depth hide nothing; `depthBias` (default 0.001 of the distance) decides what counts as on a surface, so an edge closer behind a surface than that shows as seen. Dashes run in world units. Hidden lines do not pick. | A depth test is one draw with no mesh analysis, on any scene; exact CAD hidden-line removal would need the geometry on the CPU. | A very thin wall can show an edge behind it as seen. | Lower `depthBias`, or raise it if a far model flickers. |
| Alpha to coverage on lines (`alphaToCoverage` on `LineMaterial`) | By method: works with MSAA only and falls back to blending without it; opacity comes in steps of one sample, four at 4x MSAA; lines of equal opacity use the same samples, so the later replaces the earlier at a crossing. | MSAA hardware turns alpha into a sample mask, which is what makes it independent of draw order. | Fine opacity changes band at low sample counts. | Leave it off and blend, or raise the sample count. |
| Filled helpers (`solidHead` on `ArrowHelper`, `fillOpacity` on `PlaneHelper`) | By method: a fill is flat colour with no lighting and does not pick. An opaque fill writes depth; translucent fills blend in the order added. | Helpers are guides, so they stay readable in any light and need no material or mesh. | A solid head has no shading, so its shape reads from its outline. | Use a mesh from `@margoengine/core` where lighting matters. |


| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| glTF download budget | Enforced: gltf-pro reads at most `maxDownloadBytes` (default 64 MiB, 67,108,864 B: `assetLimit`) of JSON, buffers and images per load, and decoded accessors, packed geometry and decoded images may each use 4x that (256 MiB by default); `@margoengine/gltf` reads at most 64 MiB ([asset.ts](../packages/gltf-pro/src/asset.ts), [loading.js](../packages/shared/loading.js); [accessors.test.js](../packages/gltf-pro/tests/accessors.test.js)). Khronos ABeautifulGame (a 43 MB GLB whose 33 2048x2048 textures decode to 528 MiB) is over the default image budget. | Bounds memory for any URL an app is handed. | gltf-pro names the option for the download and packed-geometry budgets, e.g. `RangeError: glTF exceeds download budget (67108864 bytes; raise the maxDownloadBytes option)`; decoded accessors and images over 4x throw `RangeError: Decoded glTF exceeds byte budget` or `RangeError: glTF images exceed decoded size limit`; the light loader throws `glTF download byte budget exceeded` or `glTF buffers exceed 64 MiB`. | gltf-pro's `maxDownloadBytes` option (ABeautifulGame loads with 160 MiB, [khronos-gallery.js](../examples/khronos-gallery.js)); for the light loader, use gltf-pro. |
| Malformed and hostile files | Enforced at each parser's trust boundary (glTF, gltf-pro with its parse worker and progressive stream, `.margo`, Draco, KTX2, meshopt, HDR, EXR, UltraHDR, FBX), checked by seeded fuzzers (`npm run fuzz`, [targets-formats.js](../scripts/fuzz/targets-formats.js); regressions in [fuzz-formats-regressions.test.js](../tests/fuzz-formats-regressions.test.js)): every input ends in a result or the package's own error. Limits added with them: a gltf-pro document nested deeper than 256 levels ([asset.ts](../packages/gltf-pro/src/asset.ts)); an EXR chunk that decodes to more than 256 MiB, or chunks too small to hold the image ([exr.ts](../packages/environment/src/exr.ts)); a Draco or KTX2 decode running longer than 10 s plus 4 s per MiB of input ([pool.ts](../packages/decoders/src/pool.ts)). How long large valid Draco and KTX2 files take to decode: not measured. | Files from a URL are untrusted: a malformed one must fail with an error the app can show, not crash, hang, read outside its bytes or claim memory its size cannot justify. | `TypeError: Invalid glTF JSON: nested deeper than 256 levels`, `RangeError: Unsupported EXR: a chunk decodes to more than 256 MiB`, `RangeError: Invalid EXR: chunks are too small for the image size`, `MargoError: Draco decode timed out after <limit> ms (corrupt data?); the decoder worker was restarted`. | The decoders' `timeout` option (`Infinity` turns the limit off). No real glTF comes near 256 levels; EXR: fewer channels per file. |
| Vertices per primitive | Enforced: gltf-pro takes up to 1,000,000 vertices per primitive (index accessors are bounded only by the decoded budget); the light `@margoengine/gltf` loader up to 1,000,000 vertices in total ([accessors.test.js](../packages/gltf-pro/tests/accessors.test.js): 1,000,002 indices decode, 1,000,002 vertices are refused). | Vertex buffers are also bound as storage buffers, and indices pass through float32, exact up to 2^24. | gltf-pro names the location: `glTF mesh 0 "part" primitive 0: Expected bounded triangle geometry`; the light loader: `RangeError: glTF exceeds one million vertices`. | gltf-pro instead of the light loader lifts the total; a primitive over 1,000,000 vertices must be split at export (for CAD, a coarser `margo-convert --linear-deflection`). |

## Geometry

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NURBS surfaces (`@margoengine/geometry/nurbs`) | Enforced by method: no trimming curves, knot insertion or degree elevation; `NurbsCurve.tessellate` halves a span at most 12 times. | Trimming needs a boundary representation, which this engine does not carry; revolves, control nets and whole patches do not. | A trimmed patch meshes untrimmed. | Cut the mesh with `@margoengine/mesh-edit`. |
| Mesh surface sampler (`@margoengine/geometry/sample`) | Enforced by method: points are independent random draws, so they can clump; there is no minimum spacing. Vertex weights are linear across each triangle. | Independent draws cost one search each and need no neighbour lookups. | Two points can land close together. | `@margoengine/scatter` for spaced placement on terrain. |
| Mesh optimisation (`@margoengine/geometry/optimize`) | Enforced by test ([optimize.test.js](../packages/geometry/tests/optimize.test.js)): shuffled grids, spheres and knots end under 0.8 cache misses per triangle on a 16-vertex first-in first-out cache (3 before); nested shells lose over 40 percent of their overdraw while the miss ratio stays within 6 percent. Frame time on a GPU: not measured. | The cache model is a simulation; real GPUs differ in cache size and batching. | Triangle order changes, so a transparent mesh that relied on it can look different. | `overdraw: false` keeps the sort off; leave the mesh out to keep its order. |
| Bending along a curve (`@margoengine/geometry/flow`) | Enforced by method: frames are sampled `segments` times (default 256) and interpolated, and only vertices move. A shape wider than the radius of a bend folds over itself. | Sampling once makes each vertex a table lookup. | A coarse mesh cuts corners; a tight bend pinches the inner side. | Add segments along the axis; raise `segments`. |
| Extrusion UVs (`uvGenerator` of `@margoengine/geometry/extrude`) | Enforced by method: the generator runs once per triangle corner on the CPU, and wall `u` comes from the outline before the bevel widens it. | Walls and caps are separate triangles, so a corner can differ per surface. | A texture on a wide bevel stretches a little across `u`. | Use `distance` and your own `u` from `shape`. |
| Split tangents (`splitTangents`, `computeTangents` with `split`) | Enforced by method: checked against Blender's MikkTSpace on two meshes, to a dot product above 0.9995 per corner with matching signs. It follows the published grouping and is not a port of the reference library, so a mesh with unusual degenerate triangles may group differently. `w` assumes v up. | Clean room: written from the paper. | A rare corner could differ from a bake on degenerate geometry. | Remove zero-area triangles first; flip v on glTF UVs. |
| Baked poses (`bakeMorphTargets`, `bakeSkin`) | Enforced by method: four joints per vertex, linear blend skinning, Float32 output. | One pose on the CPU for picking, physics or export; the same mix glTF defines. | Linear blending collapses at sharp twists, as it does on the GPU. | Bake several poses, or split the joint. |
| Delaunay triangulation (`@margoengine/geometry/delaunay`) | Enforced by method: adds no points of its own, so thin outlines keep thin triangles; crossing constraints and self-crossing rings are refused. Exact tests fall back to whole-number arithmetic, which is slower on grids and other exactly cocircular input. | Keeping the input points is what stops T-junctions; refinement would add vertices. | Cocircular input costs more time. | Add inner points with `points`; split crossing edges. |
| Colour conversion (`@margoengine/math/color-space`) | Enforced: four named spaces (`srgb`, `srgb-linear`, `display-p3`, `display-p3-linear`), D65 white only; any other name throws `TypeError`. Results are not clamped. | Those are the spaces WebGPU canvases and CSS `color()` share, and unclamped values convert back unchanged. | A colour outside the target space has channels below 0 or above 1. Below 0 the transfer curve runs on as its straight segment, not mirrored. | Call `clipToSRGB` on linear sRGB to bring a colour inside sRGB. |
| Oriented boxes (`@margoengine/math/obb`) | Enforced: non-finite values, a negative half size, a matrix that is not a rotation and a negative or non-finite `epsilon` throw. `applyMatrix4` throws `RangeError` for a projective matrix, a zero scale axis or a scale that would shear the box. `intersectsOBB` pads the axis cosines by `epsilon`, 1e-6 by default. | A sheared box is no longer a box. Near-parallel edges have a cross product close to zero, and the pad stops them reporting a false separation. | Two boxes closer than about `epsilon` times their size can report an overlap; a real overlap is never missed. | Pass 0 as `epsilon` for an exact test on boxes with no near-parallel edges, or bound a sheared object with `Box3`. |
| Segments and triangles (`@margoengine/math/line3`, `/triangle`) | Enforced by method: two directions count as parallel, and a triangle as degenerate, when the sine squared of their angle is below 1e-14 (float64 rounding). `Triangle.containsPoint` tests the point's projection on the plane, not its height above it. | Below that angle the closed forms lose all their digits, so the parallel and collapsed cases take their own paths. | A sliver thinner than about 1e-7 radians gets null barycentric weights. | Use `closestPointToPoint`, which still answers for a degenerate triangle; check `distanceToPoint` when height off the plane matters. |
| Polygon booleans and offsets (`@margoengine/geometry/polygon`) | Enforced by method: all points go onto one grid of about 2^26 steps across the input. A vertex at a crossing moves up to half a step, edges closer than a step touch, and parts under two steps wide are dropped. | One exact grid is what makes every test safe: no epsilon to tune, and no failed or crossing output at any scale. | Two features 1e-8 of the input's width apart merge. Very large plans with very fine detail lose the detail. | Run distant parts separately, or scale up the part that needs the detail. |
| Project and unproject (`@margoengine/math/project`) | Enforced by method: core's `camera.matrix` is Float32 and holds zeros until the first frame; a point at or behind the camera plane returns null; a matrix with no inverse throws `RangeError`. | One matrix serves every camera, orthographic included; null keeps a point behind the camera from showing up mirrored on screen. | Results carry float32 precision, not float64, and depth z follows the camera (WebGPU near = 1, far = 0; WebGL near = -1, far = 1). | Pass your own `{matrix}` as a Float64Array for float64 results. Take depth from `projectPoint` instead of hard-coding it. |
| Spherical harmonics (`@margoengine/math/sh`) | Enforced by method: three bands, 9 RGB coefficients, CPU only. No rotation of a coefficient set. | Three bands hold diffuse light to within a few percent, and match the layout `@margoengine/environment` reads. | A single point of light overshoots: a distant light reads 17/16 of its irradiance facing it and 1/16 facing away, where the truth is 1 and 0. Results are not clamped. | For sharp light use a real light and keep SH for the soft part. To turn a probe, project it again from rotated samples. |
| Sweep and loft (`@margoengine/geometry/sweep`) | Enforced by method: sections stay flat and are matched by their share of the way round, with no point-to-point control. A loft has no holes in its sections. | One rule fits any pair of outlines and keeps every corner. | A twisted quad is two flat triangles, so a twisted solid loses volume in proportion to the step (0.4 percent at 128 steps for a quarter turn). A sharp bend in a path pinches the profile. | Raise `steps`, round the path, or pass 3D rings with matching points and `align: false`. |
| Capsules (`@margoengine/math/capsule`) | Enforced: a negative or non-finite radius and any matrix beyond rotation, translation and uniform scale throw `RangeError`. `pushOutOfTriangle` resolves one triangle at a time, and returns null for an axis lying in a degenerate triangle. | Under other matrices the shape stops being a capsule. One triangle at a time keeps the type a shape, not a physics solver. | Several triangles at once (a corner) need repeated passes in the caller, and a push out of one triangle can move into the next. | For a full character controller with sliding and stepping use `@margoengine/physics`. |
| Tessellation (`@margoengine/geometry/tessellate`) | Enforced by method: `maxTriangles`, 5,000,000 by default, stops a tiny limit. Edges are measured in the mesh's own units, not on screen. | Plain edge length needs no camera and keeps neighbours in agreement. | Long thin triangles add many vertices along their length. Flat areas are split as finely as curved ones. | Pick the limit for the deformation, or tessellate only the part that bends. |
| GPU geometry (`@margoengine/geometry/gpu`) | Enforced by method: WebGPU only, `attach` throws `unsupported` on WebGL2; 1,000,000 vertices per item, as core. Tube and ribbon frames are walked by one GPU invocation, so that step grows with `segments`. Speed is not measured. | Each frame depends on the one before it. | CPU raycasts and exports see zeros until `read()`. Control points written by your own compute pass are lost with the device. Default bounds are never culled. | Pass `bounds`; keep `segments` to what the curve needs; call `setPoints` again after a restore if you drive points on the GPU. |
| Exact booleans (`@margoengine/mesh-edit/boolean-exact`) | Enforced by method: every side test and all topology are exact, then corners round to float64. Faces thinner than about 4e-9 of their length, or a few float64 steps, fold away; `collapsedFaces` counts them. Inputs must not intersect themselves. Measured 0.8 s for one operation on 1,728 faces and 40 to 75 s on 10,368 (work grows with faces squared). | `PolygonMesh` stores float64 corners and every face must pass the validity check, so a true result thinner than that has no valid float64 face. | A closed valid mesh that can differ from the exact solid by about 4e-9 of a face length; `MargoError` `failed` for a self-intersecting input. | `booleanMeshes` in `/modeling` is faster on clean inputs; scale thin features up, or split large meshes. |
| Modifier stack (`@margoengine/mesh-edit/modifiers`) | Enforced: array `count` 1 to 4096, screw `steps` up to 4096, lattice 2 to 16 controls per axis. Not checked: walls thicker than a concave radius fold over themselves, and a screw profile is a surface because `PolygonMesh` has no loose edges. | The stack stays pure CPU work on valid polygon meshes; those limits bound one evaluate. | `RangeError` or `TypeError` from `evaluate`; a folded wall has faces that cross, with no error. | Thin the wall, or run `booleanMeshesExact` on the parts. |
| Smoothing (`smoothMesh` in `@margoengine/mesh-edit/modeling`) | Enforced: 1 to 10,000 passes. By method: neighbors weigh equally, so uneven triangles drift along the surface. | Equal weights need no angle data and are what Taubin's method describes; cotangent weights fail on the thin triangles scans have. | Volume stays within 2% on a noisy sphere over 20 passes; very uneven meshes change shape slightly along the surface. | Run `remeshMesh` first. |
| Remeshing (`@margoengine/mesh-edit/remesh`) | Enforced: voxel grids stop at `maxCells`, 16,777,216 by default, and need a closed input. By method: isotropic output is triangles, a warped voxel quad is stored as two triangles (`quads` keeps the topology), parity counts an overlap of two parts as outside, and UVs do not carry through voxels. | Faces must be planar, and a grid has no link back to corner UVs. | `RangeError` above `maxCells`; `TypeError` for open input; `nonManifoldEdges` above 0 where two sheets pass within a voxel. | Raise `voxelSize` or `maxCells`; `fillMeshHoles` closes input; `booleanMeshesExact` unions overlapping parts first. |
| Sculpting (`@margoengine/mesh-edit/sculpt`) | Enforced: `undoLimit` 0 to 1,000. By method: each `pick` tests every triangle and each `dab` visits every vertex; each undo step stores the whole surface; output is triangles. | Dynamic topology rewrites adjacency, so plain arrays stay simpler and correct where an acceleration tree would need updating on every dab. | Dabs slow down in proportion to mesh size; memory grows with size times `undoLimit`. | Lower `undoLimit`, or sculpt parts of a mesh in separate sessions. |
| Hole filling (`fillMeshHoles` in `@margoengine/mesh-edit/modeling`) | By method: holes above 256 edges start from a center fan, not the lowest-cost search; a grid needs an even edge count and warped grid quads are stored as two triangles; new faces get planar UVs of their own. | The search costs edges cubed, and faces must be planar. | A long border fills from its center; an odd one in grid mode gets triangles. | `maxEdges` leaves large holes open for manual work. |
| High-to-low baking (`@margoengine/mesh-edit/bake`) | By method: one ray per texel at the texel center, no supersampling; overlapping UVs share texels, first triangle wins; colour reads the nearest texel; the bake runs on the calling thread. | Antialiasing would multiply ray cost, and a bake is an offline step. | Hard detail edges alias at low resolutions; `missed` counts texels whose ray found nothing. | Bake at twice the size and downscale; raise `distance` when `missed` is above zero. |
| Vertex groups (`@margoengine/mesh-edit/weights`) | By method: a brush reaches by straight-line distance, not along the surface; `skinAttributes` keeps at most 8 joints per vertex and drops the weakest; `remap` needs every edit in order. | Straight-line distance needs no surface walk per dab, and 4 influences is what glTF skinning takes. | A brush can touch both sides of a thin part; a vertex with more groups than influences loses the weakest. | Paint with a smaller radius; raise `influences` up to 8. |
| Closest point and frames (`closestPointOnSpline` in `@margoengine/splines/closest`, `SplineFrames` in `@margoengine/splines/frames`) | By method: the search samples the curve (`samples`, default the spline's `divisions`) and refines the best sample only, so passes closer together than one sample can be confused; frames are stored at `samples` steps (default 256) and blended between them; the tangent is a finite difference. | Sampling plus bisection keeps a query at `samples` curve evaluations with no per-curve setup. | A tight spiral can return a nearby pass instead of the nearest; frames drift from true rotation-minimising by less than the step size. | Raise `samples`. |
| Knot paths (`KnotPath` in `@margoengine/splines/knots`) | Enforced: 2 to 1,000,000 knots (3 minimum when closed); every knot carries the same number of data values. By method: a closed path builds an open Bezier whose last point is its first; a segment is straight only when both its knots are `linear`. | Bezier handles express auto, linear and broken tangents in one form. | `Spline.closed` is false for a closed path, so frames do not spread loop twist. | Build the curve with `Spline` and `closed: true` when you do not need broken tangents. |
| Place and deform along splines (`@margoengine/splines/mesh`) | Enforced: at most 1,000,000 instances. By method: a mesh bends in straight chords between its own vertices; normals are rotated with the frame, not re-derived; one frame lookup per distinct position along the axis. | Rotating normals needs no mesh connectivity. | A coarse mesh facets on a tight bend and a very sharp bend leaves normals slightly off. | Subdivide the mesh along its axis first. |
| Fitting (`fitSpline` in `@margoengine/splines/fit`) | Enforced: 2 to 10,000,000 points, a `tolerance` above 0. By method: the error is measured at each point's own curve parameter (an upper bound on the true nearest distance); pieces are cut at the worst point, so a curve can use a piece or two more than the fewest possible. | Cutting at the worst point is the usual way to keep fitting linear in the points. | Output may have more control points than a hand-placed curve. | Raise `tolerance`, or run the result through `KnotPath` and remove knots. |

## Entities

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduler (`@margoengine/ecs/schedule`) | Enforced: one fixed step size per `Schedule`, at most `maxSteps` (default 8) steps an update; time past that is dropped. Systems are synchronous and single threaded; the fixed phase always runs before the frame phase. | A cap stops a long stall from costing more steps than the next frame can pay for, which would snowball. | `update` returns the steps run and `schedule.dropped` holds the seconds lost. A frame system ordered before a fixed one throws MargoError `'state'`. | Raise `maxSteps`, or run a second `Schedule` for a second rate. |
| Change detection (`@margoengine/ecs/changes`) | Enforced by method: only `component.add`, `remove`, `touch` and `world.destroy` are seen. A write straight into `fields` is invisible until `touch` reports it, and a row counts as changed even when the value written is the same. 24 bytes per world slot per tracker. | `fields` are plain typed arrays, so loops over them stay at full speed; intercepting each write would cost that speed. | The entity is missing from `changed`. | Call `component.touch(entity)` after direct writes. |
| Query filters and tags (`@margoengine/ecs/query`, `world.tag`) | Enforced: `with` needs at least one term, and a `Query` cannot run inside its own `forEach`. Entities that start matching during `forEach` wait for the next call. A tag stores no fields but keeps the 8 bytes per world slot of its entity index. | The smallest `with` store is the list to walk, so there must be one. The match list is one buffer per query. | MargoError `'state'` or `TypeError`. | Use a second `Query` to nest. |
| Engine bridge (`@margoengine/ecs/engine`) | Enforced: one way, component to mesh, and one mesh per entity. Each group is whole or absent. Values pass the mesh's own setters; `sync` costs one lookup per link even when nothing moved. Parents are not copied. | The setters' checks and the Euler view of `mesh.rotation` must hold, so the bridge cannot write the store columns blindly. | `TypeError`, `RangeError` or MargoError `'disposed'` from `link`, `sync` or the constructor. | Read a mesh back by hand when something else moves it. |
| Relationships (`@margoengine/ecs/relations`) | Enforced by method: pairs carry no data of their own and live in Maps and Sets, not typed arrays. `acyclic` pays a walk up from the target on every `add`. | Pairs change rarely next to component rows, and Sets keep both directions direct to read. | A loop on an `acyclic` relation throws `TypeError`. | Keep per-pair numbers in a component on the source. |
| Growable worlds (`@margoengine/ecs/growable`, accepted difference in speed, 2026-11-05) | Enforced: at most `limit` slots, 1,000,000 at most, and a slot retires after about 4,294,967,295 / `limit` reuses. Measured ([ecs-growable.mjs](../examples/package-benchmarks/ecs-growable.mjs), Node 26, three runs on a busy machine, diagnostic): a loop over 100,000 rows takes about twice as long as on a fixed `World`, ratio 2.02 to 2.09. | Ids are 32 bits and spaced by `limit`, so they survive growth. Resizable buffers keep every array reference valid while growing; plain arrays would be replaced, and a cached `fields.x` would silently write to the old copy. A fixed `World` pays nothing. | `create` throws `RangeError` at the limit. | Use a fixed `World` when a bound is known; lower `limit` for more reuses per slot. |

## Copies of a model

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Textures of `cloneModel` copies | Shared: one GPU texture per device, image and format, freed with its last holder (`p-morph`: 7 textures for 100 copies, not 700). A second model loaded from the same file holds its own images, so it uploads its own textures. |
| `p-morph` build plus first frame (accepted only for now, open in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md#build-plus-first-frame-of-100-morphed-copies-is-still-slower-than-threes-webgl-backend)) | 154 ms, or 125 to 143 with `PBRModel.compile()` (first frame 17), against three's WebGPU 217 and WebGL 54, busy-machine diagnostic. |
| `PBRModel.compile()` | Compiles for the canvas pass under the lights and effects set when it is called. A later change to either, a batched textureless mesh, and any pass other than beauty compile on the draw as before. |

## Platform

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WebGPU first | Enforced: `Engine.create` uses WebGPU unless the app passes a fallback ([engine.ts](../packages/core/src/engine.ts), [webgl.test.js](../packages/webgl/test/webgl.test.js), [webgl-preview.test.js](../tests/webgl-preview.test.js)). | One backend keeps core + stage at 22,859 B gzip; culling, particles, sections and most effects are compute or WebGPU-only work. | `Error: WebGPU unavailable` (no fallback) or `Error: adapter unavailable` (`backend: 'webgpu'`); on the WebGL2 path, `engine.pick` and `engine.rebootDevice` throw `WebGPU required` (core is frozen, so a plain `Error`), and packages that need WebGPU throw `MargoError` code `unsupported` naming themselves when attached (`PostProcessing requires WebGPU; ...`, `VFX ...`, `Sky ...`, `Shadows ...`). On margoengine.com, a browser without WebGPU (no `navigator.gpu`, or no adapter) downloads the WebGL2 compatibility layer and runs every live demo on it (see the next row); only a browser without WebGL2 at the layer's full tier as well gets "This demo needs a browser with WebGPU: Chrome, Edge or Safari." in the canvas area with a link to [webgpu.html](../site/webgpu.html) on what to update, and downloads no demo code; the landing page draws no scene. No demo runs on the small WebGL2 preview: each needs effects, particles, skinning or compute, and all of them run on the layer. | `@margoengine/webgl` (3,154 B gzip, stays for v1.0 as the small preview, `Engine.create(canvas, {backend: 'auto', fallback: webglRenderer})`): a basic preview of core meshes, shaded per pixel with one directional light plus ambient, no textures, effects or picking. Checked in a real browser with WebGPU removed (`npm run check:no-webgpu`, part of `check:merge`: every site demo installs the layer without WebGPU, shows the message without WebGL2 too, downloads none of the layer with WebGPU, throws no uncaught error, and the preview draws two coloured boxes, read back as pixels) and in [gates-browser-tests.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/gates-browser-tests.json). The WebGL2 compatibility layer (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat`) is what the site runs without WebGPU, and the fuller fallback: it runs the WebGPU code of core and the packages as an optional download that WebGPU users never load ([webgl2-compat-roadmap.md](webgl2-compat-roadmap.md)). In React, `loadFallback` fetches the basic fallback only without WebGPU and `fallbackContent` replaces the plain message. |
| WebGPU pages alive at once | Measured on an Intel Arc 140V laptop (Edge and Chrome 156, headless, 2026-10-30): with 3 WebGPU pages alive in one browser process a new page's `requestDevice` took 10.6 s, and the 4th page never got a device or finished its pipeline compile (4 of 7 runs); 2 pages at once, one page at a time, or 4 separate browsers always started. The NVIDIA RTX A6000 desktop starts 4 at once. Enforced since then: each `Engine.create` startup step (`requestAdapter`, `requestDevice`, each pipeline compile) has a limit ([renderer.ts](../packages/core/src/renderer.ts), [core-startup-watchdog.test.js](../tests/core-startup-watchdog.test.js)). | The stall is in the driver or the browser's GPU process, not the page: the pages already drawing keep drawing every frame while the new one waits. | One `console.warn` (`Margo: still waiting for requestDevice after 8 s; see https://margoengine.com/errors#timeout`) after `startupWarning` ms (default 8,000), then a rejection with `MargoError` code `timeout` naming the step after `startupTimeout` ms (default 30,000); `backend: 'auto'` with a `fallback` draws on WebGL2 instead. Before, `Engine.create` never settled and the canvas stayed blank at 300 x 150. | Start several engines one at a time (each after the previous has drawn) and dispose those that leave the screen; the demo gallery must not start many engines at once. `signal` cancels creation; raise `startupTimeout` for a slow first compile. |
| Compute on the WebGL2 compatibility layer | Measured (Edge 156, ANGLE Direct3D 11, NVIDIA RTX A6000, 2026-10-28, [compute.html](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/compute.html) cases and a timing page). Compute entry points that store only their own texel run as fragment draws and those with a bounded number of stores as point draws, on the GPU. The rest (atomics, workgroup memory, barriers, stores in loops of unknown length) run on the CPU in JavaScript: a clustered-binning kernel over 3,456 clusters takes 1.5 ms with 16 lights, 2.8 ms with 64 and 9.4 ms with 256 (37 to 94 million loop iterations a second); a 64-wide workgroup reduction with 7 barriers runs 4.4 million invocations a second (65,536 in 14.9 ms). | WebGL2 has no compute shaders, storage buffers or atomics. | The same results as WebGPU (the layer's compute check compares both on one GPU), slower: GPU-written inputs of a CPU kernel are read back synchronously (counted in the device's `stalls`). Multisampled and external textures cannot be read by CPU-tier kernels (MargoError `unsupported`); cube textures are sampled there as on WebGPU, seamless; CPU kernels need a page that allows JavaScript compiled at run time (CSP `unsafe-eval`; nothing else in the layer does). A CPU-tier dispatch stops at its work budget, 100,000,000 invocations plus loop iterations by default (`cpuWorkBudget`), and is reported as a `GPUInternalError` coded `failed` with nothing stored. | Keep per-frame CPU-tier work under the numbers measured here; [webgl2-compat-roadmap.md](webgl2-compat-roadmap.md) lists the tiers. A transform-feedback tier for own-index stores is parked (speed only: those stores already run on the scatter tier with the same pixels, about 0.09 ms more per stored word, measured in the roadmap). |
| Package routes on the WebGL2 compatibility layer | Measured (Edge 156, ANGLE Direct3D 11, NVIDIA RTX A6000, 2026-10-29, frame wall time, native WebGPU then the layer; [routes-browser.mjs](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/routes-browser.mjs) checks the pixels). DOF at 1280 x 720: 0.72 ms, 10.1 ms on its route (913 ms on the generic CPU tier before). Splats: 10,000 in 1.2 ms, 17.9 ms (44 ms before); 100,000 in 2.1 ms, 39 ms (308 ms before). `CulledInstances`, 10,000 parts: 0.98 ms, 1.14 ms (11.7 ms before). VFX on the CPU tier, its plan's route: 5,000 particles 0.61 ms, 6.5 ms; 50,000 in 0.67 ms, 48 ms. Scatter on the CPU tier: 10,000 instances 0.56 ms, 5.4 ms; 100,000 in 0.85 ms, 40 ms. | WebGL2 has no workgroup memory, atomics or compute; each route does the same work another way. | The same pixels as native WebGPU. Splats read their projected keys back once a frame (a counted stall); `'occlusion'` culling culls against the frustum only (the same image, more parts drawn). The voxel path tracer and XR refuse the layer (MargoError `unsupported`). | Budget VFX particles and scatter instances by the per-frame times measured here (about 1 µs per particle and 0.4 µs per instance on this PC). |
| Site demos on the WebGL2 compatibility layer | Measured by `npm run visual:compat` (part of `check:merge`): every site demo and Khronos gallery model, natively and on the layer in one browser on one GPU; the per-demo table, with each pixel difference and frame cost, is [webgl2-compat-demos.md](webgl2-compat-demos.md). | WebGL2 has no compute, storage buffers or atomics; the layer runs those kernels as fragment draws, point draws or on the CPU, and Shadows, DOF, splats and culling take routes of their own. | Each demo either draws the same pixels as WebGPU (at most 0.1% of pixels more than 2 levels apart, mean at most 0.25), runs with differences the table states, or refuses the layer for a part that needs WebGPU (MargoError `unsupported`, shown over the scene). The per-sample MSAA difference is an accepted difference (Scott accepted, 2026-10-31): WebGL2 cannot read one sample of a multisampled texture, so the layer resolves it first, and DOF, the gameplay sandbox and Night Citadel differ from WebGPU through it ([the section on it](webgl2-compat-demos.md#accepted-difference-per-sample-reads-of-multisampled-textures)); at 1x MSAA they are within the parity rule. A demo's median frame on the layer must stay under 50 ms of main-thread work, or under twice its native frame when that is slower already (`npm run visual:compat:budget`, part of `check:merge`, with the GPU held exclusively; `--budget=<ms>` sets another limit, for an integrated GPU; that run is not recorded yet, and gameplay-sandbox is over the budget on the RTX A6000, see [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)). | [webgpu.html](../site/webgpu.html) explains the compatibility mode to visitors; [examples/dual-viewport.html](../examples/dual-viewport.html) draws one scene both ways with the live difference and frame times. |
| Download size of the WebGL2 compatibility layer | Measured by `npm run measure:size`'s record ([entry-sizes.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/entry-sizes.json), `splits`; the sizes gate holds both numbers, [lazy-boundary.test.js](../tests/lazy-boundary.test.js) holds the boundary), min+gzip, record at a28a2ec64. Two numbers: the base, everything `install()` loads (device, GLSL back end, WGSL front end, the render path), is 72,556 B (241,846 B minified); the compute runtime, which only a page that makes its first compute pipeline loads, is 22,093 B (69,306 B minified). Both together, as one file, are 94,104 B. A page on WebGPU downloads none of it. | The layer translates WGSL to GLSL and runs WebGPU's device model on WebGL2, so the base holds a full WGSL front end (check.ts 61 KB, parser, builtins) and the GLSL emitter. Property names are not mangled. | Accepted difference (Scott accepted, 2026-10-31; the limit itself was set 2026-10-30): the sizes gate holds the base to 73,000 B, not the 60,000 B target the roadmap once stated and no gate enforced. The base carries the full WGSL to GLSL translator and the WGSL checker, both needed on the first frame; native WebGPU always validates shaders, so a production build without the checker would behave differently. The lazy compute runtime is measured and gated separately. The five largest modules of the base by their share of the gzip bytes: device/render.ts 14.0 KB, glsl/emit.ts 13.9 KB, wgsl/check.ts 11.4 KB, device/resources.ts 5.0 KB, wgsl/builtins.ts 4.3 KB. | A page that never runs compute pays the base only. [webgl2-compat-roadmap.md](webgl2-compat-roadmap.md) tracks the size work. |
| Content Security Policy | Enforced by the browser: core compiles its Wasm kernel, so `script-src` needs `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` (as do Draco and Basis). The standard WebGPU path and the other WebGL2 tiers need no `'unsafe-eval'`, workers included (the optional WebGL2 CPU compute tier of `webgl2-compat` builds its shaders with `new Function` and needs it, or is refused): the Draco/KTX2 decoder worker loads its Emscripten code with `importScripts`, and the build replaces the `new Function` wrapper generators in the Basis glue with closures, output byte-identical ([no-eval-workers.test.js](../tests/no-eval-workers.test.js)). No COOP/COEP. Checked with zero violations on Edge, one policy on the page and every worker ([csp-check.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/csp-check.json)). | Wasm is how the kernel stays small and fast. | Without `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, `Engine.create` rejects ("Compiling or instantiating WebAssembly module violates the following Content Security policy directive") ([csp-check-negative.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/csp-check-negative.json)). | Headers for Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel and Nginx in [deploying.md](deploying.md). A Draco or Basis build you substitute for the bundled one may still call `new Function` (three.js's Basis transcoder does) and then needs `'unsafe-eval'` for its worker. |
| React app budget (what a bundler emits and the browser loads) | Measured and enforced by the bundler matrix (`npm run modern:test:bundlers`, part of `check:merge`): a Vite 8 build of the React cube page (`Canvas`, `Mesh`, `BoxGeometry`, `PbrMaterial`, `OrbitControls` from `@margoengine/react/controls`, `useFrame`; React 19) loads 94,216 B gzip before it runs (React, React DOM, core, the stage and the React bindings; budget 100,000 B), and with `@margoengine/react` installed alone the whole build emits 104,197 B gzip of JavaScript and no Wasm (budget 115,000 B). The matrix loads the built page in Edge and fails if it requests Wasm, an optional engine package or the BVH raycaster, and builds the same page with `@margoengine/react` alone in Next.js 16 (webpack and Turbopack), Rollup and esbuild: every module resolves and no optional package is emitted. Breakdown: [React page](#react-page). The build prints no warnings, without `@vitejs/plugin-react` too: `'use client'` is only on the `react-server` entries. | `@margoengine/react`'s root holds only bindings that need no optional package; each optional one is a subpath named after its package (`/controls`, `/gltf-pro`, `/shadows`, ...), and the stage's features are entries of their own (`@margoengine/stage/gltf`, ...), so no root reaches an optional package, not even through a lazy `import()` (`tests/optional-peer-reach.test.js`). | With `npm i margoengine`, `margoengine/react` re-exports every binding, so its module graph reaches gltf-pro's decoders: Vite copies the Basis (527,333 B) and Draco (192,420 B) `.wasm` to `dist` when it reads those modules, before tree-shaking. No chunk of them is emitted and the page never requests them (94,222 B gzip at load). | Install `@margoengine/react` alone, plus the packages its subpaths name (`@margoengine/controls` for `OrbitControls`): nothing else is installed or emitted. |
| Meshlets, cloth, particle fluids and soft bodies | By decision (2026-10-31): out of scope for v1.0.0. | Each is a large package of its own; `@margoengine/culling` already culls instances on the GPU and `@margoengine/physics` has `Rope`. | No such API exists; the parity matrix lists them as NOT PLANNED ([threejs-parity.md](threejs-parity.md)). | `CulledInstances` for large static assemblies, GPU particles in `@margoengine/vfx`, Rapier joints in `@margoengine/physics`. |
| No visual editor | By design: Margo is code-first. | An editor is a product of its own; the engine stays a library. | Scenes are built in code or authored in another tool. | Author in Blender and export glTF or `.margo` (`@margoengine/blender`, `tools/blender-addon`, [guides/blender-game.md](guides/blender-game.md)); inspect at runtime with `@margoengine/inspector` and its `/frame` debugger; move objects with `@margoengine/controls`'s TransformControls. A Margo Studio editor is planned after 1.0. |
| Bricked volumes | Enforced by the budget ([bricks.ts](../packages/sciviz/src/bricks.ts), [bricks.test.js](../packages/sciviz/tests/bricks.test.js)): `@margoengine/sciviz/bricks` holds at most `memoryBudget` bytes of GPU memory (default 512 MiB) and marches at most 2048 samples per ray. Measured at 4096 x 1024 x 1024 voxels (8.6 GiB as half floats, past the 2048 texture limit), 1280 x 720, RTX A6000, default budget: median 4.3-12.6 ms per frame over four views. Drawn against the same volume as one texture: largest channel difference 2 of 255. | A single 3D texture stops at the GPU's limit and costs all its bytes up front. | Past the budget, finer bricks wait and coarser ones draw; between levels values can step by what averaging removed. The page table takes one texel per full-resolution brick and must fit the 3D limit. Errors: `RangeError` naming `memoryBudget` or `brickSize`; `MargoError` code `failed` for a read that failed. | Raise `memoryBudget` or lower `detail` for more detail; frame time grows with the bricks drawn (2 GiB, closest view: median 653 ms). |
| Light-tier frame rate | Enforced ([index.ts](../packages/quality/src/index.ts)): `paceEngine` holds the light tier to an even rate of at least 60 FPS: 60 on 60, 120 and 240 Hz, 72 on 144 Hz, 83 on 165 Hz, 67 on 200 Hz, and every refresh of 75, 90 and 100 Hz. | Each frame spans a whole number of refreshes, so the rate cannot land on exactly 60 on every display, and an uneven 60 on 100 Hz would judder. | A 100 Hz display renders 100 FPS on the light tier, which asks twice the GPU work of the 50 FPS it used to get; a GPU that cannot keep up misses refreshes as it would on any uncapped tier. Not yet seen on a physical 100 Hz panel: the numbers come from a real page on a simulated 100 Hz clock. | `capFrameRate(engine, rate)` sets another rate; `?quality=high` is not paced. |
| GPU reading against `FAST_GPU_MS` | Measured (voxel sandbox, seed 1, 1920 x 1000, 2026-11-05): an Apple M6 reads 8.8 ms in Chrome 157 and 8.7 ms in Playwright WebKit 27.2 at 60 FPS, an RTX A6000 4.5 ms in Edge. | The limit is 8 ms, chosen on Plaza from an A6000, an Intel UHD and an Arc 140V. | An M6 sits just over the limit on this scene, so it stays on the light tier at 60 Hz; on a simulated 100 Hz clock it read 5.5 to 7.0 ms and stored the full tier. The full tier costs 13.4 ms of GPU time a frame in Chrome on the M6, over the 10 ms of a 100 Hz refresh. | `?quality=high` forces the tier; `localStorage.removeItem('margoQuality:' + location.pathname)` measures again. |
| Tested hardware | Committed real-GPU results come from two Windows 11 machines in Edge 155: the Intel Arc 140V laptop above and an NVIDIA RTX A6000 desktop (its own visual-baseline profile, `nvidia-ampere-msedge-155`; the voxel results above come from it). Phones: the demos were run by hand on an iPhone (Safari), with no scripted run or committed result; a Galaxy S23 Ultra report of a slow island demo is unresolved. | One developer, two machines so far. | Behaviour elsewhere follows WebGPU's guarantees but is unverified. | An Apple M6 Mac mini ran the voxel sandbox and the biome checks by script (macOS 27.2, Chrome 157 and Playwright WebKit 27.2). Untested: AMD GPUs, NVIDIA GPUs other than the A6000, other Apple silicon, Android devices other than the S23 report, Linux, ChromeOS. Results from these are welcome; [reproduce.md](whitepaper/reproduce.md) has the commands. |
| Browsers | Verified: Edge 155 (Chromium) on Windows, automated (real-GPU suites, visual regression, CSP). iPhone Safari: run by hand only (above). Firefox: not verified. macOS Safari: not verified (Playwright WebKit 27.2 ran the voxel sandbox on an Apple M6, but it is not Safari). | Same as above. | Where a browser lacks WebGPU, `Engine.create` reports it (see "WebGPU first"). | Chrome uses the same Chromium engine as Edge; the automated suites run in Edge. CSP behaviour in Firefox and Safari is unverified. |
| WebXR AR hit testing | Not measured: `@margoengine/xr` `HitTest` has never run on an AR headset or phone. It is checked against the W3C WebXR Hit Test Module's interfaces with a mocked session (hit results, transient input, anchors, failure paths: [hit-test.test.js](../packages/xr/tests/hit-test.test.js)). | No AR device is in the test setup, and immersive AR needs the native WebGPU XR binding. | `XR.isSupported('immersive-ar')` is false where the browser cannot run it; on a device that can, behaviour is unverified. | Plane detection, depth sensing and light estimation are not wrapped; read them from the native session (`xr.session`). |

### React page

What a minimal React page downloads, and why it is larger than core + stage (22,859 B gzip). The cube page of the
bundler matrix (`Canvas`, `Mesh`, `BoxGeometry`, `PbrMaterial`, `useFrame`, and `OrbitControls` from
`@margoengine/react/controls`), built by Vite 8.3.4, React 19.3 and `@margoengine/react` installed alone with
`@margoengine/controls` (2026-10-27), measured from the build's source maps (minified bytes per package; gzip is each
package's own gzip size, scaled so the parts add up to the chunk's). Core lights every scene by default
(a sun and an ambient term), so this is also the minimal lit page.

| Part | Minified B | Gzip B | Needed for a lit scene? |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `react-dom` (client) | 206,925 | 62,263 | Yes: the app's own UI runtime, not Margo's |
| `react` + `scheduler` | 11,635 | 4,430 | Yes: the app's own |
| `@margoengine/core` (engine, renderer, Wasm kernel, camera, shaders, geometry) | 49,485 | 19,056 | Yes |
| `@margoengine/react` (components, internal, assets, the shadows hook) | 14,241 | 5,488 | Yes: `Canvas`, `Mesh` and the hooks |
| `@margoengine/stage` | 2,771 | 1,405 | Not to draw (core draws and lights the cube); `Canvas` wraps its engine in the stage it hands to `onCreated` and `<Stage>` |
| Vite runtime (preload helper, module preload polyfill), app code and `@margoengine/math` (170 B) | 3,135 | 1,609 | The build's own |
| **Entry, requested before the page runs** | **288,234** | **94,251** | Budget 100,000 B gzip |
| `@margoengine/controls/orbit` + its view helpers + profiles, when `OrbitControls` mounts | 17,999 | 6,951 | Yes, for orbiting |
| **Everything the page fetches** | **306,233** | **101,202** | |

React and React DOM are 66% of the page; Margo's part (core, stage, bindings) is 25,949 B gzip (27,028 B before the
stage feature entries and the React subpaths of 2026-10-27, which took 3,089 B of minified loaders out of the stage). Nothing optional is in
the entry: `PbrMaterial` is core's material and pulls in no other package.

- **Fixed (2026-10-26):** `OrbitControls`, `MapControls` and `CadControls` loaded the `@margoengine/controls` index,
  so mounting them fetched TransformControls, DragControls, the gizmo and the `@margoengine/bvh` raycaster as one
  112,655 B (39,072 B gzip) chunk. They now load `@margoengine/controls/orbit` and `/profiles`, `ArcballControls`
  loads `/arcball` and `TransformControls` loads `/transform`: the mount costs 6,951 B gzip, and a Vite build emits
  107,027 B gzip in all instead of 135,875 B.
- **Emitted, never fetched:** the arcball chunk (3,192 B gzip). Nothing else: since 2026-10-27 neither `Canvas` nor
  the stage reaches an optional package, so there are no stand-in stubs either.
- **A textured model** (`<Gltf src="BoxTextured.glb">` from `@margoengine/react/gltf-pro`, with `@margoengine/gltf-pro`
  installed): the entry grows by
  1,750 B gzip (the `Model` binding), and mounting it fetches gltf-pro (175,257 B, 56,074 B gzip: glTF parsing, the
  PBR material and shader, compression hooks) plus the model. The Draco and Basis Wasm are emitted for files that use
  them; this one does not, and the page does not request them.
- Still on the controls index: `PointerLock` (from `@margoengine/react/controls`), because `@margoengine/controls` has no
  pointer-lock entry; a page that does not use it never emits it.

=== Known bugs and unverified features (docs/known-bugs.md) ===

# Known bugs and unverified features

What is known to be wrong or not yet proven, and what it would take to close each item. Design limits (where a
boundary is a decision, with its escape hatch) live in [limits.md](limits.md); this page lists defects and checks that
are still open.

## Boulder demo

### The robot's arm shows a copper piston through its shell at close range

- **What:** in the Boulder demo, from the nearest orbit distance (1.2 m), a copper rod shows through the upper arm shell
  and the shell has a jagged edge near the elbow. It does not show from the default view, and it does not affect the
  collision results, which use the link hulls.
- **Repro:** `npm run build:boulder`, then `node scripts/test-boulder-browser.mjs --shots=<dir> --closeups`, and open
  `boulder-high-close-right.png` and `boulder-high-close-left.png`.
- **Cause, not yet confirmed:** the piston, washers and hubs in `examples/assets/source/skinning_ik/build_robot.py` are
  not in its `NO_CROSSING` list, so the crossing check in that script does not see them.
- **Needed to close:** decide whether this model stays. If it does, add those parts to `NO_CROSSING`, fix what the check
  then reports and rebuild the GLB. If another model replaces it, this entry goes with the old model.

## Blocked on hardware we do not have

These features pass their tests against the published specifications, but the only real check is a device the project
does not own. Each entry says exactly what is needed to close it.

### USDZ export with textures: never opened in Quick Look

- **What:** `exportUSDZ` in `@margoengine/exporters` (`packages/exporters/src/usdz.ts`) writes UsdPreviewSurface
  materials with texture readers (base colour with opacity and `opacityThreshold`, metal-rough on the g and b channels,
  normal, occlusion, emissive, `st`/`st1` texcoords with the V flip, a base-colour `UsdTransform2d`, wrap modes) and
  stores each image 64-byte aligned and uncompressed.
- **Verified:** the USDZ tests (`packages/exporters/tests/usdz.test.js`) check the shader graph text, every file's
  alignment, the image bytes and a round trip through our own USD reader (`@margoengine/usdz`). OpenUSD's own checker
  (`packages/exporters/tests/validate-usdz.py`) has not been run on textured output: it needs the `usd-core` Python package, which is not
  installed on the development machines.
- **Not verified:** that Apple's renderers show the textures as intended. A non-default `normalScale` writes a normal
  scale and bias that OpenUSD's validator may flag as non-standard.
- **Needed to close:**
  1. An iPhone or iPad on iOS 17 or later, or a Mac on macOS 14 or later (Quick Look and AR Quick Look).
  2. The kit's exported files opened there, each compared with the same scene drawn by Margo: a base-colour texture with an
     alpha mask (`opacityThreshold`), a blended (alpha) texture, a metal-rough map plus a normal map at `normalScale` 1
     and 2, an occlusion plus emissive map, a base-colour texture transform (offset, scale and rotation) with repeat
     and mirror wrapping, and rotation alone at +30 and -30 degrees.
     `node scripts/make-usdz-quicklook-kit.mjs <folder> --glb` writes them (eight files: `normalScale` 1 and 2 are
     separate; 07 and 08 are the rotations), with engine-drawn reference twins.
     Texture rotation (KHR_texture_transform radians, written as `UsdTransform2d` degrees with the same sign, and read
     back the same way by `@margoengine/usdz`) is written but not yet confirmed on a device: Quick Look on iOS 27.2 drew file 06 leaning clockwise, as gltf-pro draws the same glTF
     transform (the kit's first checklist expected anticlockwise; that expectation was wrong). Files 07 (+30, should
     lean clockwise) and 08 (-30, anticlockwise) await a device re-check.
  3. `pip install usd-core`, then `python packages/exporters/tests/validate-usdz.py <file>` on the same files.
  4. The result (pass, or the difference seen) recorded here and in `docs/threejs-parity.md` (USDZExporter row).

### WebXR AR hit testing: never run on an AR device

- **What:** `HitTest` in `@margoengine/xr` (`packages/xr/src/hit-test.ts`): hit-test sources from the viewer, an input
  source or transient input, results as reference-space poses, anchors.
- **Verified:** tests against the W3C WebXR Hit Test Module's interfaces with a mocked session
  (`packages/xr/tests/hit-test.test.js`); [limits.md](limits.md) has its row.
- **Needed to close:** an Android phone with ARCore and a Chromium browser that exposes WebXR `immersive-ar` with the
  WebGPU XR binding (`XRGPUBinding`), or an AR headset with the same; then a reticle placed on a real floor and a real
  table (viewer source) and by screen tap (transient source), one placement anchored, and the result recorded here.

### Intel Arc 140V: three GPU-suite failures fixed on this PC and rechecked on Intel by the outside audit

- **Verified on Intel** (Core Ultra 7 258V, Arc 140V, driver 32.0.101.8860, main at 30bea6fa, recheck of 2026-10-27):
  the four failures of the first run (main d000e4b6) are fixed there. FFT: the Stockham passes match the host-twiddle
  f32 reference exactly (0.00 u at n = 1024 and 65536); path tracer `combinedHDR` within 1 sRGB level (was 226),
  converged after 17 frames; the Next client drew the mint cube after 598 ms (past the old 300 ms fixed wait); the voxel
  and path-tracer `test:gpu:slow-compile` twins and `modern:test:browser` with its twin pass.
- **What failed instead** (same run), and the cause and fix of each, measured on the RTX A6000:
  1. compute CPU/GPU parity, `sin, cos, atan2[16]: cpu -0.4964582920074463, gpu -0.49644696712493896` (1.13e-5 off,
     tolerance 1e-5). Cause: the WGSL builtins. WGSL allows `sin` and `cos` 2^-11 absolute error inside [-pi, pi] (and
     none promised outside), `atan2` 4096 ulp, `asin` 6.8e-5; the Arc 140V is 1.1e-5 off near 1.5 where the A6000 is
     within 3.3e-7 (the A6000 is itself 1e-5 off at |x| near 100, 133 ulp for `tanh`, 114 for `pow`). Fixed: element-wise
     functions use precise f32 versions (`packages/shared/precise-math.js`: integer Payne-Hanek reduction, minimax
     polynomials from `scripts/precise-math-coefficients.mjs`), within 1 to 2.5 ulp (pow 5) on every GPU;
     `createCompute({ fastMath: true })` keeps the builtins. The parity check is tighter now (1e-6, plus each function
     in ulp) and the fastMath path is checked against the WGSL bounds. Regression tests: `tests/precise-math.test.js`
     (the bounds over dense inputs with fused and unfused rounding and with division and sqrt at WGSL's limits), the
     GPU check `compute-precise-browser.js` (the A6000 computes the host mirror's values bit for bit), and
     `compute test:browser:spec-math`, which moves every builtin result by WGSL's whole allowed error
     (`--spec-math-error`, scripts/browser.js): the old parity check fails there as on Intel, the new one passes.
  2. voxel normal suite, `4x four-view blue`: the bottom two views black. Cause: the bevel check took "the quad and
     triangle counts did not change for 3 frames" for "every chunk is meshed"; with one mesher worker on a slower CPU
     a bevelled chunk takes several frames, so the last two chunks (the bottom views) were not on the GPU yet. Fixed:
     `VoxelRenderer.stats.pending` counts the chunks not yet on the GPU (changed, meshing, waiting for upload); the
     check waits for a frame with `pending` 0, `compiling` false and draws. Regression test: `voxel test:gpu:slow-mesh`
     delivers every worker message 150 ms late (`--worker-delay`): the old check fails there the same way, the new one
     passes.
  3. voxel-pathtracer normal suite, `traversal fisheye: depth`: 1.17e-3 relative depth error against the CPU raycast
     (assertion < 1e-4), 16379 of 16384 first hits alike. Cause: the fisheye rays came from the builtin `asin`, `sin`
     and `cos`; a ray that far off grazes a different voxel face. Fixed: the panorama and fisheye rays use the precise
     functions. Regression test: `voxel-pathtracer test:gpu:spec-math` (the projections check with every builtin at
     WGSL's error bound) fails with the builtins and passes with the fix.
- **The class:** five checks have now waited "N frames" or "N ms" for something that takes longer on a slower GPU or
  CPU. `scripts/check-fixed-waits.mjs` (run by `tests/check-fixed-waits.test.js` in `npm run verify`) fails on any new
  fixed frame count or sleep in a GPU or browser check unless it carries `// fixed-wait: <reason>`; the ones already
  there are counted in `scripts/fixed-waits-baseline.json` and only go down. `scripts/support/gpu-ready.js`
  (`waitForPipelines`) waits for the pipelines themselves.
- **Rechecked on Intel by the outside audit of 2026-10-28** (a second Intel Arc 140V laptop; the audit is the source
  for this paragraph): the compute spec-math case, the voxel normal and slow-compile cases and the voxel-pathtracer
  spec-math fisheye case all passed. The audit does not say whether the three fixes above (the precise maths, the
  `pending` count and the precise fisheye rays) were what changed them, and it reports no per-function bounds.
- **Not verified:** the precise functions' error bounds on the Intel compiler (`compute-browser.json` from an Intel
  PC), which no recheck has recorded.
- **Needed to close:** the `compute-browser.json` precise-maths results from an Intel PC, then this entry removed or
  turned into the cause found.

### Intel Arc 140V: voxel-pathtracer `denoise` case ran out of time with no output

- **What:** on the Intel Arc 140V laptop, `voxel-pathtracer test:gpu` finished every case before `denoise`, which started
  at about 172 s and printed nothing until the test runner killed the suite at 900 s (`HUNG: no result after 900 s`).
  The cases after it never ran there.
- **Measured on the RTX A6000** (shared GPU, 2026-10-29): the case renders six 480 x 300 references at 16384 samples
  and took 196 s (diffuse 14, opaque 15, materials 82, caustics 85); the longest wait for any GPU work to finish was
  1 s. The Arc ran `convergence` in 61.3 s against 13.1 s here (4.7 times slower), which puts `denoise` near 915 s there,
  more than the 728 s it had. Most likely cause: the case was simply longer than the time limit. A GPU wait that never
  resolves is not ruled out without an Arc run.
- **Done:** each scene is its own case (`denoise-diffuse`, `denoise-opaque`, `denoise-materials`,
  `denoise-caustics`; `denoise` runs all four). Every render prints a
  `progress denoise <scene>: ...` line. A case in which no GPU work finishes for `MARGO_GPU_STALL_S` (120 s) now fails
  at once, naming the case, the step and the render (`tests/progress.mjs`). Each case prints its time and its longest GPU
  wait. Regression test: `voxel-pathtracer test:gpu:stall` (`tests/stall-check.mjs`) hangs every GPU wait once the
  first render starts and expects that named failure. It fails in 17 s with the watchdog; without it the run has not
  ended at the 180 s limit.
- **Measured again on the Arc** (origin/main cb42459a, mains, Edge 156): `test:gpu` still hit its 900 s limit with no
  `GPU stall` line, so the GPU kept finishing work: the denoise references started at 147 s (diffuse), 242 s
  (opaque), 327 s (materials) and 748 s (caustics), and the caustics case was still running at 898 s. Slow, not hung.
  `denoisepeak`, `denoisehistory`, `lens`, `viewport`, `capture`, `materialtables`, `largemodels` and `native4k`
  never ran there.
- **Done (split, 2026-10-30):** the check runs as five package scripts that name their cases, each with its own limit
  in `margo.gpuTestTimeoutMinutes`; same cases, samples and tolerances. A6000 time, Arc estimate (from the run above),
  limit: `test:gpu` (agx to convergence) 57 s, about 150 s, 10 min; `test:gpu:denoise` (diffuse, opaque, denoisepeak,
  denoisehistory) 46 s, about 240 s, 10 min; `test:gpu:denoise-materials` 99 s, about 450 s, 15 min;
  `test:gpu:denoise-caustics` 109 s, about 500 s, 15 min; `test:gpu:viewport` (motion, lens, viewport, bloom, capture,
  materialtables, largemodels, native4k) 36 s, about 200 s, 10 min. `tests/voxel-pathtracer-gpu-split.test.js` fails
  if a split script is missing, if their cases are not exactly the check's case list (each once), if a script runs the
  whole check with no case named, or if check:merge would not run one when the package is affected. An unknown case
  name now fails the browser check instead of running nothing.
- **Needed to close:** run the five split scripts above on the Arc. If each passes
  inside its limit, remove this entry. If one stops with `GPU stall`, the message names the render to hunt.

### Linux (Intel UHD, Mesa): three GPU suites not finished

- **What:** on the Ubuntu test server (Intel N100 with Intel UHD, Chromium on Mesa's Vulkan driver, Node 24, main
  b92998d6, 2026-10-28) 42 of the 43 package GPU suites were started, one at a time, and 38 passed. The voxel, voxel
  path tracer and root browser suites were stopped by the heat watchdog at 82 C before they finished, so they have no
  Linux result yet. The text failure of the same run is the colour emoji entry below.
- **Needed to close:** those three suites run to the end on Linux, on a machine that stays cool under a long GPU
  run, and the results recorded here.

## Open defects

### Native glass on a display-encoded target adds its lit draw in encoded values

- **What:** without an HDR scene target (`f.settings.w` below 0.5), the lit draw of gltf-pro's native glass blends over
  the tint draw in display-encoded values. Light adds in linear values, so bright highlights over bright backgrounds
  come out too bright. `materials` `install` and `Transmission` add in linear light since 2026-11-05; only the native
  two-draw path is left.
- **Size:** encoded 0.5 + 0.5 reads 1.0; adding in linear light reads 0.69. Also, the native tint encodes the share and
  multiplies, which is exact only for a power curve: within 1 step above about 40 of 255, up to 2 steps below it.
- **Repro:** glass with a strong highlight over a bright background through `loadGLTF`, on a target with no PostStack,
  against the same scene with `Tonemap`.
- **Cause:** the blend unit reads the target as it is stored, and core's colour targets are plain `bgra8unorm` or
