The sandbox supplies phase/speed from the shared controls module.

`generateRockMesh()` produces deformed fieldstones with smooth, averaged normals
across split vertices while preserving UV seams and tangent frames.
`generateFernMesh()` produces seven curved, tapered ribbon fronds; use a
double-sided material. Both return `GeometryData` and are deterministic.
For the biome presets there are more plants: `generatePalmMesh()`, `generateBirchMesh()`, `generateAcaciaMesh()` and
`generateSnagMesh()` (a dead standing tree, empty canopy) return `{ trunk, canopy }` like `generateTreeMesh`, and
`generateCactusMesh()`, `generateReedMesh(stems = 9)` (double sided) and `generateTundraShrubMesh()` return one
`GeometryData`; each is rooted at the origin, +Y up, in metres.
Mesh levels for distance: `generateTreeMesh(kind, options)`, `generateShrubMesh`, `generateTundraShrubMesh`,
`generatePalmMesh`, `generateBirchMesh` and `generateAcaciaMesh` take `{ detail: 0 | 1 | 2 }` (default 2, the full
mesh, unchanged byte for byte). Level 1 keeps the shape with coarser lobes (a broadleaf canopy goes from 6,240 to
3,180 triangles); level 0 merges lobes into a few coarse ones for the far rings (400 triangles).
Level 1 keeps each axis of the canopy box within 20 percent of level 2; level 0 is stretched to level 2's box (conifer,
broadleaf, palm, birch, acacia and shrub canopies, within 10 percent on every axis), so far trees keep their size. An
invalid level throws a `RangeError`.

```ts
import {generateTreeMesh} from 'margoengine/procedural';
const rings = [2, 1, 0].map((detail) => generateTreeMesh('broadleaf', {detail})); // near, middle, far
```

For a cove scene there are two waterfront props, each one `GeometryData` mesh with UVs, tangents and unit normals,
local origin at the water surface (y = 0), +Y up, in metres, deterministic by `seed` (an integer, default 1):

| Call | Options (defaults) | Triangles at `detail` 2 / 1 / 0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `generateJettyMesh(options?)` | `length` 4..120 (24), `width` 1..8 (2.2), `height` above the water 0.3..4 (1.1), `ladder` (true), `seed`, `detail` | 2,768 / 1,680 / 508 |
| `generateBoatMesh(options?)` | `length` 1.5..12 (3.6), `seats` 0..4 (3), `oars` (true), `seed`, `detail` | 1,884 / 812 / 372 |

The jetty runs along +X from the shore end at x = 0, with planks, stringers, posts and a ladder at the far end. The
boat is a rowing boat centred on the origin with its bow toward +X. A wrong type throws a `TypeError` and a value out of
range a `RangeError`; the message names the range to pass.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/procedural.md]

=== @margoengine/wfc (packages/wfc/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/wfc

Import `margoengine/wfc` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/wfc` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Seeded 3D Wave Function Collapse with weighted entropy, six-direction adjacency, pinned cells and bounded restart attempts.

```ts
import {WFC} from 'margoengine/wfc';
const generator = new WFC([4,4,4], [{neighbors: [[0],[0],[0],[0],[0],[0]]}]);
const cells = generator.solve(123);
```

Tile IDs are 0..31; output is a flattened Uint8Array with X fastest, then Y, then Z. Directions are +X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z. Adjacency must be reciprocal. solve(seed, pins, attempts) retries contradictions deterministically and throws when the bounded budget is exhausted. This is local WFC propagation with restart, not an exhaustive backtracking solver or a guaranteed connected-dungeon generator; connectivity belongs in the tile rules and caller validation.

## Overlapping model (`@margoengine/wfc/overlapping`, 1.9 kB min+gzip)

Learns N x N patterns from a sample image and generates outputs in which every N x N window appears in the sample.

```ts
import {OverlappingModel} from 'margoengine/wfc/overlapping';
// 0 floor, 1 wall, 2 door; any numbers work (palette indices, packed RGBA).
const rows = ['11111111', '10000101', '10000201', '11211111', '10000001', '11111111'];
const model = new OverlappingModel({data: rows.join('').split('').map(Number), width: 8, height: 6}, {N: 3, symmetry: 8});
const image = model.solve(64, 40, {seed: 7, periodic: false});   // Float64Array of sample values, X fastest
console.log(model.patterns, model.stats.backtracks, model.stats.attempts);
```

Options: `N` 2..5, `periodicInput` (patterns wrap around the sample), `symmetry` 1..8 (rotations and reflections, in
Gumin's order); `solve` takes `seed`, `periodic` output, `backtracks` (per attempt, default 1000) and `attempts`
(default 4). Propagation is arc-consistent (supporter counts per cell, pattern and direction). On a contradiction the
latest choice is undone from the trail and forbidden in its cell (chronological backtracking); past the budget the
attempt restarts from scratch with the seed stream continuing; when the attempts run out `solve` throws. Every loop is
bounded by the budgets, so an unsatisfiable sample fails instead of hanging (the tests run one in a child process with a
timeout). A 7 x 7 maze sample with `symmetry: 1` fails every seed without backtracking and solves them all with it.
Limits: at most 4096 patterns and `cells x patterns` <= 4,194,304 (memory: 18 bytes per cell and pattern); the
min-entropy scan is O(cells) per choice, fine to about 128 x 128; no ground/pinning constraints yet; CPU only.
Example: `examples/overlapping.html`.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/wfc

=== @margoengine/splines (packages/splines/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/splines

Import `margoengine/splines` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/splines` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Piecewise 3D Catmull-Rom, cubic Bezier, cubic Hermite, uniform B-spline and Kochanek-Bartels curves, with a cached arc-length lookup, closest point, stable frames, knot editing, mesh placement and bending, and curve fitting.

```ts
import {Spline} from 'margoengine/splines';
const curve = new Spline([[0,0,0], [5,1,5], [10,0,10]]);
const point = new Float64Array(3);
curve.atDistance(curve.length / 2, point);
curve.tangent(0.5, point);
```

Bezier curves require 3n+1 points and are open. Hermite requires one tangent per point; Catmull-Rom and Hermite can be closed. at uses t in 0..1; atDistance uses world units. Returned default output is reused, so provide an output buffer to retain multiple results. After editing points, call updateArcLengths. Arc lengths/tangents are numerical approximations controlled by divisions.

## More curve types

`kind: 'bspline'` is the uniform cubic B-spline: smoother than Catmull-Rom (continuous curvature) but it only pulls toward interior points, so it does not pass through them; open curves start and end exactly at the first and last point. `kind: 'kochanek-bartels'` passes through every point and adds `tension`, `continuity` and `bias`, each -1 to 1 and 0 by default (all zero is Catmull-Rom).

```ts
const camera = new Spline(waypoints, {kind: 'kochanek-bartels', tension: 0.3, bias: -0.2});
const smooth = new Spline(waypoints, {kind: 'bspline', closed: true});
```

## Closest point (`@margoengine/splines/closest`)

```ts
import {closestPointOnSpline} from 'margoengine/splines/closest';
const hit = closestPointOnSpline(curve, [3, 1, 4]);
// hit.t (0..1), hit.arc (world units along the curve), hit.point, hit.distance
```

It samples the curve (`samples`, default the spline's `divisions`), then bisects on the slope of the distance around the best sample. A curve that passes close to itself (a tight spiral) needs `samples` high enough to tell the passes apart. `distanceAt(spline, t)` and `parameterAt(spline, distance)` convert between `t` and arc length.

## Stable frames and roll (`@margoengine/splines/frames`)

```ts
import {SplineFrames} from 'margoengine/splines/frames';
const frames = new SplineFrames(curve, {up: [0, 1, 0], roll: (t) => t * 0.5});
const frame = frames.frameAt(curve.length * 0.25);
// frame.position, frame.tangent, frame.normal, frame.binormal (binormal = tangent x normal)
```

Frames are carried along the curve by double reflection (rotation-minimising), so they do not flip where a fixed up vector would (a curve passing through the up direction). `roll` is radians about the tangent: a function of `t`, or one value per knot (`knotCount(curve)`, blended linearly). A closed curve's twist is spread over its length so the last frame meets the first (`closeLoop: false` turns that off). Frames are sampled at `samples` (default 256) steps and blended in between.

## Knot editing (`@margoengine/splines/knots`)

```ts
import {KnotPath} from 'margoengine/splines/knots';
const path = new KnotPath([
  {position: [0, 0, 0], data: [1]},
  {position: [4, 3, 0], data: [2]},
  {position: [8, 0, 0], mode: 'linear', data: [4]},
]);
path.insertAt(0, 0.5);                 // split the first segment; the curve does not move
path.setMode(1, 'broken', {tangentOut: [0, 2, 0]});
const spline = path.toSpline();        // a Bezier Spline
const width = path.dataAt(0.7)[0];     // per-knot numbers blended along the curve
const [a, b] = path.split(2);          // two paths sharing knot 2
```

Modes: `auto` (smooth through the knot), `linear` (handles point at the neighbors; a segment between two linear knots is straight) and `broken` (the stored `tangentIn` and `tangentOut`, so a corner can point any way). `insertAt` keeps the shape by turning the new knot and its two neighbors `broken`; pass `false` as the third argument to insert an `auto` knot and let the curve reshape. A closed path builds an open Bezier whose last point is its first.

## Place and deform along a spline (`@margoengine/splines/mesh`)

```ts
import {placeAlongSpline, deformAlongSpline} from 'margoengine/splines/mesh';
const posts = placeAlongSpline(curve, {spacing: 2.5, fit: true, forward: 'z'});
// posts.matrices: count column-major 4x4 matrices, ready for an instance buffer
const pipe = deformAlongSpline(curve, positions, {axis: 'z', normals, fit: 'stretch'});
// pipe.positions, pipe.normals
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/splines.md]

=== @margoengine/animation (packages/animation/README.md) ===

# Margo Engine Animation

Import `margoengine/animation` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/animation` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional WebGPU skeletal animation and morph targets, isolated from core and stage.

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
import {loadGLTF} from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';
import {Animation} from 'margoengine/animation';
const stage = await createStage('#viewport', {backend:'webgpu',capacity:2048});
const model = await loadGLTF(stage.engine, '/RobotExpressive.glb');
const animation = Animation.attach(model);
animation.play('Walking');
animation.playing = false;
animation.seek(0.5);
animation.destroy();
model.destroy();
stage.dispose();
```

Parses glTF skins, joint hierarchies and inverse bind matrices. Samples STEP, LINEAR (quaternion slerp), and CUBICSPLINE tracks. Animation advances in seconds before the engine updates world matrices. A compute pass blends position/normal/tangent morphs before skinning and writes the vertex draw buffer. Bone matrices use read-only storage buffers, bounded by the GPU's storage limits rather than a fixed bone count.

Every skinned or morphed primitive of a device, across all its Animations, lives in a few shared storage buffers and deforms in one compute dispatch per buffer page and influence format (100 morphed models with two primitives each: one dispatch, not 200). Copies of one asset primitive (`cloneModel`) share one copy of its morph deltas and skin influences. A primitive's deformed vertices start `primitive.deformedOffset` bytes (a multiple of 256) into `primitive.deformed`; gltf-pro, shadows, TAA, selection and picking read them there, and a custom reader binds or copies from that offset.

Use `animation.setMorph(nodeIndex, targetIndex, weight)` for manual expressions. Play a clip by name/index; set `loop:false` for one-shot playback. Up to eight influences per vertex are supported through paired `JOINTS_0`/`WEIGHTS_0` and optional `JOINTS_1`/`WEIGHTS_1`. Higher sets reject explicitly. No blending between clips is included.

Four-influence primitives keep their 32-byte influence records and the arithmetic of the per-primitive shader, bit for bit. An eight-influence primitive uses a 64-byte record and a second, lazily created compute pipeline; both formats can coexist in one model. Weights normalize across all present sets, including assets whose positive weights are entirely in the secondary set. Joint indices accept unsigned 8-bit or 16-bit accessors; weights accept Float32 or normalized unsigned 8-bit/16-bit accessors. Both sets require matching vertex counts, valid palette indices, nonnegative weights, and a positive combined sum.

Single-clip playback reuses sample buffers, quaternion arrays, palette matrices, and inverse-bind views. The animation hot path allocates no new typed arrays, quaternion copies, or GPU resources. Device restoration recreates both pipeline variants and the shared buffers. `sampleTrack()` retains its independently owned return value by default; an optional seventh `target: Float32Array` argument lets other consumers reuse their own output storage.

`createMaterialAnimation(model, {clip?, loop?})` plays a clip's `KHR_animation_pointer` STEP tracks on base-color `KHR_texture_transform` offset and scale (what `@margoengine/exporters` writes from `materialAnimations`): `seek(seconds)` writes the sampled UV transform into every primitive material of the targeted glTF material, and `dispose()` releases its claim on those properties. Given the opt-in `pointers` option, `Animation` also plays those channels, with every other `KHR_animation_pointer` channel it supports (see below); without it, it skips them and counts them in the clip's duration.

The separate `@margoengine/animator` package adds gameplay states, blend trees, additive masks and foot IK while reusing this pass's palette buffers. `sampleTrack()` is exported for animation consumers (matrix products: `@margoengine/math/mat4`).

Animation installs an optional `model.prepareDeformation` encoding hook. GPU
picking and explicit CPU snapshots use it to update the same skin/morph output
after a seek, bone edit or weight change without needing a beauty frame. Queries
do not advance playback time. The hook survives device restoration; disposal
removes only the animation instance's own hook. No CPU skinning copy is added to
the playback path.

Run the character demo at `/examples/robot-expressive.html` (also `character-animation.html`). RobotExpressive is by Tomás Laulhé with morphs by Don McCurdy (CC0). It is not a Khronos sample.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/animation.md]

=== @margoengine/animator (packages/animator/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/animator

Import `margoengine/animator` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/animator` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional gameplay animation on the existing `@margoengine/animation` skinning pass. Named states select clips, 1D trees interpolate neighboring samples, and 2D trees use normalized inverse-square distance weights with exact sample reproduction. State transitions crossfade a captured pose into the destination. Masked additive layers apply translation/scale/quaternion and morph deltas relative to a sampled reference pose. A zero reference scale component contributes an identity scale delta on that axis. Primitives sharing a node must have matching morph target counts, as required by glTF.

```ts
import {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
import {loadGLTF} from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';
import {Animation} from 'margoengine/animation';
import {Animator, addCCDChain, type CCDChain} from 'margoengine/animator';
const engine = await EngineKernel.create(document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('#viewport')!, {backend:'webgpu'});
const model = await loadGLTF(engine, '/hero.glb'); // clips named Idle, Walk, Run
const animation = Animation.attach(model);
const animator = Animator.attach(animation, {
  initial:'locomotion', parameters:{speed:0},
  states:{
    locomotion:{parameter:'speed', samples:[{value:0,clip:'Idle'},{value:1,clip:'Walk'},{value:3,clip:'Run'}]},
    idle:'Idle'
  },
  transitions:[{from:'locomotion',to:'idle',when:p=>p.speed<0,duration:0.15}]
});
animator.parameters.speed = 2;
engine.start();
```

For a 2D state use `{parameters:['strafe','forward'],samples:[{value:[0,0],clip:'Idle'},...]}` with unique coordinates. Parameters default to zero. 1D samples must be strictly increasing. Clips loop independently in seconds (`Animation.options.loop` false holds the last frame). `playing = false` pauses state time and crossfades; `Animation.options.speed` scales them, as for Animation playback. `transition(state,duration)` switches states explicitly; predicates are evaluated in declaration order, at most once per frame. Add a layer with `addLayer({clip:'Aim',weight:0.5,mask:[upperBodyNodeIndex,...]})`. Masks use glTF node indices. The returned function removes the layer; mutable weights are validated each frame. `referenceTime` defaults to zero.

`addFootIK({hip,knee,ankle,pole,raycast,offset,probeHeight})` requires a direct three-node leg chain. The callback receives a world-space origin above the current ankle and a downward ray. Return `{position,normal?}` or `null`; supply terrain collision data or an existing BVH. For a BVH raycast, adapt its result to `{position}` or `null`. Normals align the ankle's local +Y with the terrain. Bones/ancestors require positive uniform scales. Unreachable targets clamp to the leg's reach; the pole chooses the knee bend direction. `solveTwoBoneIK()` is also exported as a standalone analytical solver.

## CCD chains (any length)

`addCCDChain(animator, chain)` adds a Cyclic Coordinate Descent IK chain (Wang and Chen 1991) for arms, spines, tails, tentacles or fingers, solved every frame after the pose, additive layers and foot IK. Each sweep goes from the last joint to the first; every joint turns, on its own, so the end effector moves toward the target, then its limit is applied. `joints` lists glTF node indices from the first joint to the last, each the child of the one before. The Animator keeps the chain object and reads `target`, `rotation`, `pole`, `weight` and the solve settings every frame, so move the target by writing into it:

```ts
const joint = (name: string) => model.asset.doc.nodes!.findIndex((node) => node.name === name);
const grab = () => console.log('reached');
const reach: CCDChain = {
  joints: [joint('Shoulder'), joint('Elbow'), joint('Wrist')], // glTF node indices
  target: [0.4, 1.3, 0.5],                   // world space; mutate it per frame
  rotation: null,                            // optional world rotation (x, y, z, w) for the last joint
  pole: [0.3, 1.0, -0.5],                    // optional: the elbow bends toward this point
  tip: [0, 0.08, 0],                         // optional effector offset in the last joint's space
  limits: [
    { type: 'cone', angle: 1.6, twist: [-0.5, 0.5] },        // shoulder: swing cone + twist range
    { type: 'hinge', axis: [1, 0, 0], min: -2.6, max: 0 },  // elbow: one axis, one range
    { type: 'euler', min: [-0.6, -0.3, -1], max: [0.6, 0.3, 1] }, // wrist: per-axis angles (XYZ)
  ],
  iterations: 16, tolerance: 0.001, weight: 1,
  onSolve: (result) => { if (result.reached) grab(); },
};
const remove = addCCDChain(animator, reach);
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/animator.md]

=== @margoengine/kinematics-constraints (packages/kinematics-constraints/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/kinematics-constraints

Import `margoengine/kinematics-constraints` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/kinematics-constraints` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Standalone capsule, sphere and convex hull avoidance for IK targets and two-bone chains. The package projects targets out of proxy volumes, checks elbow and link clearance, and searches a shoulder swivel angle through a caller-supplied IK evaluator. It has no engine, renderer, physics, or Wasm dependency. ESM exports and declarations are tree-shakable; core, stage, animation, and the existing IK kernels remain unchanged.

Version `1.0.0` is source-only and has not been published to npm. From the repository root:

```sh
npm ci
npm run build --workspace @margoengine/kinematics-constraints
npm run test --workspace @margoengine/kinematics-constraints
npm pack --workspace @margoengine/kinematics-constraints --pack-destination test-results
```

Install the resulting tarball in another project with `npm install ./margoengine-kinematics-constraints-1.0.0.tgz`. No core peer dependency is required. The package is Apache-2.0 licensed.

## Interactive arm demo

From the repository root, run:

```sh
npm run modern:dev:extensions
```

Open [http://127.0.0.1:5173/examples/kinematics-constraints.html](http://127.0.0.1:5173/examples/kinematics-constraints.html). If Vite reports a different port, use that port with the same path. Drag the orange request across the torso, overhead, and across the waist. Switch from the capsule torso to a mixed scene with an additional sphere and capsule rail; every full-chain acceptance checks all active volumes.

The compact controls demonstrate full-chain `solve()` versus target-only `resolveTarget()`. Target-only mode hides the arm and explicitly certifies only the green target sphere. The full-chain readout separates the accepted physical gap, accepted pole angle, allowed `min(π, speed * dt)` pole window, actual accepted pole step, accepted hand displacement, and requested-target contact. Hand motion can be nonzero while the transported pole coordinate is unchanged; a held pose reports zero for both accepted displacements. Before solving, the demo conditions large requested translations toward a nominal 0.75 m/s using the configured damping response. This reduces large catch-up steps without rejecting a successful solve after its history has advanced; obstacle/reach projection can still alter displacement, so it is not a certified Cartesian or joint velocity limit. Raw requests outside the operational reach band remain diagnostic. A rejected conditioned request can advance through a smaller local step only if another complete `solve()` succeeds; otherwise the controller holds its last accepted pose. Exact angular overshoot is not exposed by the package and is not invented by the HUD.

Advanced settings expose the caller's live/fixed positive time step, angular search budget, required gap, and target damping time. Changing the scene, required gap, or damping constructs a new solver and starts from a newly validated initial pose; changing speed or search budget preserves solve history. Fixed time is per caller update and is not a display-frame-rate guarantee. The optional 25° shoulder/torso yaw assist is an application adapter, not a feature of the package: the rotationally symmetric torso capsule remains in the same frame while a proposed shoulder position and its complete link chain are checked before being committed together. Rejected shoulder candidates retain the accepted root and pose.

The [demo controller](../../examples/kinematics-constraints-controller.js) includes an analytical elbow callback with reused vector storage. It transports the last accepted bend reference between reach directions, so overhead and cross-body motion keep one continuous angle convention. Pointer rays meet a curved drag surface in front of the torso and waist. The demo renders analytical proxies directly, without character skinning, continuous collision detection, joint acceleration limits, or a physical safety guarantee. Reused buffers do not guarantee that the JavaScript runtime or renderer performs no allocations.


For a motion report, expand **Record a problem**, click **Start recording**, reproduce the issue, then click **Stop recording**. The stopped JSON is readable in the panel and can be downloaded explicitly. The temporary recorder keeps the latest 3,600 frame snapshots plus bounded control actions, including raw, paced and final retry targets, accepted and candidate poses, clearance, pole/hand steps, and caller settings. It stays disabled until started, stores only local in-memory numeric snapshots, and never uploads or saves automatically. Clear removes the captured trace from the panel.


## Controller integration

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/kinematics-constraints.md]

=== @margoengine/rigging (packages/rigging/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/rigging

Import `margoengine/rigging` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/rigging` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Rigging and animation authoring for characters made in Margo or anywhere else: smooth automatic skin weights, weight painting with undo, the skin checks game engines need before export, IK chains with poles and retarget presets that play Mixamo, Godot and Roblox clips on any humanoid. Everything here is plain data in, plain data out: no engine, renderer or GPU is needed, core is never imported, and an app that does not import this package ships none of it.

## Automatic weights (bone heat)

`boneHeatWeights(mesh, joints)` gives every vertex smooth weights from a rest skeleton, by bone heat diffusion (I. Baran and J. Popović, "Automatic rigging and animation of 3D characters", SIGGRAPH 2007). Each joint moves the vertices around its bone, the segment from the joint to each child (a point at a leaf joint), and weights blend smoothly across joints. Weights are 0 or more and sum to 1 per vertex. Heat only reaches a vertex from bones it can see, so an arm's weight does not leak into the hip it hangs beside.

```ts
import { boneHeatWeights, checkSkin, type RigJoint } from 'margoengine/rigging';

// Any triangle mesh (positions xyz, optional indices) and a rest skeleton in the same space.
const positions = new Float32Array([0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0]);
const indices = new Uint32Array([0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3]);
const joints: RigJoint[] = [
  { name: 'hips', parent: -1, position: [0.5, 0, 0] },
  { name: 'spine', parent: 0, position: [0.5, 1, 0] },
  { name: 'head', parent: 1, position: [0.5, 2, 0] },
];
const weights = await boneHeatWeights({ positions, indices }, joints, { visibility: false });
const { joints: JOINTS_0, weights: WEIGHTS_0 } = weights.toInfluences(4); // glTF's four strongest per vertex
console.log(JOINTS_0.length, WEIGHTS_0.length); // 16 16
console.log(checkSkin({ weights: weights.toInfluences(4), joints }).ok); // true
```

Options, each with its default:

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `skip` | `[]` | Joints (indices or names) that move no vertices, such as a root at the feet. |
| `visibility` | `true` | Heat only from visible bones; uses `@margoengine/bvh`, loaded on first use. `false` takes the nearest bone (faster; fine for convex parts). Or pass `(from, to) => boolean`. |
| `heat` | `1` | Heat constant c in H = c / d². Larger keeps vertices closer to their nearest bone. |
| `weld` | `1e-6` | Vertices closer than this fraction of the mesh size are one point, so weights cross UV seams and split faces. |
| `tolerance` | `1e-6` | Largest weight error per vertex when a bone's solve stops. |
| `maxIterations` | `2000` | Conjugate-gradient iterations per bone; a `MargoError` with code `failed` when not enough. |
| `threshold` | `1e-4` | Weights below this share are dropped before renormalising. |
| `signal` | none | `AbortSignal`; the promise rejects with its reason. The solve yields to the event loop every 30 ms. |

Vertices at one position always get the same weights. Pass `joints` from `@margoengine/exporters/skin`'s `humanoidJoints()`, or turn any glTF skeleton into joints with `rigJoints(retargetRig(model))`.

## Weight painting

`WeightPainter` paints a `WeightMap` with brush dabs: `add`, `subtract`, `replace` (toward `value`) and `smooth` (toward the neighbours' average). Each dab keeps every vertex it touches summing to 1: when one bone gains or loses weight, the other unlocked bones on that vertex make up the difference. Locked bones never change. Every stroke returns its undo.

```ts
import { WeightMap, WeightPainter } from 'margoengine/rigging';

const mesh = { positions: new Float32Array([0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0]), indices: new Uint32Array([0, 1, 2]) };
const map = new WeightMap(3, 2, [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]);
const painter = new WeightPainter(map, mesh, { parents: [-1, 0], locked: [] });
const stroke = painter.stroke({ mode: 'add', bone: 1, center: [0, 1, 0], radius: 0.8, strength: 0.5, falloff: 'smooth' });
painter.smoothAll({ iterations: 2, strength: 0.5 });
stroke.undo(); // undo strokes newest first
painter.normalize();
```

| Stroke field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | required | `add`, `subtract`, `replace` or `smooth`. |
| `bone` | required except for `smooth` | The bone painted. |
| `center`, `radius` | required | Brush sphere in mesh space. |
| `strength` | `0.5` | Amount at the centre (0-1). |
| `value` | `1` | `replace`'s target weight. |
| `falloff` | `smooth` | `smooth` (smoothstep), `linear` or `constant`. |

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/rigging.md]

=== @margoengine/tween (packages/tween/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/tween

Import `margoengine/tween` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/tween` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Numeric property interpolation and easing; `update` steps the existing tracks in place and creates no per-track objects.

```ts
import {Tween, easeInOutCubic} from 'margoengine/tween';
const timeline = new Tween();
const cancel = timeline.to(object, 'opacity', 1, {duration: 0.5, easing: easeInOutCubic});
timeline.update(1 / 60);
```

Times are seconds. delay, onComplete, zero-duration tracks and cancellation are supported. A new track for the same object/property cancels the old one. Callback-created tracks begin next update; clear cancels all tracks. Completed/cancelled tracks compact in place. Track creation and callbacks can allocate; the in-place stepping above does not cover them. Targets are numeric writable properties; for colours, quaternions and paths use `array`, `path` or `custom` (below). CSS strings are not parsed.

## Repeat, yoyo, easings, springs, timelines, colours, paths

```ts
import {Tween, Timeline, Spring, easeOutBack, cubicBezier, parseHexColor, toHexColor, slerpArray, catmullRomPath} from 'margoengine/tween';
declare const light: {intensity: number}, door: {angle: number}, camera: {position: number[]}, node: {rotation: number[]};
const tween = new Tween();
tween.to(light, 'intensity', 3, {duration: 1, repeat: Infinity, yoyo: true, easing: cubicBezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)});
const colour = parseHexColor('#ff0000');
tween.array(colour, parseHexColor('#0000ff'), {duration: 2}); // toHexColor(colour) while it runs
tween.array(node.rotation, [0, 0.7071, 0, 0.7071], {duration: 1, interpolate: slerpArray}); // quaternions
tween.path(camera.position, catmullRomPath([[0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 0], [3, 2, 1]]), {duration: 3});
tween.custom((progress) => console.log(progress), {duration: 1, easing: easeOutBack});

const timeline = new Timeline({repeat: 1})
  .to(door, 'angle', 1.5, {duration: 0.6})
  .label('open')
  .to(light, 'intensity', 3, {duration: 0.4, at: 'open'})
  .call(() => console.log('opened'))
  .play();

const spring = new Spring({stiffness: 120, damping: 12});
spring.target = 1;
const frame = (dt: number) => { tween.update(dt); timeline.update(dt); return spring.update(dt); };
```

- `repeat` (integer or `Infinity`), `yoyo` and `onRepeat` work on every tween kind.
- Easings: `ease{In,Out,InOut}` of `Quad`, `Cubic`, `Quart`, `Quint`, `Sine`, `Expo`, `Circ`, `Back`, `Elastic`, `Bounce`, plus `cubicBezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)` (CSS timing function) and `steps(n)`.
- `Spring` steps the exact damped-oscillator solution, so any frame time is stable and a new `target` keeps the velocity.
- `Timeline` chains tweens and callbacks with labels (`at: 'open+0.2'`), `seek`, `pause`, `reverse`, `speed`, `repeat` and `yoyo`. A property's start value is read when the playhead first reaches its entry; seeking back restores values. Callbacks run on `update`, never on `seek`.

## smoothDamp: follow a moving target

`smoothDamp(current, target, velocity, smoothTime, maxSpeed, dt, out)` eases a vector (a camera, a follower, a hand) toward a target with no oscillation, and keeps its `velocity` between frames so a moving target stays smooth. It is a critically damped spring solved exactly, so any frame time is stable, and it works on `Float32Array`, `Float64Array` or plain arrays of any length without creating objects.

```ts
import {smoothDamp} from 'margoengine/tween';
const position = new Float32Array(3), velocity = new Float32Array(3), target = new Float32Array([0, 1.6, 4]);
const frame = (dt: number) => smoothDamp(position, target, velocity, 0.3, 6, dt, position); // 0.3 s to arrive, at most 6 units/s
frame(1 / 60);
```

- `smoothTime` is roughly the seconds to arrive. Zero lands on the target at once and zeroes `velocity`.
- `maxSpeed` limits the length of the whole velocity vector (units per second), so the direction of travel is kept. Pass `Infinity` for no limit; 0 holds the point still.
- Each component matches a `Spring` with stiffness `(2 / smoothTime)^2` and damping `4 / smoothTime`, so a velocity heading toward the target can overshoot once, as the spring does.
- `dt` 0 copies `current` to `out` and leaves `velocity` alone; a negative, NaN or infinite `dt`, a non-finite value or mismatched lengths throw `RangeError`. A very long `dt` arrives at rest instead of producing NaN.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/tween

## Speed

10,000 `spring.update(dt)` calls take 0.28 ms in Node on the development PC, with no allocation per call, so a spring per object is fine:

```ts
import {Spring} from 'margoengine/tween';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/tween.md]

=== @margoengine/cinematic (packages/cinematic/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/cinematic

Import `margoengine/cinematic` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/cinematic` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

`rig.setOrbitOffset(yaw, pitch, distance, height = 0)` writes the retained camera
offset in place from orbit angles (no new vector is created). The sandbox uses this
public method after its shared locomotion step.

A virtual camera with analytically integrated critically damped follow and look-at springs plus additive screen shake.

```ts
import {Cinematic} from 'margoengine/cinematic';
const rig = Cinematic.attach(engine, {offset: [0,3,6], damping: 6});
rig.follow(player);
rig.shake(0.2, 0.4);
```

follow accepts a live mesh from the attached engine or a world-position tuple. Mesh targets use world transforms. Shake amplitude is in world units and duration is seconds; it does not alter the settled spring position. The frame plugin owns camera position/target while attached, so disable competing camera controls. dispose detaches it.

Scope the rig with `using` (it calls `dispose()` and returns the camera to your controls):

```ts
import {Cinematic} from 'margoengine/cinematic';
{
  using rig = Cinematic.attach(engine, {offset: [0, 3, 6]});
  rig.follow([0, 1.6, 0]);
  rig.update(1 / 60);
}
```

Errors name their fix: a bad argument throws `RangeError` or `TypeError` (for example `Invalid camera delta; pass a finite delta of 0 or more seconds`), and attaching a rig twice throws `MargoError` with code `attached`.

Set `ground: (x,z) => height` to keep the camera arm above a CPU heightfield.
`clearance` defaults to 0.65 world units. The rig checks both its desired arm and
the resulting damped/shaken camera, without changing your requested `offset`.
For a below-target orbit, it raises the rendered aim point with the camera so
terrain clearance preserves upward look instead of forcing the view back down.
Six samples along each arm suit broad terrain; narrow ridges and buildings need
collision geometry. Heights must be finite. Ground handling is disabled by default.

Walls and ceilings: set `collide: (origin, direction, distance) => hitDistance | null`. Each frame
the rig asks for the first obstacle along the arm from the look-at point to the (damped, shaken,
ground-lifted) camera; on a hit the camera moves in at once to `clearance` short of it, and once the
arm is clear it eases back out at the follow damping. The spring state and your `offset` are
unchanged. The arrays passed in are reused each frame. Any scene query fits, for example a sphere
cast against the physics world (so the near plane does not clip into the wall):

```ts
const rig = Cinematic.attach(engine, {offset: [0, 3, 6], clearance: 0.3,
  collide: (o, d, max) => physics.shapeCast({shape: 'sphere', radius: 0.2}, [o[0], o[1], o[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1], [d[0], d[1], d[2]], {maxDistance: max, excludeDynamic: true})?.distance});
```

or `@margoengine/bvh`'s Raycaster (`firstHitOnly`, `far = max`) over the level. Exclude the followed
character from the query, and start it above the floor if the look-at point sits on it (the arm
starts at the target, usually the character's feet).

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/cinematic

=== @margoengine/cutscene (packages/cutscene/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/cutscene

Import `margoengine/cutscene` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/cutscene` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

A timeline sequencer for cutscenes and in-game cinematics: tracks of keys and clips in a JSON document, a pure
`evaluate(t)` that gives the whole scene state at any time, and a player with play, pause, reverse, speed, scrubbing,
skip and fast-forward that fires every event in order. It renders nothing itself and imports nothing heavy: apply the
state to your camera, objects, animation mixer, audio and UI.

```ts
import { Camera } from 'margoengine/core';
import { CutscenePlayer, type CutsceneDocument } from 'margoengine/cutscene';

const intro: CutsceneDocument = {
  format: 'margo-cutscene',
  version: 1,
  duration: 6,
  markers: [{ time: 3, name: 'reveal' }],
  tracks: [
    {
      type: 'camera',
      id: 'cam',
      keys: [
        { time: 0, position: [0, 2, 8], target: [0, 1, 0] },
        { time: 3, position: [5, 3, 4], target: [0, 1, 0], ease: 'easeInOutCubic' },
        { time: 4, position: [0, 1.6, 2], target: [0, 1.5, 0], fov: 35, cut: true },
      ],
    },
    { type: 'transform', id: 'door', target: 'door', keys: [{ time: 3, rotation: [0, 0, 0, 1] }, { time: 4, rotation: [0, 0.7071, 0, 0.7071] }] },
    { type: 'animation', id: 'hero', target: 'hero', clips: [{ start: 0, duration: 6, clip: 'Walk', loop: true, length: 1.2 }] },
    { type: 'audio', id: 'music', clips: [{ start: 0, duration: 6, sound: 'theme', fadeIn: 1 }] },
    { type: 'subtitle', id: 'subs', clips: [{ start: 1, duration: 2, text: 'Someone left the door open.', speaker: 'Ada' }] },
    { type: 'event', id: 'cues', events: [{ time: 3.5, name: 'spawnBats', data: { count: 12 } }] },
  ],
};

const camera = new Camera();
const player = new CutscenePlayer(intro);
player.on('event', (event) => console.log('event', event.name, event.data));
player.on('marker', (marker) => console.log('marker', marker.name));
const done = player.play();

// Each frame:
player.update(1 / 60);
const state = player.state;
if (state.camera) {
  camera.position = state.camera.position;
  camera.target = state.camera.target;
  camera.fov = state.camera.fov;
  camera.up = state.camera.up;
}
// state.transforms.door.rotation, state.animations, state.audio, state.subtitles: apply them the same way.

player.skip(); // "Skip cutscene": jumps to the end and still fires spawnBats and the marker, in order.
await done; // true: it finished
```

## Tracks

Every track has an `id` (unique in its timeline) and may be `muted`. Key tracks interpolate between keys sorted by
`time`, holding the first value before the first key and the last after the last; `ease` on a key shapes the move into
it (`'linear'` default, `'step'`, `'smoothstep'`, any `ease*` easing of `@margoengine/tween` such as
`'easeOutBack'`, or cubic-bezier points `[x1, y1, x2, y2]`). Clip tracks hold spans `start` + `duration` (start
inclusive, end exclusive) that may overlap.

| Track | Fields | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `camera` | `keys: [{time, position, target, fov?, roll?, ease?, cut?}]`, `path` (`'catmull-rom'` default, `'linear'`) | `camera`: `position`, `target`, `fov` (degrees, default 60), `roll`, `up` |
| `transform` | `target`, `keys: [{time, position?, rotation?, scale?, ease?}]` | `transforms[target]`; each channel among the keys that set it; rotations slerp |
| `property` | `target`, `property`, `keys: [{time, value, ease?}]` (a number or an array) | `properties[target][property]` |
| `animation` | `target`, `clips: [{start, duration, clip, speed?, offset?, loop?, length?, blendIn?, blendOut?}]` | `animations`: clip name, clip time and blend weight |
| `audio` | `clips: [{start, duration, sound, volume?, offset?, fadeIn?, fadeOut?}]` | `audio`: sound, time into it, volume |
| `subtitle` | `clips: [{start, duration, text, speaker?}]` | `subtitles` |
| `event` | `events: [{time, name, data?}]` | fired by the player |
| `timeline` | `clips: [{start, duration, timeline, speed?, offset?}]` naming one of the document's `timelines` | the nested timeline's state, merged in |

Camera keys with `cut: true` jump instead of moving there, and the Catmull-Rom path never bends across a cut, so one
track holds a whole edit. The first unmuted camera track wins; a later transform or property track wins a channel two
tracks key. Markers name points in time; `state.marker` is the last one passed.

Nested timelines live under `timelines` and are placed by timeline clips with their own speed and offset; they may
nest (up to 16 levels, no cycles). Their tracks report paths like `intro/sfx`. A nested clip cut by the window of
its timeline clip still enters and exits, at the window's edges.

## Evaluating, scrubbing and seeking

```ts
import { Cutscene } from 'margoengine/cutscene';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/cutscene.md]

=== @margoengine/controls (packages/controls/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/controls

Import `margoengine/controls` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/controls` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

`stepLocomotion(state, actions, delta, height, options?)` provides ground-following
character movement with normalized diagonals, damped speed and heading, and a
50 ms movement-step limit. Retained state is `[x,y,z,heading,cameraYaw,cameraPitch,
gaitPhase,speed]`; actions are `[strafe,forward,lookX,lookY,sprint]`.
Options include `bounds: [minX,maxX,minZ,maxZ]`, `minHeight`, `walkSpeed` (3.4),
and `runSpeed` (7). Bounds and minimum height are omitted by default. Look values
are angular deltas; pitch stays between -1.4 (look up) and 0.9 radians (look down).
Use `Cinematic` ground clearance to keep upward-looking cameras above terrain. Height samples must
be finite. The caller owns input bindings, character meshes and gait animation.

```ts
import {stepLocomotion} from 'margoengine/controls';

const state = new Float32Array(8);                    // x, y, z, heading, cameraYaw, cameraPitch, gaitPhase, speed
const actions = new Float32Array([0, 1, 0, 0, 0]);    // strafe, forward, lookX, lookY, sprint: walk forward
const ground = (x: number, z: number) => 0.1 * Math.sin(x) * Math.cos(z); // any finite height sampler
for (let frame = 0; frame < 60; frame++) stepLocomotion(state, actions, 1 / 60, ground, {bounds: [-50, 50, -50, 50]});
console.log(state[0], state[2]);                      // where the walker is after one second
```

Bad inputs throw a `RangeError` that says what to pass (finite numbers, bounds with min below max).

Orbit, map, trackball, arcball, fly, first-person and pointer-lock camera controls plus an interactive transform gizmo and drag controls for Margo Engine, each tree-shakable on its own. `DragControls` uses `@margoengine/bvh` (a peer dependency) for its hits.

Build from source with `npm run build` in `packages/controls`.

```ts
import {Engine, box} from 'margoengine/core';
import {OrbitControls, TransformControls} from 'margoengine/controls';

const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);
const mesh = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box());

// Passing the engine attaches to engine.canvas and updates before every render.
const orbit = OrbitControls.attach(engine);
orbit.enableDamping = true;

const gizmo = TransformControls.attach(engine, {mode: 'translate', translationSnap: 0.25});
gizmo.attach(mesh);
gizmo.addEventListener('dragging-changed', event => {orbit.enabled = !event.value;});
addEventListener('keydown', event => {if (event.key === 'r') gizmo.setMode('rotate');});

engine.start();

// On teardown (engine.dispose() also disposes both):
gizmo.dispose(); orbit.dispose();
```

Drag core meshes and gltf-pro models (a model moves by its `root`), with the mouse or touch:

```ts
import {Engine, box} from 'margoengine/core';
import {DragControls, OrbitControls} from 'margoengine/controls';
import {loadGLTF} from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';

const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const mesh = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box());
const part = await loadGLTF(engine, '/part.glb');
const drag = DragControls.attach(engine, [mesh, part]);          // created before OrbitControls: a grab stops the orbit drag
const orbit = OrbitControls.attach(engine);
drag.plane = [0, 1, 0];                                        // slide on the ground; default 'view' faces the camera
drag.axis = [1, 0, 0];                                         // or only along world X
drag.addEventListener('dragstart', event => console.log(event.object, event.hit)); // hit: a bvh RaycasterHit
drag.addEventListener('hoveron', () => {engine.canvas.style.cursor = 'grab';});
drag.addEventListener('hoveroff', () => {engine.canvas.style.cursor = '';});
```

## Walkthroughs and simple games: `@margoengine/controls/walk`

`WalkControls` is a Wasm-free kinematic first-person walker: eye height held above the floor, stairs, slopes, walls,
glass, jump and crouch, keyboard + mouse, gamepad and touch, and an orbit "dollhouse" view and back. It collides on the
CPU against the cached triangle trees of the `@margoengine/bvh` Raycaster (core meshes, gltf-pro and materials models),
so it costs nothing unless you import its entry. A whole recipe: [docs/guides/walkthrough.md](../../docs/guides/walkthrough.md).

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {loadGLTF} from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';
import {WalkControls} from 'margoengine/controls/walk';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/controls.md]

=== @margoengine/cameras (packages/cameras/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/cameras

Import `margoengine/cameras` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/cameras` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Orthographic projection and exactly vertical (top-down and bottom-up) views for core's camera, for CAD, plans, maps
and isometric views. Culling, `engine.pick`, selection, bvh rays, TAA and every pass that reads `camera.matrix` see the
same view. It uses core's `camera.project` and `camera.up` hooks.

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {CameraProjection} from 'margoengine/cameras';

const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, {camera: {position: [0, 40, 0], target: [0, 0, 0]}}); // straight down
const projection = CameraProjection.attach(engine); // orthographic, framed like the perspective view at the target

projection.mode = 'perspective';             // toggle at any time; vertical views keep working
projection.mode = 'orthographic';
projection.height = 12;                      // or fix the visible world height (resize widens with the aspect)
projection.zoom = 2;
projection.fit(model.bounds);                // frame a box: [minX, minY, minZ, maxX, maxY, maxZ], animated
```

- **Fitting**: `fit(bounds, {aspect, duration, padding})` takes the flat bounds array models carry (no slicing into
  min/max). Orthographic: the view direction and distance stay, the box centre moves to the view centre and `zoom` is
  set so the box's projected outline (not a bounding sphere) fills the view less `padding` (default 1.1), honouring
  `height` or `left`/`right`/`top`/`bottom`. Perspective: core's `fitToBoundingBox`. `aspect` defaults to the engine
  canvas, `duration` to 0.3 s; the engine advances the animation (after `attach(camera)` call `onPreUpdate(delta)`
  yourself). Throws `Bounds exceed far` when the box does not fit the default depth range (`camera.far` deep).

- **Parameters**: `left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom` (all four replace `height` and
  the canvas aspect, so update them on resize), `zoom` (divides the frustum about its centre), `near`, `far` (eye-space, may be negative).
  Without `height` or bounds the visible height is `2 · distance · tan(fov / 2)`: the perspective framing at the target,
  so `fitToBoundingBox`, core's `CADCameraControls` and `@margoengine/controls` dolly become ortho zoom and pan tracks
  the cursor exactly. Without `near`/`far` the depth range is `camera.far` deep and centred on the target (Blender's
  convention), so zooming in never clips a model at the eye.
- **Fixed size.** With an explicit `height` or all four bounds, `projection.fixedOrthographic` (also readable on the
  attached camera) is true: dolly changes only the distance, so `@margoengine/controls` zoom-to-cursor adds no pan.
- **Depth** is reversed-Z on WebGPU (near 1, far 0) like core, and -1..1 on WebGL. Orthographic depth is linear.
- **Vertical views**: core's `Camera.update` throws `Vertical camera` when the view is parallel to `camera.up`, which with the default +Y up means looking straight up or down. With the plugin,
  such a view renders exactly vertical with screen up = `up` (default `[0, 0, -1]`, north up looking down; it needs a
  horizontal component). While attached, `camera.up` reads as `up` for such views (horizontal part at most 1e-9 of the
  distance) and as the world up (`[0, 1, 0]`) otherwise; assigning `camera.up` sets that world up. The position is
  not moved, and passes that rebuild the view (shadows, SSAO, gltf-pro) read `camera.up` too. Orbit controls stay
  1e-6 rad from the pole, so orbiting never snaps the roll.
- **Culling** is exact and stays on: core derives the culling planes from the matrix the `project` hook builds. No
  `culling: false` and no extra cost.
- **Detecting it**: `camera.matrix` is orthographic when entries 3, 7 and 11 are zero.
- `attach(camera)` drives a camera without an engine; `dispose()` (or `engine.removePlugin('cameras')`) restores core's
  `project` (unset) and a plain `up` field. Attaching to a camera whose `project` is already set throws.

Errors name their fix. Argument problems throw `RangeError` or `TypeError` (for example `Invalid fit; pass min <= max, aspect > 0, duration >= 0 and padding >= 1, all finite`). Branch on `error.code` for the rest: `attached` (a projection or camera already in use) and `state` (a `FloatingOrigin` used before `engine.use(origin)`).

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/cameras.md]

=== @margoengine/input (packages/input/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/input

Import `margoengine/input` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/input` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Semantic actions combine keyboard codes, mouse buttons and relative motion, gamepad axes/buttons, and touch controls.

```ts
import {Input} from 'margoengine/input';
const input = new Input({jump: [{type: 'key', code: 'Space'}]});
input.update();
const {pressed, value} = input.state('jump');
```

Call update once per simulation tick. State objects are reused. Opposing bindings sum and clamp to -1..1; gamepad axes use a configurable deadzone. createStick(parent, id) creates a pointer-captured virtual stick; bindTouchButton(button, id) supports pointer and keyboard activation. rumble(durationMs, strength, gamepadIndex) returns false when no actuator is available. dispose removes listeners and owned stick elements. Editable fields do not trigger gameplay key-down actions. Mouse motion is relative, not an absolute screen cursor.

## Chords, contexts, rebinding and prompts

```ts
import {Input, bindingLabel} from 'margoengine/input';
const input = new Input(
  {
    jump: [{type: 'key', code: 'Space'}],
    save: [{type: 'key', code: 'KeyS', modifiers: ['ctrl']}],
    confirm: [{type: 'key', code: 'Enter'}],
  },
  {contexts: {game: ['jump'], menu: ['confirm']}},
);
input.setContext('game', false); // a menu opened: jump reads 0 and releases; confirm keeps working
const prompt = bindingLabel(input.actions.save[0]); // "Ctrl+S"; gamepad buttons use 'xbox' | 'playstation' | 'generic' names
const binding = await input.captureBinding({signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)}); // "press a key to rebind"
input.rebind('jump', [binding]);
localStorage.setItem('bindings', JSON.stringify(input.exportBindings()));
input.importBindings(localStorage.getItem('bindings')!); // unknown actions are ignored; invalid data changes nothing
input.resetBindings();
```

- `modifiers` (`'shift' | 'ctrl' | 'alt' | 'meta'`) on a `key` binding makes a chord: the key counts only while every modifier is held.
- `contexts` (option) group actions; an action owned by contexts reads 0 unless one is enabled. Unlisted actions are always active.
- `captureBinding` resolves with the next key (with held modifiers), mouse button or gamepad button; Escape or the signal rejects with `AbortError`.

## Gestures

```ts
import {Gestures} from 'margoengine/input';
declare const canvas: HTMLCanvasElement;
let zoom = 1;
using gestures = new Gestures(canvas, {swipeDistance: 60});
gestures.on('pinch', (e) => (zoom *= e.scale!));
gestures.on('swipe', (e) => console.log(e.direction, e.velocity));
gestures.on('doubletap', () => (zoom = 1));
```

Touch and pen only (mouse never triggers them, so they never fight orbit controls): `tap`, `doubletap`, `swipe` (direction and px/s), two-finger `pinch` (scale since the last event) and `rotate` (radians). Thresholds are options with defaults. Set `touch-action: none` on the element.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/input

=== @margoengine/ui (packages/ui/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/ui

Import `margoengine/ui` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/ui` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Game UI that is drawn inside the engine, so it works in fullscreen and in exported games, with no DOM on top of the
canvas:

- **Widgets:** panels, labels, buttons, toggles, sliders, progress and health bars, lists, inventory grids, menus,
  dialogs, toasts and tooltips.
- **Layout:** anchors, flex-style rows and columns, grids, scrolling, safe areas.
- **Scaling:** a reference resolution, the device pixel ratio and the user's text size, with text that stays sharp
  because it is drawn by `@margoengine/text` as signed distance fields.
- **Themes:** a good-looking dark theme by default, a light theme, a high contrast theme, and `createTheme` for your own.
  All status colours come from the colour-blind-safe Okabe-Ito palette and meaning never rests on colour alone.

The package is optional and tree-shakable and adds nothing to core. `Ui` holds the widgets and produces a list of
rectangles and text in pixels; it touches neither the GPU nor the DOM, so it runs in Node and in tests.
`UiRenderer` is the engine plugin that draws that list on WebGPU. On the WebGL2 backend it warns once and draws nothing.

```ts
import { Engine } from '@margoengine/core';
import { Ui, UiRenderer, Menu } from '@margoengine/ui';

const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const ui = new Ui(); // dark theme, 1 UI unit = 1 CSS pixel, system font
UiRenderer.attach(engine, ui); // steps the UI every frame and draws it over the finished frame

ui.add(
  new Menu({
    title: 'Paused',
    items: [
      { label: 'Resume', onSelect: () => ui.toast('Back in the game') },
      { label: 'Quit', onSelect: async () => (await ui.confirm('Quit to the title screen?')) && location.reload() },
    ],
  }),
);
```

## Building a screen

Every widget is a class you construct with an options object. Put them in a `Panel` (a column by default) and add the
panel to `ui`. Layout options are on every widget.

```ts
import { Ui, Panel, Label, Button, Toggle, Slider } from '@margoengine/ui';

const ui = new Ui();
const settings = new Panel({
  background: 'surface',
  border: true,
  shadow: true,
  padding: 24,
  gap: 12,
  width: 360,
  anchor: 'center',
  children: [
    new Label({ text: 'Settings', size: 'title' }),
    new Slider({ text: 'Volume', value: 0.8, onChange: (e) => console.log('volume', e.value) }),
    new Toggle({ text: 'Subtitles', checked: true, onChange: (e) => console.log('subtitles', e.value) }),
    new Button({ text: 'Done', variant: 'primary', onClick: () => settings.removeFromParent() }),
  ],
});
ui.add(settings);
```

`on(type, handler)` works on every widget and returns a function that unsubscribes; it is also disposable, so
`using off = button.on('click', fn)` ends the subscription at the end of the block. Option callbacks (`onClick`,
`onChange`, `onSelect`) are shortcuts for `on('click' | 'change' | 'select', ...)`.

## Layout

Sizes are UI units. By default one unit is one CSS pixel; see Scaling.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `direction` | `'column'` | `'row'`, `'column'`, `'stack'` (children anchored over each other) or `'grid'` |
| `gap` | `0` | space between children; a number or `[column gap, row gap]` |
| `align` | stretch (column), center (row) | cross-axis placement: `'start'`, `'center'`, `'end'`, `'stretch'` |
| `justify` | `'start'` | main-axis placement: `'start'`, `'center'`, `'end'`, `'space-between'`, `'space-around'`, `'space-evenly'` |
| `padding`, `margin` | `0` | a number, `[vertical, horizontal]` or `[top, right, bottom, left]` |
| `width`, `height` | `'auto'` | a number, `'auto'` (fit content), `'fill'` or a percentage such as `'50%'` |
| `minWidth`, `maxWidth`, `minHeight`, `maxHeight` | none | bounds in UI units |
| `grow`, `shrink` | `0`, `1` | shares of the free or missing main-axis space |
| `alignSelf` | the parent's `align` | cross-axis placement of this child |
| `anchor` | `'stretch'` in a stack | `'top-left'`, `'top'`, `'top-right'`, `'left'`, `'center'`, `'right'`, `'bottom-left'`, `'bottom'`, `'bottom-right'` or `'stretch'`; `margin` is the distance from the edges |
| `position` | `'flow'` | `'absolute'` takes the child out of a row or column and anchors it |
| `offset` | `[0, 0]` | shift after layout, for animation |
| `bleed` | `false` | in a stack, ignore the parent's padding and the safe area |
| `columns`, `cellWidth`, `cellHeight` | `1`, widest, tallest | for `direction: 'grid'` |
| `overflow` | `'visible'` | `'hidden'` clips; `'scroll'` clips and scrolls on the main axis |

The screen layer is a stack, so a widget with an `anchor` sits at that corner or edge of the screen, inside the safe area:

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/ui.md]

=== @margoengine/viewcube (packages/viewcube/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/viewcube

Import `margoengine/viewcube` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/viewcube` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

A CAD orientation cube for Margo Engine: a small cube in a corner of the view that turns with the camera. Click a face,
edge or corner and the camera animates around its target to that view (Top, Front, Right, ..., the twelve edge views
and the eight isometric corners), keeping the distance. With `@margoengine/cameras` it also toggles perspective and
orthographic projection.

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {CameraProjection} from 'margoengine/cameras';
import {OrbitControls} from 'margoengine/controls';
import {ViewCube} from 'margoengine/viewcube';

const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);           // the canvas needs a parent element; the cube is placed in it
const projection = CameraProjection.attach(engine, {mode: 'perspective'});
OrbitControls.attach(engine);                             // or core's CADCameraControls
const cube = ViewCube.attach(engine, {projection});       // omit projection to hide the toggle

cube.view('top');                                      // 'top' | 'bottom' | 'front' | 'back' | 'left' | 'right' | 'iso'
cube.view([1, 1, 0]);                                  // any direction from the target toward the camera
cube.view('front', 0);                                 // jump without animating
cube.setProjection('orthographic');
cube.dispose();                                        // engine.dispose() also disposes it
```

Options: `container` (default: the canvas's parent; made `position: relative` if it is static), `corner`
(`'top-right'` default, `'top-left'`, `'bottom-right'`, `'bottom-left'`), `size` (cube edge in CSS pixels, 80),
`duration` (seconds, 0.4), `projection` (a CameraProjection, or anything with `mode`), `labels` (face names, for
translation), `flip` (false; also a public field: clicking the view already shown turns to the opposite one, as
Blender's navigation gizmo and SolidWorks' "Normal To" pressed twice do; Autodesk's ViewCube keeps the view).
`@margoengine/controls` navigation profiles carry it: `ViewCube.attach(engine, {...BLENDER.viewCube})`. The toggle
also follows projection changes made elsewhere (Blender's numpad 5 through a profile) on the next frame.
`cube.element` is the widget root for your own styling.

- **Orientation.** World Y is up, front is +Z, right is +X (glTF and Blender exports). Top shows X right and -Z up,
  bottom X right and +Z up, from whichever side the camera comes, because the animation interpolates azimuth and
  elevation the way OrbitControls moves. Top and bottom are exactly vertical: on the pole the cube sets `camera.up` to
  the screen up of the way it came (arrow keys turn it there) and puts the previous up back as soon as the camera
  leaves the pole, or on `dispose` (then 1e-6 rad off the pole, same image). An up it did not set is left alone, such as
  a CameraProjection's vertical `up`. OrbitControls and CADCameraControls leave an exact pole at azimuth 0, so after a
  top view reached from the side they start from the front.
- **Engine views.** `ViewCube.attach(engine, {view: {camera, viewport}})` turns that view's camera and sits in the chosen corner of its rectangle (the cube's container must cover the canvas). One cube per view.
- **Controls.** The cube writes `camera.position` (and `camera.up` on the poles); OrbitControls, MapControls and core's CADCameraControls read
  the camera each frame, so they keep working. Any other camera change during an animation (a drag, a wheel) cancels it.
  A running `fitToBoundingBox` animation is cancelled when a view starts.
- **Accessibility.** The root is a labelled group. The six faces are buttons named "Front view", "Top view", ...; only
  faces turned toward the viewer are in the tab order (screen readers reach all six). Arrow keys step the view 45°
  around and over the target, Home goes to the isometric view, Enter or Space activates the focused face. Edge and
  corner hot spots are pointer targets with tooltips. The projection toggle is a button with `aria-pressed`.
- **Rendering.** Plain DOM and CSS 3D transforms: no GPU work, no extra pass, crisp text at any DPR, works on WebGPU
  and WebGL2. The cube turns in a frame-graph step after every control has moved the camera, so it never lags a frame,
  and touches the DOM only when the orientation changed.

Why a separate package and not `@margoengine/controls`: the cube is a DOM widget that drives any camera controller
(including core's CADCameraControls, which does not use controls) and optionally `@margoengine/cameras`; keeping it
out leaves controls' bundle and dependencies unchanged.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/viewcube.md]

=== @margoengine/selection (packages/selection/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/selection

Import `margoengine/selection` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/selection` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Visible core and PBR selection outlines using Jump Flood Algorithm distance fields or circular morphological dilation. `Selection.set` discovers glTF Pro/FBX buffers from their loader-owned mesh nodes; no separate outline registration is required.

```ts
import {Selection} from 'margoengine/selection';
const selection = Selection.attach(engine, {algorithm: 'jfa', width: 3, color: [1,0.5,0]});
selection.set([mesh]);
```

`Picking.attach(engine)` enables faster `engine.pick(x, y)` in canvas CSS pixels:

```ts
import {Picking} from 'margoengine/selection';
const picking = Picking.attach(engine);
const mesh = await engine.pick(x, y);
```

The standard core PBR draw writes a second `r32uint` attachment in the same pass, with no extra draw calls. A pick copies a clipped 3×3 neighborhood from that frame when camera, mesh identities, geometry, transforms, visibility, materials and frame-graph revision match. Otherwise it renders a 3×3 micro frustum, rejecting each instance's bounding sphere before batching the survivors. The sphere test stays conservative under nonuniform scale, mirrored transforms and hierarchy shear. Zero means background; stored IDs are core slots plus one, so slot zero remains selectable.

The center wins. For an empty center, orthogonal neighbors win before diagonals, with a deterministic tie order. Coordinates and neighbors are bounded to the canvas. Readback remains asynchronous and one pick may be pending at a time. A reusable 768-byte staging buffer accommodates WebGPU's 256-byte row pitch. Device restoration recreates resources; removal or engine disposal frees them.

`Picking.attach(engine, {capture: false})` leaves the frame untouched (no second color target, no per-frame mesh snapshot) and renders the culled 3x3 pass for every pick; use it when picks are rare and frame rate matters more. Custom scene pipelines fall back to the micro pass; sections also use that pass so mutable core clipping uniforms stay current. Other mutable custom shader effects should render their changed state before picking. The cached ID texture costs four bytes per viewport pixel; the package remains optional and tree-shakable.

## Many points at once

`picking.pickMany(points)` answers many canvas CSS pixels from one GPU readback, where a loop of `engine.pick` waits for one
readback each. It answers what `engine.pick` answers, as `PickHit`s, in
order, with null for a miss or a point off the canvas. All points read the scene as it is at the call's turn in the pick
queue. Pass a `view` as the second argument to pick through it; with several views and no `view`, points outside the first
point's view are picked one at a time.

```ts
import {Picking} from 'margoengine/selection';
const picking = Picking.attach(engine);
const hits = await picking.pickMany([[10, 20], [64, 64], [120, 40]]);
const meshes = hits.map((hit) => hit?.mesh ?? null);
```

## Lines in picks

`LinePicking.attach(picking, lines)` from `margoengine/lines/pick` makes fat lines answer `engine.pick`, `picking.pick` and `pickMany`, in one depth test with the meshes, with `hit.line` and `hit.segment` set. See the [lines README](../lines/README.md#gpu-picking).

`picking.addOverlay(overlay)` is the hook it uses: an overlay draws into the 3 x 3 pick tile after every mesh, with IDs from `firstId`, and `pickHit(index)` turns an ID back into a hit. Up to 8 overlays; each owns 2^28 IDs. While one is registered, picks use the 3 x 3 pass rather than the cached ID texture.

## Marquee, lasso, hover and face/edge/vertex picking

`SelectionTool` drags a rubber band (or, with `shape: 'lasso'`, a free-form outline) over the canvas: Shift + drag replaces
the selection, Shift + Ctrl adds, Shift + Alt removes. It stops a matching press from reaching later listeners, so create it
before the camera controls. `HoverHighlight` outlines the mesh under the mouse with its own `Selection`. `selectInRect` and
`selectInPolygon` are the same tests as plain functions, and `pickElement` returns the face, nearest vertex and nearest edge
under a pixel. Both selection modes test each mesh's projected bounding sphere: `mode: 'center'` (default), `'overlap'` (a
crossing window) or `'contain'` (a window).

```ts
import {Picking, Selection, SelectionTool, HoverHighlight, pickElement} from 'margoengine/selection';
import type {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/selection.md]

=== @margoengine/audio (packages/audio/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/audio

Import `margoengine/audio` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/audio` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Web Audio listener, global and positional sounds, encoded-file loading and a frequency analyser for Margo Engine.

Build from source with `npm run build` in `packages/audio`.

```ts
import {AudioListener, Audio, PositionalAudio, AudioVoicePool, AudioAnalyser} from 'margoengine/audio';

const listener = AudioListener.attach(engine, {volume: 0.8}); // follows engine.camera every frame; resumes on the first click or key press

const engineSound = new PositionalAudio(listener, {
  mesh: truck, refDistance: 2, distanceModel: 'inverse', rolloffFactor: 1.2,
  coneInnerAngle: 90, coneOuterAngle: 220, coneOuterGain: 0.3, muteWhenHidden: true,
});
engineSound.setBuffer(await listener.load('/sounds/engine.ogg'));
engineSound.loop = true;
engineSound.fadeIn(0.5);

const music = new Audio(listener, {volume: 0.4});
music.setMediaElementSource(document.querySelector('audio')).play();

// A sound on an editor timeline: starts at timeline second 4, follows play, pause, scrubbing and timeline speed.
const cue = new Audio(listener, {volume: 0.6, loop: false, timelineStart: 4});
cue.setBuffer(await listener.load('/sounds/cue.ogg'));
engine.onFrame(() => cue.sync(timeline.seconds, timeline.playing, timeline.speed));

// Footsteps and block sounds: 6 voices share one buffer; a 7th overlapping play steals the oldest voice.
const steps = new AudioVoicePool(listener, await listener.load('/sounds/step.ogg'), {voices: 6, refDistance: 2});
steps.play([x, y, z], {volume: 0.7, playbackRate: 0.9 + Math.random() * 0.2});

const analyser = new AudioAnalyser(music, 1024);
engine.onFrame(() => meter.style.width = `${analyser.getAverageFrequency() / 2.55}%`);

// On teardown (engine.dispose() does this too):
engine.removePlugin(listener.name);
```

## Cancel a load, and clean up with `using`

```ts
import {AudioListener, Audio} from 'margoengine/audio';

using listener = new AudioListener({volume: 0.8}); // disposed at the end of the block
const buffer = await listener.load('/sounds/step.ogg', {signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)}); // rejects with an AbortError
using step = new Audio(listener).setBuffer(buffer);
step.play();
```

Errors carry a stable `code` (`error.code`): `disposed` for a sound used after `dispose()`, `state` for `play()` before a source is set, `unsupported` when Web Audio or `fetch` is missing, `failed` for an HTTP or decoding failure. Each message says what to do.

## How it works

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/audio.md]

=== @margoengine/mixer (packages/mixer/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/mixer

Import `margoengine/mixer` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/mixer` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Audio mixing and effects on Web Audio, as a sibling of `@margoengine/audio`: a tree of buses with fader, mute, solo, sends and ducking; an effects chain (equaliser, filter, compressor, limiter, delay, convolution reverb); positional emitters; and deterministic offline rendering so a chain can be rendered and its numbers compared in a test. Nothing touches `AudioContext` at import time, and the package adds nothing to core.

```ts
import { Mixer, renderOffline, measure } from 'margoengine/mixer';

// Live: mix before the listener, so the camera-following AudioListener from margoengine/audio stays the last stage.
//   using mixer = new Mixer(listener.context, {destination: listener.input, buses: {...}});
// Offline (runs in a browser; the same calls work on a live AudioContext):
const buffer = await renderOffline({ seconds: 2, sampleRate: 48000, mixer: { effects: [{ type: 'limiter', ceiling: -1 }] } }, ({ context, mixer }) => {
  mixer.createBus('music', { gain: -6, effects: [{ type: 'eq', bands: [{ type: 'lowshelf', frequency: 120, gain: 3 }] }] });
  mixer.createBus('voice');
  const reverb = mixer.createBus('room', { effects: [{ type: 'reverb', seconds: 1.5, mix: 1 }], soloSafe: true });
  mixer.bus('voice').send(reverb, { gain: -9 });

  const tone = new OscillatorNode(context, { frequency: 220 });
  mixer.route(tone, 'music');
  tone.start(0);
  tone.stop(2);

  // Lower the music by 12 dB from 0.5 s to 1.2 s for a line of dialogue.
  const duck = mixer.bus('music').duck({ amount: 12, attack: 0.05, at: 0.5 });
  duck.release({ at: 1.2, seconds: 0.3 });
});
const { peak, rms } = measure(buffer.getChannelData(0));
```

## Buses

`new Mixer(context, {destination, gain, effects, buses})` makes a `master` bus and any buses you list. `mixer.createBus(name, {parent, gain, muted, solo, soloSafe, effects})` adds one that feeds its parent (default master). Each bus is `input -> effects -> fader -> duck -> mute/solo gate -> output`.

- **Gain** in dB: `bus.setGain(-6, {at, seconds})`. Changes move smoothly (about 20 ms) unless the context has not started or `seconds` is 0, so there are no clicks and an offline render starts at the right level.
- **Mute and solo**: `bus.setMuted(true)`, `bus.setSolo(true)`. While anything is soloed, only soloed buses, their ancestors (which carry the sound on), their descendants (which feed them) and `soloSafe` buses such as reverb returns stay audible. `audibleBuses(states)` is that rule as a pure function.
- **Sends**: `bus.send(other, {gain, pre})` copies part of a bus to another (after the gate by default, so muting the bus mutes the send; `pre` taps before the fader). A send that would make a loop throws `RangeError`.
- **Ducking**: `bus.duck({amount, attack, at})` lowers a bus and returns a handle; `handle.release({at, seconds})` brings it back. Overlapping ducks hold the deepest one. You decide when to duck (when a voice starts); there is no automatic sidechain.
- **Routing**: `mixer.route(source, bus)` connects an AudioNode, or anything with `getOutput()` such as `Audio` and `PositionalAudio` from `margoengine/audio`, to a bus after removing its other connections. Configure the sound's filters first.
- **Scheduling** uses AudioContext time: every `at` is `context.currentTime` seconds (default now), and `mixer.now` reads the clock.
- `bus.peak()` reads the current output peak (it adds an AnalyserNode on first use).

## Effects

Effects are plain objects, so a chain can be stored as JSON: `bus.setEffects([...])`, or `createEffect(context, spec)` for one effect.

| `type` | Settings (defaults) | Built from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `eq` | `bands: [{type: 'peaking', frequency, q, gain}]`, 1 to 16 bands | one BiquadFilterNode per band |
| `filter` | `filter`, `frequency`, `q`, `gain` | BiquadFilterNode |
| `compressor` | `threshold` -24, `knee` 30, `ratio` 4, `attack` 0.003, `release` 0.25 | DynamicsCompressorNode |
| `limiter` | `ceiling` -1 dB, `release` 0.05 | DynamicsCompressorNode, ratio 20, knee 0 |
| `delay` | `time` 0.3 s (at least 128 samples), `feedback` 0.35 (at most 0.95), `mix` 0.3 | DelayNode with a feedback loop; echo k lands exactly at k times `time` |
| `reverb` | `seconds` 2, `decay` seconds/2, `preDelay` 0, `mix` 0.25, `seed` 1, or a recorded `impulse` | ConvolverNode, `normalize = false` |

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/mixer.md]

=== @margoengine/physics (packages/physics/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/physics

Import `margoengine/physics` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/physics` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).
