Rigid-body physics for Margo Engine on [Rapier](https://rapier.rs): a fixed-step engine plugin with interpolation, colliders (compound and convex-decomposed ones included), joints (rope and spring included), ropes and chains, ray-cast vehicles, scene queries, collision events and a character controller.

Build from source with `npm run build` in `packages/physics`.

It exports `Physics` (the world: bodies, colliders, joints, queries and events), `PhysicsBody`, `PhysicsJoint`, `CharacterController`, `Vehicle` and `Rope`. The React components in `@margoengine/react/physics` are `<Physics>`, `<RigidBody>`, the collider components (`CuboidCollider`, `BallCollider` and others), `useJoint`, `usePhysics`, `useBeforePhysicsStep` and `useAfterPhysicsStep`. Rapier is not bundled: you install `@dimforge/rapier3d-compat` (Apache-2.0) yourself and pass the initialized module in.

```ts
import RAPIER from '@dimforge/rapier3d-compat';
import {Engine, PbrMaterial, box} from 'margoengine/core';
import {Physics, collisionGroups} from 'margoengine/physics';

await RAPIER.init();
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);
const physics = new Physics(engine, {rapier: RAPIER}); // registers itself with engine.use()

const floor = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box(20, 1, 20)).setPosition([0, -0.5, 0]);
physics.addBody(floor, {type: 'fixed'});                 // box collider fitted to the geometry

const crate = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box()).setMaterial(new PbrMaterial({color: '#c08040'})).setPosition([0, 5, 0]);
const body = physics.addBody(crate, {colliders: {shape: 'box', restitution: 0.3, density: 2}});
body.applyImpulse([0, 2, 0]);

// Hinge with limits and a motor.
const frameBody = physics.addBody(null, {type: 'fixed', position: [2, 1, 0], colliders: []});
const doorMesh = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box(1, 2, 0.1)).setPosition([2.5, 1, 0]);
const door = physics.addBody(doorMesh, {colliders: {shape: 'box', halfExtents: [0.5, 1, 0.05]}});
physics.addJoint(frameBody, door, {type: 'revolute', anchorB: [-0.5, 0, 0], axis: [0, 1, 0], limits: [0, Math.PI / 2], motor: {targetVelocity: 1}});

// Queries return the core Mesh that was hit.
const hit = physics.raycast(engine.camera.position, [0, -1, 0]);
hit?.mesh; hit?.distance; hit?.point; hit?.normal;

// Events with the meshes involved.
physics.on('contactstart', ({meshA, meshB}) => {});
physics.on('intersectionstart', ({bodyA, bodyB}) => {}); // sensors

// Character controller on a kinematic capsule, driven once per fixed step.
const input = {x: 0, z: 1}; // from your keyboard or gamepad handling
const playerMesh = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box(0.6, 1.6, 0.6)).setPosition([-2, 1, 0]);
const player = physics.addBody(playerMesh, {type: 'kinematicPosition', colliders: {shape: 'capsule', halfHeight: 0.5, radius: 0.3}});
const controller = physics.createCharacterController(player, {maxSlopeClimbAngle: Math.PI / 4, autostep: {maxHeight: 0.3, minWidth: 0.2}, snapToGround: 0.2});
physics.on('beforestep', dt => controller.move([input.x * 4 * dt, -9.81 * dt, input.z * 4 * dt]));

engine.start(); // each frame's delta drives the accumulator
// On teardown: physics.dispose(), engine.removePlugin('physics') or engine.dispose().
```

## Ropes, vehicles and compound shapes

```ts
import RAPIER from '@dimforge/rapier3d-compat';
import {Engine, box} from 'margoengine/core';
import {Physics, Rope, Vehicle} from 'margoengine/physics';

await RAPIER.init();
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const physics = new Physics(engine, {rapier: RAPIER});
physics.addBody(null, {type: 'fixed', position: [0, -0.5, 0], colliders: {shape: 'box', halfExtents: [50, 0.5, 50]}});

// A rope hung from a fixed hook, carrying a crate. rope.points() is the polyline for @margoengine/lines.
const crate = physics.addBody(null, {position: [0, 3, 0], colliders: {shape: 'box', halfExtents: [0.3, 0.3, 0.3]}});
const rope = new Rope(physics, {start: [0, 6, 0], end: [0, 3.3, 0], segments: 10, attachStart: 'fixed', attachEnd: crate});
const polyline = rope.points();

// Rope and spring joints between two bodies.
const hook = physics.addBody(null, {type: 'fixed', position: [3, 5, 0], colliders: []});
const bob = physics.addBody(null, {position: [3, 4, 0], colliders: {shape: 'sphere', radius: 0.2, mass: 2}});
physics.addJoint(hook, bob, {type: 'spring', restLength: 1, stiffness: 50, damping: 5}); // or {type: 'rope', length: 1.5}
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/physics.md]

=== @margoengine/physics2d (packages/physics2d/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/physics2d

Import `margoengine/physics2d` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/physics2d` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

2D rigid-body physics for Margo Engine on [Rapier](https://rapier.rs): a fixed-step engine plugin with interpolation, bodies that drive sprites, box, circle, capsule and polygon colliders, joints, scene queries, collision events, a character controller and tile map colliders in one call. Rapier is not bundled: you install `@dimforge/rapier2d-compat` (Apache-2.0) yourself and pass the initialized module in.

World units are sprite pixels, y points down and angles are radians, clockwise on screen. `pixelsPerMeter` (default 32) maps them to Rapier's metres, so a 16 pixel tile is half a metre. Mass, density, force and impulse use Rapier's units.

```ts
import RAPIER from '@dimforge/rapier2d-compat';
import {Physics2D} from 'margoengine/physics2d';

await RAPIER.init();
const physics = new Physics2D(null, {rapier: RAPIER}); // or new Physics2D(engine, ...) to step with the engine

// A tile map: tiles with collision shapes (or a `solid: true` property) become one fixed body.
physics.addTileMap({
  tileWidth: 16, tileHeight: 16,
  tilesets: [{firstGid: 1, tileCount: 1, tileWidth: 16, tileHeight: 16, tiles: [{id: 0, properties: {solid: true}}]}],
  layers: [{type: 'tile', name: 'ground', width: 8, height: 4, data: new Uint32Array(32).fill(1, 24)}],
});

// A body that drives a sprite: each frame the interpolated pose is written to sprite.x, sprite.y and sprite.rotation.
const sprite = {x: 64, y: 0, rotation: 0};
const crate = physics.addBody(sprite, {colliders: {shape: 'box', width: 16, height: 16, restitution: 0.2}});
physics.on('contactstart', ({bodyA, bodyB}) => {});
physics.update(1 / 60); // or let the engine call it every frame
crate.applyImpulse([0, -2]);
physics.raycast([64, 0], [0, 1])?.point;

// A hinge with limits, and a character on a kinematic body.
const pole = physics.addBody(null, {type: 'fixed', position: [32, 8], colliders: []});
physics.addJoint(pole, crate, {type: 'revolute', anchorB: [-8, 0], limits: [-1, 1]});
const hero = physics.addBody({x: 20, y: 40, rotation: 0}, {type: 'kinematicPosition', colliders: {shape: 'capsule', radius: 5, height: 20}});
const controller = physics.createCharacterController(hero, {snapToGround: 2});
physics.on('beforestep', dt => controller.move([60 * dt, 200 * dt]));
```

It exports `Physics2D`, `Body2D`, `Joint2D`, `CharacterController2D`, `interactionGroups` and `tileMapColliders`, the collider list `addTileMap` builds. `addTileMap` accepts a `TileMapData` from `@margoengine/tilemap`, or any object of the `TileMapSource` shape. Whole-cell solid tiles merge into outline loops so bodies slide across tile seams without catching; other collision shapes (rectangles, ellipses, polygons, polylines), tile flips and layer offsets are kept. Very fast bodies on a tile map need `ccd: true`, because outlines have no thickness.

Queries (`raycast`, `overlapPoint`, `overlapShape`, `castShape`) see every collider added or moved since the last step: they bring Rapier's broad phase up to date with a zero-length step first, which moves nothing and raises no events.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^1.0.0, Rapier peer optional.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/physics2d

=== @margoengine/ragdoll (packages/ragdoll/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/ragdoll

Import `margoengine/ragdoll` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/ragdoll` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Ragdolls for animated characters, on `@margoengine/physics` (Rapier). Give it the hips of a skeleton and it builds one
capsule body per bone, joined at the bone origins with swing and twist limits. While the character is animated the
bodies follow the bones as kinematic hit boxes that push the world; `activate()` makes it limp, keeping the momentum the
animation gave each bone; `deactivate(seconds)` blends the bones back to the animation. Core and physics stay the same
size: an app that does not import this package ships none of it.

```ts
import RAPIER from '@dimforge/rapier3d-compat';
import { EngineKernel } from 'margoengine/core';
import { loadGLTF } from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';
import { Animation } from 'margoengine/animation';
import { Animator } from 'margoengine/animator';
import { Physics } from 'margoengine/physics';
import { Ragdoll } from 'margoengine/ragdoll';

await RAPIER.init();
const engine = await EngineKernel.create(document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('#viewport')!);
const physics = new Physics(engine, { rapier: RAPIER });
physics.addBody(null, { type: 'fixed', colliders: { shape: 'box', halfExtents: [20, 0.1, 20] } });
const model = await loadGLTF(engine, '/hero.glb'); // a skinned character with a Run clip
Animator.attach(Animation.attach(model), { initial: 'run', states: { run: 'Run' } });

// After the Animator, so it runs after the animation each frame.
const hips = model.nodes.find((node) => node.name === 'Hips')!;
const ragdoll = Ragdoll.attach(physics, { root: hips });

// A hit: go limp and push the bone that was struck.
const head = ragdoll.bones.find((part) => part.node.name === 'Head');
ragdoll.activate();
head?.body.applyImpulse([0, 2, -30]);

// Two seconds later, get up: hand the bones back to the animation over half a second.
setTimeout(() => ragdoll.deactivate(0.5), 2000);
engine.start();
```

## What it builds

`Ragdoll.attach(physics, {root})` walks every node under `root`. A node with children becomes a bone; its capsule runs
from the node's origin toward its children's centre (the farthest child when that centre is at the origin). End nodes
and bones shorter than `minLength` (fingers, toes) are left out with their children and keep their animation. The
radius is `thickness` times the length, or half the distance the children sit off the bone's line when that is more,
so a pelvis between the legs and a chest between the arms come out round. Mass is the capsule volume times `density`.
The pose at construction is the rest pose the joint limits measure from: build it in a T or A pose, or the first frame
of a clip.

Each body's frame is its bone's world frame, so a body's origin is its joint with the parent bone, and the bone's world
pose is the body's pose. `ragdoll.bones` lists the parts, parents first; `bones[0]` is the root. Each part has its
`node`, `body` (a `PhysicsBody`; apply impulses to it), `joint` (null on the root), `parent` index, `length` and
`radius`. Every body's `userData` is `{ragdoll, node}`, so a raycast hit tells you which bone was struck.

For full control, list the bones yourself instead of `root`: each is a node or `{node, joint, length, radius, mass}`.
One bone is the root, and every other bone's parent node must be in the list.

```ts
const node = (name: string) => model.nodes.find((n) => n.name === name)!;
const custom = Ragdoll.attach(physics, {
  bones: [
    node('Hips'),
    { node: node('Spine'), joint: { type: 'cone', swing: 0.4, twist: [-0.3, 0.3] } },
    { node: node('Head'), length: 0.25, radius: 0.1 },
    node('LeftUpLeg'),
    { node: node('LeftLeg'), joint: { type: 'hinge', axis: [1, 0, 0], limits: [0, 2.4] } },
  ],
});
```

## Joints

| Joint | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `{type: 'cone', swing, twist}` | A ball joint. The bone stays inside a cone of half angle `swing` radians around its rest direction and twists about its own axis between `twist[0]` and `twist[1]` radians. Shoulders, hips, spine, neck. Defaults `swing` π/4, `twist` [-π/6, π/6]. |
| `{type: 'hinge', axis, limits}` | One axis of rotation, `axis` in the bone's local frame, turning between `limits` radians from the rest pose. Knees, elbows. Default `limits` [-3π/4, 0]. Uses Rapier's revolute joint with both frames aligned at rest (Rapier 0.21 or later). |
| `{type: 'free'}` | A ball joint with no limits. |

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/ragdoll.md]

=== @margoengine/navmesh (packages/navmesh/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/navmesh

Import `margoengine/navmesh` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/navmesh` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Dependency-free navigation: A* chooses a polygon corridor, the funnel algorithm pulls it taut, reciprocal ORCA selects collision-avoiding agent velocities in XZ, a `Crowd` manager walks agents along routes with area costs, off-mesh links and obstacles, and `@margoengine/navmesh/build` generates the walkable polygons from level triangles.

```ts
import {NavMesh} from 'margoengine/navmesh';
const mesh = new NavMesh([[0,0,0], [10,0,0], [0,0,10]], [[0,1,2]]);
const path = mesh.path([1,0,1], [2,0,2]);
```

Polygons must be strictly convex, planar and nonvertical. Neighbor polygons share vertex-index edges; welded coordinates with different indices do not link. Outside or disconnected endpoints return null. Paths use supplied endpoint heights and portal vertex heights. The bounded open set uses a binary heap (4096 polygons maximum). Shared-edge portals are oriented from the source polygon, independently of polygon winding or center-to-center alignment. Agent radii are handled by avoid(), not by corridor inset: build an already-eroded walkable mesh (the generator below does). ORCA expects current velocities and preferred velocities for all reciprocal agents, uses seconds, and bounds output by maxSpeed; when no velocity avoids every neighbor it returns the one that breaks the constraints least. Static-wall constraints are not generated here; a neighbour with `reciprocal: false` (an obstacle, a player) leaves all of the avoidance to the agent.

## Crowds, area costs, off-mesh links and obstacles

```ts
import {Crowd, NavMesh} from 'margoengine/navmesh';

// Two 4 x 4 m rooms with a 1 m gap between them (x 4 to 5).
const nav = new NavMesh(
  [[0,0,0], [4,0,0], [4,0,4], [0,0,4], [5,0,0], [9,0,0], [9,0,4], [5,0,4]],
  [[0,1,2,3], [4,5,6,7]],
);
nav.addOffMeshLink([3.8,0,2], [5.2,0,2]); // a jump across the gap, both ways
nav.setAreaCost(nav.locate([7,0,2]), 3); // the second room is mud: routes avoid it when they can

const crowd = new Crowd(nav, {neighborDistance: 5, maxNeighbors: 10, timeHorizon: 2});
const guard = crowd.addAgent({position: [1,0,1], radius: 0.4, maxSpeed: 3.5});
const visitor = crowd.addAgent({position: [8,0,3], radius: 0.4});
guard.setTarget([8,0,1]);
visitor.setTarget([1,0,3]);
const removeCrate = crowd.addObstacle({position: [2,0,2], radius: 0.5}); // agents steer around it
crowd.on('arrive', (agent) => console.log('arrived', agent.id));
let last = performance.now();
const frame = (now: number) => {
  crowd.update(Math.min(0.1, (now - last) / 1000));
  last = now;
  // guard.position, guard.velocity and guard.state ('moving', 'offmesh', 'arrived', ...) drive your character.
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
};
requestAnimationFrame(frame);
console.log(nav.route([1,0,1], [8,0,1])?.offMesh, removeCrate);
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/navmesh.md]

=== @margoengine/ecs (packages/ecs/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/ecs

Import `margoengine/ecs` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/ecs` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

A sparse-set ECS with packed Float32, Float64, Int32, Uint32 and Uint8 component fields.

```ts
import {World} from 'margoengine/ecs';
const world = new World(1024);
const position = world.component({x: Float32Array, y: Float32Array});
const entity = world.create();
position.add(entity, {x: 10});
const results = new Uint32Array(world.capacity);
const count = world.query([position], results);
```

Numeric entity IDs include a generation, so destroyed/reused slots reject stale handles. Removal swaps the last dense row into the removed row: call component.index(entity) before using a row index. Queries write into caller-owned storage and reject undersized output. Integer writes reject truncation and overflow. A `World` has a fixed capacity; a `GrowableWorld` grows. This is a sparse-set implementation, not a second archetype storage engine.

## Growable worlds

`GrowableWorld` (from `margoengine/ecs/growable`) doubles its slots when `create` runs out, so you do not have to guess a capacity. Everything else works as in a `World`.

```ts
import {GrowableWorld} from 'margoengine/ecs/growable';
const world = new GrowableWorld({capacity: 1024});
const position = world.component({x: Float32Array});
const {x} = position.fields;
const results = world.allocate(Uint32Array); // keeps up with the capacity
for (let i = 0; i < 5000; i++) position.add(world.create(), {x: i});
console.log(world.capacity, x.length); // 8192 8192
console.log(world.query([position], results)); // 5000
```

| `new GrowableWorld` option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `capacity` | `1024` | Slots at the start |
| `limit` | `1000000` | Most slots it may grow to, at most 1,000,000; past it `create` throws `RangeError` |

Growing moves nothing: arrays sit on resizable buffers, so `component.fields`, arrays taken from them and ids all stay valid, and arrays only get longer. A `Uint32Array` you made yourself stays its size, so make query outputs with `world.allocate(Uint32Array)`. Ids are spaced by `limit`, and an id must fit 32 bits, so a slot retires after about 4,294,967,295 / `limit` reuses (4,294 at the default) and the world grows past it; lower `limit` for a world that churns entities hard. Resizable arrays cost speed: a loop over 100,000 rows took about twice as long as on a plain `World` (0.25 to 0.31 ms against 0.12 to 0.15, Node 26, busy machine, [ecs-growable.mjs](../../examples/package-benchmarks/ecs-growable.mjs)). When a bound is known, use a `World`.

## Query filters and tags

`world.query` intersects components. `Query` (from `margoengine/ecs`, or `margoengine/ecs/query` alone) adds `without` and `optional` terms, and `world.tag()` makes a component with no fields.

```ts
import {Query, World} from 'margoengine/ecs';
const world = new World(1024);
const position = world.component({x: Float32Array});
const health = world.component({value: Float32Array});
const frozen = world.tag();
const entity = world.create();
position.add(entity, {x: 1});
const stuck = world.create();
position.add(stuck, {x: 2});
frozen.add(stuck);
const moving = new Query(world, {with: [position], without: [frozen], optional: [health]});
moving.forEach((id, rows) => {
  position.fields.x[rows[0]] += 1;
  if (rows[1] >= 0) health.fields.value[rows[1]] -= 1; // -1: this entity has no health
});
const results = new Uint32Array(world.capacity);
console.log(moving.run(results), frozen.has(stuck)); // 1 true
```

| `new Query` term | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `with` | required | An entity must have all of these; at least one |
| `without` | none | An entity must have none of these |
| `optional` | none | Never changes the match; `forEach` gives its row, or -1 |

`run(output)` writes the ids into your array. `forEach(visit)` passes the `with` rows, then the `optional` rows, in one reused `Int32Array`. It takes the match list first and looks rows up just before each call, so `visit` can add, remove and destroy; entities that stop matching are passed over, and new matches wait for the next call. A `Query` cannot run inside its own `forEach`; use a second one to nest. Tags store no field data, only the 8 bytes per world slot every component uses for its entity index.

## Systems and scheduler

`Schedule` (from `margoengine/ecs`, or `margoengine/ecs/schedule` alone) runs named systems in a dependable order. Each `update(delta)` runs the fixed phase, then the frame phase. A `fixed: true` system runs once per step the elapsed time pays for, so physics stays deterministic at any frame rate. Everything else runs once per update.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/ecs.md]

=== @margoengine/fsm (packages/fsm/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/fsm

Import `margoengine/fsm` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/fsm` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Hierarchical states preserve common ancestors during transitions, bubble events from leaf to root, and expose previous/state/blend for cross-fades.

```ts
import {StateMachine} from 'margoengine/fsm';
const machine = new StateMachine({game: {}, idle: {parent: 'game'}, run: {parent: 'game'}}, 'idle', {}, [
  {from: 'idle', to: 'run', event: 'move', duration: 0.2}
]);
machine.send('move');
machine.update(1 / 60);
```

State hooks receive context; update hooks also receive delta seconds. Guards can decline an event transition. Hierarchy cycles and unknown states are rejected. goto changes state directly. Recursive transitions from enter/exit hooks are rejected. Cross-fade progress is a timer for the caller's animation mixer; this package does not own animations.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/fsm

=== @margoengine/behavior (packages/behavior/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/behavior

Import `margoengine/behavior` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/behavior` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Game AI for agents: behaviour trees with a typed blackboard and async tasks, utility-AI scoring, and steering and
flocking behaviours. No rendering, no globals, nothing runs on import; it works the same in the browser, a worker or
Node. For states with cross-fades use `@margoengine/fsm`; for walking on a navigation mesh with ORCA avoidance use
`@margoengine/navmesh`'s `Crowd`. Both work with this package (below).

## Behaviour trees

```ts
import { BehaviorTree, action, blackboardKey, condition, cooldown, reactiveSelector, sequence, wait } from 'margoengine/behavior';

const enemyNear = blackboardKey('enemyNear', false);
const tree = new BehaviorTree(
  reactiveSelector(
    sequence(condition('enemyNear'), cooldown(1, action('attack'))),
    sequence(action('walkToNextPoint'), wait(2)),
  ),
  {
    seed: 42,
    handlers: {
      conditions: { enemyNear: (tick) => tick.blackboard.get(enemyNear) },
      actions: {
        attack: () => 'success',
        // An async action is a task: it runs over several ticks, and its signal aborts when the branch is halted.
        walkToNextPoint: async (tick) => {
          await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 500));
          return !tick.signal.aborted;
        },
      },
    },
  },
);
tree.blackboard.set(enemyNear, true);
const status = tree.tick(1 / 60); // 'success' | 'failure' | 'running'
```

Call `tick(delta)` once per frame or fixed step. Each tick walks the tree from the root, depth first; after the root
finishes, the next tick starts it again. Nodes:

| Node | Builder | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sequence | `sequence(...)`, `reactiveSequence(...)` | children in order until one fails |
| selector | `selector(...)`, `reactiveSelector(...)` | children in order until one succeeds |
| random selector | `randomSelector(children, weights?)` | a selector whose order is drawn from the seeded stream (by weight) each time it starts |
| parallel | `parallel(children, {success, failure})` | ticks every child; `'all'`, `'any'` or a count (defaults `success: 'all'`, `failure: 'any'`) |
| utility | `utility([{score, child}], {inertia, threshold})` | utility-AI selector: runs the best-scoring option each tick (ties go to the first) |
| inverter | `inverter(child)` | flips success and failure |
| repeater | `repeater(child, {count, until})` | runs the child again, one run per tick, `count` times (default forever) or until it returns `until` |
| cooldown | `cooldown(seconds, child)` | after the child finishes, fails without running it for `seconds` |
| guard | `guard(condition, child)` | checks a condition every tick and runs the child only while it holds |
| timeout | `timeout(seconds, child)` | fails, halting the child, when it runs longer than `seconds` |
| condition | `condition(name)` | a named condition handler: true is success |
| action | `action(name)` | a named action handler, sync or async |
| wait | `wait(seconds)` | running for `seconds`, then success |

Plain sequences and selectors have memory: they resume at the child that was running. Reactive ones re-check the
earlier children every tick and halt the running one when an earlier child decides (the usual "abort lower priority").
Halting a node aborts the `signal` of every action under it, so `fetch`, timers and loaders stop with the branch.

Handlers receive a `tick` with `blackboard`, `context` (the `context` option: your agent, entity id or world),
`delta`, `time`, `random` and `signal`. Actions return `'success'`, `'failure'`, `'running'`, a boolean, nothing
(success) or a promise of one of these. A rejected promise is not swallowed: the next `tick` throws `MargoError`
`'failed'` with the error as its `cause`; return `'failure'` for an expected failure.

Deterministic: time is the sum of the deltas you pass (durations count from the tick a node starts on), and all
randomness comes from one mulberry32 stream seeded by `seed` (default 0). The same description, seed, handlers and
deltas give the same statuses and the same trace on every run and every machine. Promise-based actions settle when
their work settles, so a replay that must match exactly should resolve them from your own simulation.

### Saving, loading and validating trees

Every node is plain JSON (leaves name their handlers), so a tree is saved with `JSON.stringify` and loaded with
`parseTree`:

```ts
import { BehaviorTree, action, parseTree, sequence, treeDocument, validateTree, wait } from 'margoengine/behavior';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/behavior.md]

=== @margoengine/save (packages/save/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/save

Import `margoengine/save` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/save` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Save games, scene files and prefabs: a versioned JSON document of entities with stable ids, components and
references; prefab definitions with instances, overrides and nesting; a tested migration registry for schema
changes; validation that names every problem and its fix; loading into your world that is all or nothing; optional
gzip; and storage adapters for memory, localStorage, IndexedDB and files behind one promise-based interface with
AbortSignal.

```ts
import { Migrations, loadGame, memoryStorage, saveGame, type SaveDocument } from 'margoengine/save';

const level: SaveDocument = {
  format: 'margo-save',
  version: 2,
  meta: { title: 'Chapter 1', playTime: 754 },
  prefabs: {
    door: {
      entities: [
        { id: 'frame', components: { mesh: 'door.glb', locked: false } },
        { id: 'handle', parent: 'frame', components: { opens: { $ref: 'frame' } } },
      ],
    },
  },
  entities: [
    { id: 'player', transform: { position: [0, 0, 0] }, components: { health: { hp: 80, max: 100 }, target: { $ref: 'gate' } } },
    { id: 'gate', prefab: 'door', transform: { position: [0, 0, -8] }, components: { locked: true } },
  ],
};

const storage = memoryStorage(); // or webStorage(), indexedDBStorage(), fileStorage('./saves') from margoengine/save/node
await saveGame(storage, 'slot-1', level); // validated, gzipped where CompressionStream exists, written in one step

const migrations = new Migrations(2).register(1, (old) => ({ ...old, version: 2 }));
const loaded = await loadGame(storage, 'slot-1', { migrations }); // decoded, migrated, validated; null when empty
```

## The document

`{format: 'margo-save', version, entities, prefabs?, meta?}`. `version` is your schema version. Each entity has a
stable `id`, and optionally a `name`, a `parent` (an id), a local `transform` (`position`, unit-quaternion
`rotation`, `scale`) and `components`: any JSON by component name. A reference to another entity is
`{"$ref": "id"}` anywhere inside a component; references, parents and prefab overrides all use ids, so a save
survives reordering and stays diffable.

## Prefabs

A prefab is a list of entities with ids local to it; its `root` (default the first) becomes the instance. An entity
with `prefab: 'door'` expands to the prefab's entities: the root merged into the instance (the instance's own
components, name, transform and parent win), and the others as `gate/handle`, `gate/...`, with their parents and
local references re-pointed at the copies. `overrides` change the copies by prefab-local id as JSON Merge Patches
(RFC 7386: objects merge, other values replace, `null` removes a key); `null` for a whole entity removes it and its
children. Prefabs may contain instances of other prefabs (ids like `cart/load/lid`), without cycles, up to 32
deep.

```ts
import { expandSave, parseSave } from 'margoengine/save';

const flat = expandSave(parseSave({
  format: 'margo-save',
  version: 1,
  prefabs: { crate: { entities: [{ id: 'box', components: { mass: 2 } }, { id: 'lid', parent: 'box', components: {} }] } },
  entities: [{ id: 'c1', prefab: 'crate', overrides: { lid: { components: { colour: 'red' } } } }],
}));
// [{ id: 'c1', components: { mass: 2 }, ... }, { id: 'c1/lid', parent: 'c1', components: { colour: 'red' }, ... }]
```

## Loading into a world, all or nothing

```ts
import { loadWorld, type WorldAdapter } from 'margoengine/save';

const scene = new Map<string, { id: string; components: Record<string, unknown> }>();
const adapter: WorldAdapter<{ id: string; components: Record<string, unknown> }> = {
  create: (entity) => ({ id: entity.id, components: entity.components }), // build off-screen
  commit: (handles) => {
    scene.clear();
    for (const [id, object] of handles) scene.set(id, object); // swap the new world in
  },
  destroy: () => {}, // undo one create
};
loadWorld({ format: 'margo-save', version: 1, entities: [{ id: 'a' }, { id: 'b', parent: 'a' }] }, adapter);
```

`loadWorld(document, adapter, {migrations, components, signal})` validates, migrates and expands everything before
building anything, then calls `create` for every entity (parents first), `link` for every entity once all exist
(with `resolve(id)` for references) and `commit` once. If any step throws or the signal aborts, it calls `destroy` for
everything built, latest first, and throws `MargoError` `'failed'` with the cause: a bad file never leaves a
half-loaded world.

For an `@margoengine/ecs` World, `saveEcs(world, components)` writes the entities that hold the named components and
`ecsAdapter(world, components)` loads them back; a value that does not fit a field (a fraction in an `Int32Array`
field) undoes the whole load.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/save.md]

=== @margoengine/net (packages/net/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/net

Import `margoengine/net` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/net` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Bounded snapshot interpolation for position, quaternion and velocity, with capped dead reckoning.

```ts
import {SnapshotBuffer, createSnapshot} from 'margoengine/net';
const buffer = new SnapshotBuffer(32);
const output = createSnapshot();
// buffer.push(timeSeconds, position, quaternion, velocity)
buffer.sample(renderTimeSeconds, output);
```

Position interpolation is cubic Hermite using endpoint velocities; rotations use shortest-arc slerp. Ordered snapshots are copied into a preallocated ring, quaternions normalized, and duplicate/out-of-order timestamps return false. Extrapolation uses last velocity up to maxPrediction (default 0.25 seconds), then holds. Before the oldest sample, the oldest pose is held. Outputs are reused by default; supply your own to retain results. This is interpolation/prediction, not transport, authority, rollback or packet security.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/net

=== @margoengine/netcode (packages/netcode/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/netcode

Import `margoengine/netcode` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/netcode` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Game networking for any game, not only voxels: one schema describes your state and inputs, an authoritative server
runs the game at a fixed tick rate, and clients predict their own player, reconcile with the server and draw everyone
else interpolated. It runs in browsers, Node, Deno and workers (no platform APIs), it is optional and tree-shakable,
and core and the stage never import it. Clean-room code from public descriptions of the techniques (see "Sources").

```ts
import { defineGame, defineSchema, GameClient, GameServer, LoopbackNetwork } from '@margoengine/netcode';

// One schema for both ends. Quantized floats are small on the wire; maps are entity collections sent as deltas.
const schema = defineSchema({
  types: {
    Input: { x: { type: 'quantized', min: -1, max: 1, bits: 8 }, y: { type: 'quantized', min: -1, max: 1, bits: 8 } },
    Box: { x: 'f32', y: 'f32' },
    State: { boxes: { type: 'map', of: 'Box', maxSize: 64 } },
  },
} as const);

// One deterministic step for both ends: the server runs it authoritatively, clients run it to predict.
const game = defineGame({
  schema,
  state: 'State',
  input: 'Input',
  tickRate: 30,
  initial: () => ({ boxes: new Map() }),
  join: (state, id) => void state.boxes.set(id, { x: 0, y: 0 }),
  leave: (state, id) => void state.boxes.delete(id),
  step(state, inputs, _tick, dt) {
    for (const [id, input] of inputs) {
      const box = state.boxes.get(id);
      if (box) (box.x += input.x * 5 * dt), (box.y += input.y * 5 * dt);
    }
  },
});

// A simulated network: 60 ms each way, 20 ms of jitter, 5% loss. Swap in a real transport for a real game.
const network = new LoopbackNetwork({ latency: 60, jitter: 20, loss: 0.05, seed: 1 });
const now = () => network.time;
const server = new GameServer(game, { now });
network.listen().onconnection = (connection) => server.accept(connection);

const joining = GameClient.join(game, network.connect(), { now, input: () => ({ x: 1, y: 0 }) });
let client: Awaited<typeof joining> | undefined;
joining.then((joined) => (client = joined));
for (let frame = 0; frame < 300; frame++) {
  network.advance(1000 / 60); // one frame of virtual time
  if (network.time >= (server.tick + 1) * game.tickMs) server.step();
  client?.update();
  await null; // let the join promise settle
}
console.log('me', client?.predicted.boxes.get(client.player), 'server', server.state.boxes.get(client?.player ?? 0));
```

In a real game the server calls `server.run({ signal })` (real-time ticks) and the client calls `client.update()` every
frame; the loop above drives both by hand so the example runs anywhere, at once, the same way every time.

## What it does

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/netcode.md]

=== @margoengine/voxel-net (packages/voxel-net/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/voxel-net

Import `margoengine/voxel-net` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/voxel-net` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Multiplayer for `@margoengine/voxel` worlds: an authoritative Node server, a client that runs in browsers and Node,
and headless bots for load tests. Clean-room code with no third-party runtime package: the WebSocket server (RFC 6455)
is written here on `node:http` and `node:crypto`. Optional and tree-shakable; core and the stage never import it.
Design and decisions: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md). Measured capacity: [bench/results.json](bench/results.json) and
`docs/voxel-net-capacity-2026-10-21.md`.

```ts
// Server (Node)
import { VoxelServer } from 'margoengine/voxel-net/server';
const server = new VoxelServer({ blocks, generator: { seed: 7 }, flight: true });
await server.listen(8787, '0.0.0.0');

// Client (browser): the world fills from the server; lighting and the renderer follow world.onChunk as usual.
import { connectVoxelNet, Keys } from 'margoengine/voxel-net';
const client = connectVoxelNet('ws://127.0.0.1:8787', world, { name: 'Ada', view: 6 });
engine.onFrame((_, dt) => {
  client.update(dt, { keys: Keys.forward | Keys.jump, yaw, pitch }); // moves client.player at 1/120 s steps
  const [x, y, z] = client.renderPosition; // the camera follows this
  for (const other of client.samplePlayers().values()) drawBox(other.snapshot.position, other.snapshot.rotation);
});
client.edit(x, y, z, 0); // shown at once; the server confirms it or sends the cell back
```

## How it works

- **Server** (`./server`): one `VoxelWorld` holds the chunks within the *simulation distance* (default 3 chunks across,
  2 up and down) of some player: physics runs and edits are accepted there. Chunks a client can only see (its *view*,
  default 6 chunks across and 3 up and down; a client may ask for 2 to 8) are sent from a cache of finished messages
  (default 256 MiB). Worker threads run the generator (`noiseTerrain` options, or your own `VoxelGenerate` module) and
  `encodeChunk` in one job. A chunk whose generation fails goes to `server.onError` and is tried again after 250 ms,
  then 500 ms; after 3 failures the players who need it are closed with 1011 and a reason naming the chunk. Edited
  chunks stay in memory, up to `maxEditedChunks`; past it they go to your `store` (see below).
- **Tick**, 20 per second: each player's queued movement steps and edits in the order they came, then each client's
  view, then one corked write per client: corrections, block changes in chunks it has, nearby players (within 96
  blocks, `EntityCodec` deltas against the last message), and up to 64 chunks or 128 KiB, nearest first.
- **Movement**: the client runs `VoxelCharacter` at fixed 1/120 s steps with quantized inputs (`Keys` bits, a 16-bit
  yaw) and sends them every 6 steps with the position it reached. The server runs the same steps; when it disagrees by
  more than 1/64 block it sends a correction, which the client applies and replays its later steps on. A client can
  only spend steps it has had time for (120 per second, 0.5 s of slack).
- **Edits**: shown at once on the client; the server checks rate (10 per second, bursts of 5), reach (6 blocks from the
  eye plus 1 of slack), that a placed block replaces air, liquid or a plant and overlaps no player, and that a break hits
  a block, then sends the change to every client holding that chunk. A refused edit sends the cell back.
- **Other players**: `client.samplePlayers()` interpolates each one from a `@margoengine/net` `SnapshotBuffer`, 100 ms
  behind the newest snapshot. `other.name` holds its display name (see below).
- **Wire format** (`.`): one type byte and a varint body per WebSocket message. `encodeClientMessage`,
  `decodeClientMessage`, `encodeServerMessage` and `decodeServerMessage` check every length; chunks, block changes
  and players carry the `@margoengine/voxel/codec` bytes. Chunks go out without light (clients light them).
- **Bots** (`./bot`): `VoxelBot.connect({url, blocks})` joins with the same client, walks, jumps, swims and edits;
  it decodes only the chunks within one chunk of itself.
- **File store** (`./file-store`, Node): `new FileChunkStore(dir)` is a `ChunkStore` with one deflated file per chunk; pass
  it as the server's `store` and edits survive a restart.

## Connections, login and saved edits

Every limit has a safe default; set them on `new VoxelServer({...})`.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/voxel-net.md]

=== @margoengine/bvh (packages/bvh/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/bvh

Import `margoengine/bvh` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/bvh` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Triangle bounding volume hierarchy (`MeshBVH`, `shapecast`, `intersectsGeometry`), spatial queries and a CPU `Raycaster` for Margo Engine.

Build from source with `npm run build` in `packages/bvh`.

All-hit and nearest traversal share a conservative node-slab test. Exact parallel axes use finite spatial slack;
an infinite ray range cannot disable node rejection through infinity/NaN arithmetic. Tiny nonzero axes whose
reciprocal overflows retain division-based interval calculation rather than being treated as parallel. Hits still
use the exact triangle predicate, with full layered-hit results available for transparent picking. This changes
query correctness and traversal cost without changing mesh data, public signatures or the serialized BVH format.

```ts
import {Engine, box} from 'margoengine/core';
import {MeshBVH, Raycaster, buildAsync, computeGeometryBVHAsync} from 'margoengine/bvh';

// Engine picking: canvas CSS pixels in, sorted hits out.
const raycaster = new Raycaster();
canvas.addEventListener('pointerdown', event => {
  raycaster.setFromEngine(engine, event.offsetX, event.offsetY);
  const [hit] = raycaster.intersectEngine(engine); // {mesh, distance, point, normal, faceNormal, faceIndex, barycoord, frontFace}
});

// A loaded gltf-pro PBRModel uses its current GPU skin/morph pose.
// This explicit asynchronous query reads back only deformed vertices.
const [animatedHit] = await raycaster.intersectModel(model);

// Keep big builds off the main thread; the Raycaster then uses the cached BVH.
await computeGeometryBVHAsync(bigGeometry);

// Direct queries on raw data or a Geometry.
const bvh = MeshBVH.build({positions, indices});           // or MeshBVH.fromGeometry(geometry)
bvh.raycastFirst({origin: [0, 5, 0], direction: [0, -1, 0]}, {side: 'front'});
bvh.intersectsSegment([0, 0, 0], [0, 5, 0], {includeFace: face => face !== receiverFace});
bvh.closestPointToPoint([1, 2, 3], {maxDistance: 0.5});
bvh.intersectsSphere([0, 0, 0], 0.25);
bvh.intersectsBox({min: [-1, -1, -1], max: [1, 1, 1]}, boxMatrix);
bvh.intersectsBVH(otherBVH, otherToThisMatrix, (faceA, faceB) => {});
bvh.collectFrustum(frustumPlanes(viewProjectionTimesWorld)); // face indices

// Worker build with zero-copy results, then store or ship the tree.
const tree = await buildAsync({positions, indices}, {transfer: true});
const bytes = tree.toArrayBuffer();            // one buffer, 16-byte header
const again = MeshBVH.fromArrayBuffer(bytes, {positions});
```

PBR models and materials meshes honor live `side: 'front' | 'back' | 'double'` in ordinary engine raycasts and
deformed snapshot queries, including mirrored nodes. Ordinary engine raycasts also test each instance;
the asynchronous pose snapshot retains its existing non-instanced primitive transform. `raycaster.side`
can still override material sides.

## Segments and face filters

`intersectsSegment(start, end, {side, includeFace})` says whether a triangle crosses the segment between two
points, ignoring contact within a relative 1e-7 of either end, so a shadow test can stop exactly at a light that sits
on a surface. `includeFace` receives the source face index (also accepted by `raycastFirst` and `raycast`) and
returning false skips that face, for example the receiver's own triangles.

Restored trees (`deserialize`, `fromArrayBuffer`, the `MeshBVH` constructor) are checked to be one packed tree, so
corrupt node links throw instead of looping.

## How it works

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/bvh.md]

=== @margoengine/geometry (packages/geometry/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/geometry

Import `margoengine/geometry` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/geometry` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

`wireframePositions(data, offsetY = 0)` expands distinct triangle edges into a
contiguous line-position stream with an optional vertical lift for terrain debug views.

`pbrVertexStream(data, occlusion?)` packs the 80-byte PBR vertex layout used by
`ScatterInstances`, retaining normals, tangents and both UV slots. RGB defaults to
white tint; alpha stores baked ambient occlusion, independently of albedo and
opacity. Tangents must be present; occlusion callbacks must return finite 0..1.
`footprintRadius(data)` measures the maximum local XZ distance from the origin.

Pure-CPU, tree-shakable geometry for Margo Engine: primitives, curves, shapes, extrusion, triangulation and mesh utilities.

Build from source with `npm run build` in `packages/geometry`.

```ts
import {Engine, PbrMaterial} from 'margoengine/core';
import {CatmullRomCurve3, Path, Shape, computeTangents, extrudeGeometry, sphereGeometry, toGeometry, tubeGeometry} from 'margoengine/geometry';

// Radius, width segments, height segments.
const sphere = computeTangents(sphereGeometry(1, 48, 24));
engine.createMesh().setGeometry(toGeometry(sphere)).setMaterial(new PbrMaterial({color: '#f97316'}));

// A rounded plate with a hole and a beveled edge.
const plate = new Shape([[-2, -1], [2, -1], [2, 1], [-2, 1]]);
const hole = new Path(); hole.absarc(0, 0, 0.5, 0, Math.PI * 2, true);
plate.holes.push(hole);
const solid = extrudeGeometry(plate, {depth: 0.4, bevelThickness: 0.1, bevelSize: 0.05, bevelSegments: 3});

// A tube along a centripetal Catmull-Rom spline.
const path = new CatmullRomCurve3([[0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 0], [3, 1, 1], [4, 4, 2]]);
const tube = tubeGeometry(path, 128, 0.1, 12);
```

Every function returns a plain `GeometryData` (`positions`, `normals`, `uvs`, `indices`, optional `tangents` and `groups`) made of typed arrays. `toGeometry(data)` hands positions, normals and indices to core's `Geometry`; core has no UV or tangent slots, so those stay on `GeometryData` for packages that use them.

## What it includes

| Functions |
| --- |
| `boxGeometry`, `planeGeometry`, `circleGeometry`, `ringGeometry` |

=== @margoengine/mesh-edit (packages/mesh-edit/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/mesh-edit

Import `margoengine/mesh-edit` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/mesh-edit` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional, tree-shakable CPU polygon editing, UV allocation and pixel painting for Margo. Input meshes retain indexed positions, caller face IDs and independent normalized top-left UVs at every polygon corner. Commands return owned geometry and explicit old-to-new component provenance; caller document metadata is excluded.

```ts
import { createPrimitiveMesh, extrudeMeshFace, compilePolygonMesh } from 'margoengine/mesh-edit';
const mesh = createPrimitiveMesh('cube', 'box');
const edit = extrudeMeshFace(mesh, 'box-face-0', 0.25);
const geometry = compilePolygonMesh(edit.mesh);
```

Inset a face (default `amount` 0.24, a centroid fraction from 0.001 to 0.95), then bevel the whole closed mesh (default `amount` 0.12, from 0.001 to 0.45):

```ts
import { createPrimitiveMesh, insetMeshFace, bevelPolygonMesh } from 'margoengine/mesh-edit';
const cube = createPrimitiveMesh('cube', 'box');
const inset = insetMeshFace(cube, 'box-face-0', 0.3);
const beveled = bevelPolygonMesh(cube, 0.1);
console.log(inset.mesh.faces.length, beveled.mesh.faces.length);
```

Callers own selection intent, locks, visibility, motion/opacity policy, IDs, undo and texture storage. Margo owns component transform geometry and the UV/paint algorithms below. No engine instance, DOM or GPU is needed. Supply `createId` for deterministic face IDs; otherwise commands call `crypto.randomUUID()` only when creating faces. Empty and duplicate generated IDs reject before exposing output.

The original parity commands retain existing behavior: extrusion acts along the local face normal, inset and whole-mesh bevel use centroid fractions, and `cutMeshFace` bisects one face at opposite-edge midpoints. Cut vertices propagate through neighboring incident edges; each face interpolates its own UVs. Bevel requires closed two-manifold geometry and returns an unchanged owned mesh with a diagnostic for unsupported open/nonmanifold inputs. Supported faces are simple planar convex polygons with 3-64 corners; collinear boundary corners remain valid. Compile produces flat normals and fan triangles, preserving source face and corner-vertex identity. Drawn knife cuts, selected-edge bevels and concave n-gons (split into convex faces) are in the `modeling` entry below; equal-width inset is `insetMeshRegion`.

`meshSelectionVertices(mesh, selection)` resolves explicit object, vertex, canonical edge or face selections. `transformMeshComponents(mesh, selection, worldDelta, {worldMatrix, snapStep})` applies a public affine world delta to those shared vertices once. Unselected positions and all corner UVs remain exact; optional snapping affects only selected vertices in world space. Warped convex polygons become persisted deterministic source triangles, retaining the source face ID on one descendant. Collapsed, crossed, concave or folded projections reject atomically. Mirrored object matrices and half-turn rotations work; reflected edit deltas reject explicitly. Results add exact `edgeMap`, created/removed edges and triangulation diagnostics. Geometry-only shaping never repacks or paints an atlas.

`traceMeshQuadRing(mesh, {faceId, corner})` traverses opposite edges of connected quads with transported edge orientation. `cutMeshQuadRing(mesh, seed, fraction)` accepts `0 < fraction < 1`, splits each geometric edge once, independently interpolates each incident face's UVs and returns the new ring's ordered vertices and edges. Open strips end at geometric boundaries. Nonquad continuation, nonmanifold or inconsistent winding and ambiguous/self-crossing paths reject. This API performs a coherent adjustable ring split; callers own preview, confirm/cancel and selection remapping.

`vertexMap[oldIndex]` lists output descendants, including retained identities where present. `faceMap[oldId]` lists retained and descendant faces. Created vertices are new identities even when they are mapped descendants; removed vertices name discarded input indices, including welded duplicates that still map to a retained output vertex. Bevel replaces all vertex identities and maps each old vertex to its incident face corners. UV seams never weld merely because positions coincide.

Tests import the built public package. Run `npm test --workspace @margoengine/mesh-edit` from the engine repository.

## Modeling: edge bevel, loop slide, dissolve, weld and bridge

Bevel selected edges, cut a loop and slide it, dissolve, merge by distance and bridge two open loops, from the
`margoengine/mesh-edit/modeling` entry (`@margoengine/mesh-edit/modeling`), so apps that only paint or move components
never load it. Edge IDs are `"low:high"` vertex pairs (see `polygonMeshEdges`):

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/mesh-edit.md]

=== @margoengine/compute (packages/compute/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/compute

Import `margoengine/compute` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/compute` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

GPU compute without the WebGPU boilerplate, for data science and for engine work. It feels like NumPy: N-dimensional
typed arrays with views and broadcasting, element-wise expressions that fuse into a single kernel, reductions and
statistics along axes, scans, sorting, selection and histograms. It also runs your own WGSL kernels, with bindings
read from the source. Optional entries add matrix products (`/linalg`), Fourier transforms (`/fft`), convolution
(`/signal`), reproducible random numbers (`/random`), sparse matrices and solvers (`/sparse`), gradients
(`/autodiff`), data larger than GPU memory (`/stream`), kernels inside an engine's frame (`/frame`), subgroup
kernels for reductions, scans and sorts (`/subgroups`), neural networks (`/nn`), graph algorithms (`/graph`) and workgroup sizes measured per adapter (`/autotune`).

The package is optional and tree-shakable, adds nothing to core, and needs no engine: without one it opens a
headless device of its own. Without WebGPU (Node, an older browser, a blocklisted GPU) the same code runs on the CPU.


```ts
import { createCompute } from '@margoengine/compute';

using gpu = await createCompute(); // disposed (arrays and device freed) at the end of the block
const x = gpu.array(new Float32Array([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]));
const sorted = await gpu.sort(x).read(); // Float32Array [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9]
const mean = await x.mean().item(); // 3.875
const z = x.sub(x.mean()).div(x.std()); // one fused kernel; nothing runs until it is read
console.log(sorted, mean, await z.read());
```

## Arrays

`gpu.array(data, { dtype, shape })` uploads a TypedArray or a plain array. The dtype comes from the TypedArray:
floats give `f32` (Float64Array is converted), signed integers give `i32`, unsigned integers give `u32`, and
Float16Array gives `f16` on GPUs with `shader-f16` (check `gpu.f16`). Plain arrays default to `f32`. The second
argument may be just the dtype. Creation helpers: `zeros`, `ones`, `full`, `arange`, `linspace`, `eye`.

`read()` resolves the elements in C order (`{ offset, length, signal }` reads part of them), and `item()` resolves the
one value of a single-element array. Disposing an array frees its GPU memory; disposing the context frees every array
it made.

```ts
import { createCompute } from '@margoengine/compute';

using gpu = await createCompute();
const m = gpu.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], { shape: [2, 3] });
const counts = gpu.zeros(10, 'u32');
const steps = gpu.arange(0, 1, 0.25); // f32 [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
console.log(m.shape, counts.size, await steps.read());
```

Views cost no copy: `reshape(2, -1)`, `transpose()` or `.T`, `slice(...)` (an index, `[start, stop, step]` with
negative steps, or `null` for a whole dimension), `expandDims`, `squeeze` and `broadcastTo`. A view reads through
its strides, inside the same fused kernel.

```ts
import { createCompute } from '@margoengine/compute';

using gpu = await createCompute();
const m = gpu.array(Float32Array.from({ length: 12 }, (_, k) => k), { shape: [3, 4] });
console.log(await m.T.read()); // the transpose, read in its own C order
console.log(await m.slice(null, [1, 3]).read()); // columns 1 and 2: [1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10]
console.log(await m.slice([null, null, -1]).read()); // the rows reversed
```

## Fused expressions

Element-wise methods return lazy `Expr`essions, which follow NumPy's broadcasting and type promotion. Nothing runs
until you `read()` or `eval()` the expression or hand it to a reduction, and then the whole tree compiles into one
kernel, so no intermediate array is ever written. Constants travel in a uniform, so changing one does not recompile.

The element-wise methods:

- **Arithmetic:** `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div` (true division; integers give f32), `floorDiv`, `mod` (NumPy sign
  rules), `pow`, `minimum`, `maximum`, `clip`, `abs`, `neg`, `sign`, `square`.
- **Maths:** `sqrt`, `rsqrt`, `reciprocal`, `exp`, `exp2`, `expm1`, `log`, `log2`, `log1p`, the trigonometric and
  hyperbolic functions, `atan2`, `hypot`, `degrees`, `radians`.
- **Rounding:** `floor`, `ceil`, `round` (ties to even), `trunc`.
- **Comparison and logic** (all give u32 0/1): `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`, `eq`, `ne`, `and`, `or`, `xor`, `not`,
  `isnan`, `isinf`, `isfinite`.
- **Integer bits:** `bitAnd`, `bitOr`, `bitXor`, `bitNot`, `shiftLeft`, `shiftRight`, `popcount`.
- **Conversion:** `astype(dtype)`, `bitcast(dtype)`.

`gpu.where(cond, a, b)` selects element-wise. `gpu.map(x, 'WGSL expression')` covers anything the methods do not.

```ts
import { createCompute } from '@margoengine/compute';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/compute.md]

=== @margoengine/sciviz (packages/sciviz/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/sciviz

Import `margoengine/sciviz` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/sciviz` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Scientific visualisation for Margo Engine, WebGPU:

- **Volume rendering:** transfer functions, gradient lighting, clip planes, slices, and isosurfaces extracted by
  marching cubes on the GPU.
- **Scatter plots:** millions of points with level of detail.
- **Surface and line plots:** with axes, nice-number ticks, labels and colour bars.
- **Colour maps:** perceptual maps computed from their published definitions.

Layers read `@margoengine/compute` GPU arrays in place, so data computed on the GPU is drawn without a trip to the
CPU. The package is optional and tree-shakable, and adds nothing to core. The points, lines, labels, controls and
compute packages load with `import()` only when a figure uses them.

```ts
import { Figure } from '@margoengine/sciviz';

const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
const fig = await Figure.create(canvas); // engine, camera, orbit controls and dark theme, running
const n = 100_000;
const x = Float32Array.from({ length: n }, () => Math.random() * 10);
const y = Float32Array.from({ length: n }, () => Math.random() * 10);
const z = x.map((v, i) => Math.sin(v) * Math.cos(y[i]));
await fig.scatter({ x, y, z, color: z }, { colormap: 'coolwarm' });
fig.colorbar('coolwarm', [-1, 1], { label: 'sin x cos y' });
```

## Figures

`Figure.create(canvas, options)` sets up everything with zero configuration:

- a WebGPU engine on the canvas;
- the theme's background;
- a camera framing the plot box;
- orbit controls (drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, right-drag to pan).

`Figure.attach(engine)` adds a figure to an engine you already have. Axes and tick labels load and draw in the
background; `await fig.ready()` waits for them and rejects if they failed. A figure maps data units into a box, with data
z pointing up. The box spans the union of its layers' bounds, or fixed `limits`. Axes draw the box outline, grid
lines at the ticks and HTML tick labels.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `'3d'` | `'3d'` box you orbit, or `'2d'` chart (see 2D charts) |
| `margin` | see 2D charts | space around a 2D chart's plot area, in CSS px |
| `theme` | `'dark'` | `'dark'` or `'light'` chrome and background |
| `axes` | `true` | box, grid and tick labels |
| `titles` | `{ x: 'x', y: 'y', z: 'z' }` | axis titles |
| `ticks` | `5` | about how many ticks per axis |
| `grid` | `true` | grid lines on the floor and back walls |
| `aspect` | `[1, 1, 0.75]` | relative size of the plot box |
| `limits` | data bounds | fixed `[xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax]` (`[xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax]` in 2D) |
| `pointBudget` | `2_000_000` | most scatter points drawn per frame |
| `scale` | linear | `{ x, y, z }`: `'linear'`, `'log'` or `'date'` per axis |
| `legend` | shown for 2+ named layers | `false`, `true`, or a corner such as `'top-left'` |
| `tooltips` | `true` | hover tooltips; `false`, or `(hit) => string \| null` for your own text |
| `controls` (create only) | `true` | orbit controls (3D) |

## Layers

| Call | Draws |
| --- | --- |
| `await fig.scatter({ x, y, z?, color?, size? }, { colormap, range, size, edl, shape })` | point cloud with level of detail; `color` values go through the colour map |
| `await fig.line({ x, y, z?, color? }, { width, colormap })` | fat line with round joins |
| `fig.surface(z, { nx, ny, x, y, colormap, range, contours, grid, opacity })` | height field coloured by height, contour lines, NaN holes |
| `fig.volume(data, { dims, bounds, colormap, range, opacity, density, mode, quality, shading, clip })` | ray-marched volume; `mode: 'mip'` for maximum intensity |
| `volume.slice('x' \| 'y' \| 'z', position)` | a plane through the volume, coloured by its map |
| `brickedVolume(fig, source, options)` from `/bricks` | a volume larger than one texture or the memory budget, loaded by view ([below](#bricked-volumes)) |
| `await fig.isosurface(data, level, { dims, bounds, color })` | GPU marching cubes; `layer.update(level)` re-extracts |
| `fig.colorbar(colormap, range, { label, ticks })` | HTML colour bar at the canvas edge |

Data may be TypedArrays, plain arrays, or `GpuArray`s from `@margoengine/compute`. Make GPU arrays on the
figure's engine with `createCompute({ engine: fig.engine })`. A surface, volume or isosurface reads a GPU array on
the GPU; give such layers a `range`, since their min and max are not read back for you.

```ts
import { Figure } from '@margoengine/sciviz';
import { createCompute } from '@margoengine/compute';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/sciviz.md]

=== @margoengine/mcp (packages/mcp/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/mcp

A [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server for Margo Engine. It lets AI coding tools (Claude
Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Copilot, any MCP client) read Margo correctly and check the code they write for it.
It runs on your machine over stdio, has no dependencies, and is separate from core (core grows by zero bytes).

```sh
npm i -D @margoengine/mcp typescript
```

The server serves a snapshot of the READMEs, API reports, docs and example list from the version you installed, so
the answers match your code, not the latest page on the web. The same material is at
[margoengine.com/llms.txt](https://margoengine.com/llms.txt) and
[llms-full.txt](https://margoengine.com/llms-full.txt) for tools that read a URL instead.

## Tools

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `search_docs` | Ranked full-text search over READMEs, API declarations, docs and examples. Takes a task ("orbit camera") or an exact name (`createStage`). Filters: `kind`, `package`, `limit`. |
| `list_packages` | Every package with its layer and a one-line description. Core is frozen; features live in optional packages, so this is how a model finds the right one. |
| `get_package` | One package's README, its API report (every export with its declaration, per entry point) or both. Accepts `sciviz`, `@margoengine/sciviz` or `margoengine/sciviz`. |
| `list_examples` | The runnable example pages and starter projects, with what each shows. |
| `check_snippet` | Type-checks TypeScript, TSX or JavaScript against the real package types in your project, strict, with your own `typescript`. The snippet is compiled, never run. Returns line, column, code and message for each problem. |

Rendering a scene to a PNG is not a tool. The repository's browser harness needs Playwright, a Vite dev server and a
real GPU behind the shared GPU lock, none of which a published package can bring along, and a scene needs a bundler
step before any browser can load it. Use the visual checks in the repository (`npm run visual:check`) for pictures.

## Set up

Every client starts the same command. `--root` names the project whose `node_modules` has `typescript` and the
`@margoengine` packages; `check_snippet` type-checks against those. It defaults to the folder the client starts the
server in.

### Claude Code

```sh
claude mcp add margoengine -- npx -y @margoengine/mcp
```

Or share it with the team in `.mcp.json` at the project root:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "margoengine": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@margoengine/mcp"] }
  }
}
```

### Claude Desktop

Open Settings, Developer, Edit Config, and add the server to `claude_desktop_config.json`. Claude Desktop does not
start servers in your project, so name it with `--root`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "margoengine": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@margoengine/mcp", "--root", "/path/to/your/project"]
    }
  }
}
```

On Windows, write the path with forward slashes or doubled backslashes. Restart Claude Desktop.

### Cursor

Add the same block to `.cursor/mcp.json` in the project (or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project), then enable
`margoengine` under Settings, MCP:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "margoengine": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@margoengine/mcp"] }
  }
}
```

### Copilot and other clients

Any client that starts a stdio server works: command `npx`, arguments `-y @margoengine/mcp`. In VS Code, put the
block in `.vscode/mcp.json` under the key `servers` instead of `mcpServers`.

## Use it from code

The server is a plain function from messages to responses, so you can embed it or test against it.

```ts
import { createMargoServer, serveStdio } from '@margoengine/mcp';

const server = await createMargoServer({ projectRoot: '.' });
await serveStdio(server); // reads JSON-RPC lines from stdin, writes responses to stdout
```

```ts
import { createMcpServer, createTools, loadCorpus } from '@margoengine/mcp';

const server = createMcpServer({ tools: createTools({ corpus: await loadCorpus() }) });
const answer = await server.handle({
  jsonrpc: '2.0',
  id: 1,
  method: 'tools/call',
  params: { name: 'search_docs', arguments: { query: 'orbit camera', limit: 3 } },
});
console.log(answer);
server.dispose();
```

Options and defaults:

| Option | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `createMargoServer({ corpus })` | the corpus the package ships | Documentation to serve. |
| `createMargoServer({ projectRoot })` | the current directory | Where `check_snippet` finds `typescript` and the Margo packages. |
| `serveStdio(server, { input, output, signal })` | `process.stdin`, `process.stdout`, none | Streams to use; abort the signal to stop. |
| `checkSnippet(code, { language, strict, timeoutMs, signal })` | `ts`, `true`, 60000, none | The type check on its own. |

## Errors

=== @margoengine/react (packages/react/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/react

React 18 and 19 components and hooks for Margo Engine: a native canvas, pointer events, Suspense, stable mesh refs and
frame callbacks. There is no custom reconciler: `<Canvas>` creates one engine, and its children are ordinary React
components that edit it.

Import it as `margoengine/react` (from the `margoengine` package, every binding in one import) or from this package
alone: `@margoengine/react` holds the bindings that need no optional package (`Canvas`, `Mesh`, geometry, materials,
hooks, views, `Sun`, `Center`), and a binding that needs `@margoengine/<name>` comes from `@margoengine/react/<name>`
(`OrbitControls` from `/controls` with `@margoengine/controls` installed, `Gltf` from `/gltf-pro`, `Shadows` from
`/shadows`; the full list is in [SCENE.md](SCENE.md)). Optional parts load only when a component needs them, so an
unused feature costs nothing.

Installed alone (plus the packages your subpaths name, such as `@margoengine/controls` for `OrbitControls`), it builds
with Vite, webpack, Turbopack (Next.js), Rollup and esbuild and keeps the build to what you import. The cube page with orbit controls requests 94,251 B gzip at load
and 101,202 B once `OrbitControls` mounts, and emits no Wasm. React and React DOM are about 66% of that; Margo's part
(core, stage, bindings) is 25,949 B gzip. The breakdown is in [limits.md](../../docs/limits.md#react-page).


**What you get from this page:** a React app with a lit mesh in about five minutes, then the components, hooks,
controls, physics, XR and Next.js notes, the rule for React state against the frame loop, and a troubleshooting list.
For a textured, shadowed scene with click-to-select, follow the [React first scene guide](../../docs/guides/react-first-scene.md).

Contents: [Install](#install), [First scene](#first-scene), [Components](#components), [Models and environment](#models-and-environment),
[Batching, views, lights and voxels](#batching-views-lights-and-voxels), [Hooks](#hooks), [Controls](#controls),
[Physics](#physics), [XR](#xr), [Next.js](#nextjs), [State vs the frame loop](#state-vs-the-frame-loop),
[Build warnings](#build-warnings), [Testing and size](#testing-and-size), [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

## Install

Package name: `@margoengine/react`, version `1.0.0`. **It is not on npm yet**, so `npm install @margoengine/react` does
not work today. Two routes do. Both start from a clone of the repository (see [Install](../../README.md#install) in the
main README for Git LFS and Node.js: 22.12+ to use the package, 24.18+ to build it from the repository).

**Route 1: a Vite app of your own, from local tarballs.** In the clone:

```sh
npm ci
npm run pack:packages
```

`pack:packages` builds every package and writes one `.tgz` file each to `test-results/`. Then, in a new folder next to
the clone (shown for a shell that expands `*.tgz`, such as Git Bash, macOS or Linux):

```sh
mkdir my-react-app && cd my-react-app
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install ../margoengine/test-results/*.tgz react react-dom vite @vitejs/plugin-react typescript @types/react @types/react-dom
```

On the machine that wrote this page, packing took about a minute and the install 8 seconds. Add an `index.html` with
`<div id="root"></div>` and `<script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx"></script>`, put the first scene below in
`src/main.tsx` (add the `createRoot` line at the end), and run `npx vite`.

**Route 2: use the examples inside the clone.** `npm ci`, `npm run build:packages`, then
`npm run dev --workspace @margoengine/react-viewer` for the resizable Vite example.

**TypeScript with this package alone.** The types check under a strict `tsconfig.json` (`"skipLibCheck": false`)
without the optional peers; options typed by a peer you have not installed are `any` until you install it.

**After 1.0.0 is published**, `npm install margoengine react react-dom` replaces the tarballs and nothing else changes.
[SCENE.md](SCENE.md) lists the optional peers each component uses.

## First scene

A box lit by the default sun, with a click handler:

```tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { Canvas, Stage, Mesh, BoxGeometry, PbrMaterial, Model } from 'margoengine/react';

export function App() {
  return (
    <Canvas style={{ height: 400 }}>
      <Stage camera={{ position: [0, 2, 5] }}>
        <Mesh position={[0, 1, 0]} onClick={() => {}}>
          <BoxGeometry args={[1, 1, 1]} />
          <PbrMaterial color="#84d6bd" />
        </Mesh>
        <Suspense fallback={null}>
          <Model src="/model.glb" />
        </Suspense>
      </Stage>
    </Canvas>
  );
}

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(<App />);
```

The `Model` line needs a `.glb` file at `public/model.glb`; delete it for a scene with only the box.

=== Examples (examples/README.md) ===

# Margo Engine examples

## Example pages

- `examples/boulder.html`: A robot climbs a wall: IK that keeps its arms clear of the wall and itself
- `examples/animation-formats.html`: Collada skins and glTF animation pointers
- `examples/batched-mesh.html`: Many shapes drawn in one call
- `examples/character-animation.html`: A walking robot with blendable expressions
- `examples/clipping-planes.html`: Section planes on every material
- `examples/depth-texture.html`: A depth texture that any material can sample
- `examples/flight-helmet.html`: The Khronos Flight Helmet with PBR materials
- `examples/khronos-gallery.html`: Khronos glTF sample assets
- `examples/gallery/index.html`: The Harrow Head gallery: live pages by feature ([direction](gallery/DIRECTION.md))
- `examples/kinematics-constraints.html`: Arm clearance check with the kinematics package
- `examples/minimap.html`: A second camera view as a minimap
- `examples/robot-expressive.html`: The same character study as a standalone page
- `examples/scene-targets.html`: Several render targets with named outputs
- `examples/split-screen.html`: Two players, two views, render layers
- `examples/texture-formats.html`: TGA, TIFF, KTX and DDS textures
- `examples/tokyo-diorama.html`: A street corner animated in Blender and played back by the animation package
- `examples/weather.html`: Weather presets that blend: rain, snow, hail, lightning, wind and wet or snowy ground
- `examples/windy-meadow.html`: Grass, wind and a changing sky
- `examples/molten-words/index.html`: Any typed word as dripping liquid chrome
- `examples/cathedral-light/index.html`: Sun through stained glass into a dusty hall, with a time-of-day slider
- `examples/biomes/index.html`: A 4 km landscape from a biome map: climate controls, a Koppen and layer map, biome painting and height and mask exports
- `examples/blender-loader/`: Loading a `.margo` file exported from Blender
- `examples/usdz-loader/`: Loading USDZ and USDA files
- `examples/webxr-orbit/`: A WebXR session around a simple scene

## Projects

- `examples/vite/`: Starter app with Vite and TypeScript
- `examples/react-viewer/`: A model viewer in React
- `examples/next/`: A Next.js app
- `examples/gameplay-sandbox/`: A small third-person game
- `examples/voxel-sandbox/`: A voxel world

## Scripts and workloads

- `examples/package-benchmarks/`: Workloads that measure individual packages
- `examples/assets/`: Models and textures used by the examples, with their credits

Run from a repository checkout: `npm run build:packages`, then `npm run dev:examples` (pages) or the command in each project table.
